<header>DE LA CITÉ JAMATHAY, ALIAS JANSU 361</header>

En ceste cité siet un des douze barons dou grant Kaan, car elle est esleue por un des douze sajes. Il sunt ydres. Lor monoie ont de carte et sunt au grant Chan, et meser Marc Pol meisme, celui de cui trate ceste livre, seingneurie ceste cité por trois anz. Il vivent de mercandies et d'ars, car il i se font arnois de chevaliers et d'omes d'armes en grandisime quantité : car je voz di tout voirmant que en ceste cité et environ por s'apartinence demorent maintes homes d'armes. Il ne a autre couse que à mentovoir face. Nos partiron de ci et vos conteron des deus grant provence que do Catai meisme sunt ; elle sunt ver Ponent, et por ce que il hi a bien couse da conter, voz en conteron de elles tous lor costumes et lor usance, et conteron de le une avant que est apellé Nanghin. » (Ed. Soc. Géog., p. 160.)

Mandeville qui suit Odoric, nous dit, qu'en quittant l'île des Pygmées :

« On entre dans le Roiaume de Janchan, qui contient 12. Provinces ; dans les quelles on divise tout l'Empire des Tartares : on nomme la Capitale de ce Roiaume Janchan : c'est une ville marchande très riche, & qui paie de grosses sommes à son Roi : car ils disent eux mêmes, qu'ils donnent cinquante mille Cumans en florins d'or. Il y a dans la ville de Janchan un convent de freres Mineurs, & trois Églises, dont le revenu est de 12. Cumans ; un Cuman est dix mille pieces ; & le tribut annuel cinquante fois cinquante mille pieces : car c'est là justement la somme, qui est contenue dans un Cuman : & cinq lieuës de cette ville il y en a une autre appelée Méke, où d'un bois blanchatre, l'on fait des vaisseaux qui ressemblent à des Palais, tant il y a de chambres. » (Bergeron, col. 17.)

« Qvand on a passé la riviere de Kiang, on rencontre une fort grande écluse prés du Chasteau de Quacheu, où commence un canal fait à la main, sur lequel on vient dans cette ville d'Yangcheu. <header>ODORIC</header>

(1) Yang-tcheou, 揚州, famous city of Kiang-sou, at 32° 26' 32" lat., and 117° 04' 13" long. obs. of the missionaries.

Under the Mongols, it was a "circuit capital" (Yang-tcheou loú) dependent on the great government of Hô-nân (the "south of the Hoang-hô"), and of Kiâng-pě (the "north of the Kiâng"). However, according to the official history of the Mongol dynasty (K. 59, fol. 19), in the beginnings of the thirteenth year of tchi-youan (end of 1275, beginning of 1276) it was established as a "capital of a particular government, reporting to Taï-tou (the Mongol capital: tchi taï toû toû fou). Furthermore, it was also established as the "administrative general government of Kiâng hoaï, and other places" (Kiang hoaï tèng tchoù hîng tchoûng tchoû sing). It was not until 1277 that it became the "Circuit" of Yang-tcheou with a general administration (Yoûng-tcheou loú thoung koùan foù). In 1278, they attached to it the "Directorate of general safety of the Circle of Hoaï toung" (of the Orient of Hoaï: Hoaï-toung tao siouen weï ssé). In 1282, this "provincial general safety directorate," with the general administration of this circuit itself, was attached to the province of Tchi-li." (Yuen sse, K. 59, fol. 19). Each year one sees a change made in its administrative organization, which we believe useless to report here. One counted there a population of 249,466 families and of 1,471,194 mouths, including women and children who had not yet reached virile age." (Pauthier, Marc Pol, pp. 466, 467).

Marco Polo was governor of this city for three years:

->*Here the account of the city of Yangui.*<-

> "When one leaves Tingui, he went towards Yseloc for one day through a very beautiful country where there are castles and villages enough, and then he finds a noble and great city which is called Yangui; and know that it is so great and so powerful that it well has under its lordship twenty-seven cities, great and good and of great merchandise."

(1) Yang-tcheou, 揚州, ville célèbre du Kiang-sou, par 32° 26' 32" lat., et 117° 04' 13" long. obs. des missionnaires.

Sous les Mongols ce fut un « chef-lieu de circuit » (Yang-tcheou loú) dépendant du grand gouvernement du Hô-nân (le « midi du Hoang-hô »), et du Kiâng-pě (le « nord du Kiâng »). Toutefois, selon l'histoire officielle de la dynastie mongole (K. 59, fol. 19), dans les commencements de la treizième année tchi-youan (fin de 1275, commencement de 1276) on l'établit « chef-lieu d'un gouvernement particulier, relevant de Taï-tou (la capitale mongole : tchi taï toû toû fou). De plus on l'établit aussi « gouvernement général administratif de Kiâng hoaï, et autres lieux « (Kiang hoaï tèng tchoù hîng tchoûng tchoù sing). Ce ne fut qu'en 1277, qu'il devint le « Circuit » de Yang-tcheou avec une administration générale (Yoûng-tcheou loú thoung koùan foù). En 1278, on y rattacha la « Direction de sûreté générale du Cercle de Hoaï toung » (de l'Orient du Hoaï : Hoaï-toung tao siouen weï ssé). En 1282, cette « Direction de sûreté générale provinciale », avec l'administration générale de ce propre circuit, fut rattachée à la province de Tchi-li. » (Yuen sse, K. 59, fol. 19). Chaque année on voit un changement opéré dans son organisation administrative, que nous croyons inutile de rapporter ici. On y comptait une population de 249,466 familles et de 1,471,194 bouches, comprenant les femmes et les enfants qui n'avaient pas encore atteint l'âge viril. » (Pauthier, Marc Pol, pp. 466, 467).

Marco Polo fut trois ans gouverneur de cette ville :

->*Ici devise de la cité de Yangui.*<-

> « Quant l'en se part de Tingui, il ala por Yseloc une journée por mout belle contrée là où il a chastiaus et casaus asez, et adonc treuve une noble cité et grant qe est appelés Yangui ; et sachiés q'ele est si grant et si poisant qe bien a sout sa seignorie vingt sept cités grant et boines et de grant mercandies.

## To the Most Polished Lord RESPONDENT.

Phoebus excites you, DIETSCHI, with swift impetus,
And a better spirit, stirring your breast with inspired
Divinity, sets you apart from the wandering
Crowd of the ancients.
The Cecropian <note>i.e., Athenian, referring to Plato</note> old man enjoys himself with charming
Pleasures: they think the highest rewards of glory
Have been granted to the highest summits of the good
For those who preside over the clamorous forum,
And ambiguous scepters. The leaders of the rigid portico
Seek the languid title of virtue and its form,
And those who examine your school, O good DIOGENES.
Lofty-voiced PLATO considers the forms with
Multi-turned care for the good: they praise the heaps of money
Which an wicked thirst for shining silver holds.
My DIETSCHI, the masculine force of your wit,
Illumined by a sacred ford, brings forth a higher judgment,
And proves the lively exercise of virtue
By a stable faith.
Rise up into the midst with vigor, stand as a man
In your ETHICAL contest, and, weakening the savage
Snares, loosen the sophisms twisted
With countless folds.
Thus the bright Father of the Castalian spring <note>i.e., Apollo</note>
Will confer an untiring mind upon the work of virtue,
And, with the pathless ways removed, will uncover the approach
To the face of the highest good.

<note>For the sake of fellowship, in congratulation.</note>
<note>Magister Johannes Eichhorn, Student of Medicine.</note>

The youth of excellent character had already progressed to the more mature flower of adolescence, and had obtained not only a stature of body but also a greater firmness of judgment with increasing age, wherefore he did not deflect from the path of virtues, in which he was happily proceeding; he did not hold the parent whom he had used as an instructor in low esteem, but followed him with the same honor and obedience as when a boy. Fortune displayed her luxury to him; luxury birthed insolence; insolence excluded honesty; he, laughing at this, reported it to be smoke. Wealth, honor, and glory solicited his eyes; he looked down on everything with a high brow. Venus laughed; he judged her instruments to be weeping; the abundance of gold and silver tested his soul; he shone like an unmoved star; he saw the prosperous and favorable winds of fortune of the Pharisees; he repressed his affections with prayers and fasts, and preferred to live in poverty than to possess many riches unjustly. O therefore you blessed youth, to whom no youth can be equal! O you fortunate one, who so liberated and vindicated your intellect from ignorance, your will from the innate lust for sinning, and your affections from inordinate disturbances. What more shall I say, A. H., when the magnitude of the matter demands silence? Where shall I stop the course of my navigation as this north wind rises? I come to his mature age, nor do I find words with which I might worthily express it; I say this one thing, that he was an exemplar of all virtues and good morals. Or we speak of other things, and not of dignities, and then males and females succeed with an equal scale (law "If," law 6, Book "Concerning passed over [heirs]"). From the aforesaid it is clear the Abbot concludes that in the right of primogeniture, males failing, the firstborn [female] succeeds, but this conclusion to me, with respect, does not seem true. I am moved by the authority of the gloss of the Archdeacon in the chapter "With most devout," 11th question, 3rd [part], where the gloss says that by law a female does not succeed in a kingdom. If custom be to the contrary, therefore [this is what] the doctors hold, mostly Vicentius in the said chapter "Signified." The Lord of San Gemini affirms the same, reporting Innocent [IV] to hold thus in the said chapter "Grand," "Concerning the supplementing of the negligence of prelates," chapter "Laymen," Book 6, and Albericus touches upon it in the proemium of the Digest.

Secondly, I am moved because public offices are interdicted to females because of [the requirement for] honesty (law "Female," Digest "Concerning rules of law"). But to be a queen, duchess, etc., with all royal jurisdiction is to have a public office (law 1, paragraph "Public law," Digest "Concerning justice and law"). Therefore a female does not succeed in a kingdom, nor a duchy. The said chapter "Signified" does not stand in the way, because I answer that there the sister succeeds the brother in a county not by reason of law but by the custom of Galicia properly, [this is what] the doctor [says] in the said chapter "Signified." The said chapter "Beloved" does not stand in the way, because that text proves the part [in favor of my position], for that text says there that public legal offices of jurisdiction are interdicted to females unless by approved custom [or] privilege as in the Gallican country. Lo! The text proves a female does not succeed by law in a kingdom. And in the same way, one responds to the text of the said chapter "With most devout," as the gloss says there. From the aforesaid, I infer a conclusion against Nicolaus, that whether males exist or not, the firstborn daughter does not succeed in a kingdom nor in the right of primogeniture unless the contrary is proved by privilege or custom. I ask whether the custom that the firstborn succeeds is valid. I answer [that] either we speak of a kingdom or principality, or of patrimony or inheritance. In the first case, all conclude the custom is valid, mostly Albericus in the proemium of the Digest and Baldus in the law "From this law," Digest "Concerning justice and law," and the reason is because the human race desires peace and quiet (law "Unique" and [it is] noted there on the principle, Digest "Concerning the abolishing of lapses," and it is noted in the chapter "Foundations," "Concerning election," Book 6). From the aforesaid, the conclusion is clear that even in inheritance and patrimony the custom of primogeniture is valid. I ask whether a king can divide kingdoms or baronies among sons, or whether the sons, the king father consenting, can divide kingdoms among themselves. Codice de furibus cum similibus mihi non plus primum membrum nicolaus tali ratione quia ubique agitur de successione feudali animi pariter succedit patruus cum nepote ex filio praedefuncto quemadmodum iure romano. capitulo primo et ibi notatur in glossa de gradibus. succedit in feudo et in capitulo primo de successione feudi. secus si ageretur de successione transversalius ut dicto capitulo primo de gradibus et in successione feudali. ¶ Amplectamur nunc iura et rationes pro nepote et primo facit quod primogenitus per suos transmisit ius primogeniturae in eius filium eundemque nepote iure divino ius primogeniturae potuit vendi et cedi ut in esau iacob probat genesis. vicesimo quinto per Ioannem andream et hostiensem in capitulo de voto et iuramento dixi et quibus praecedentibus ergo potuit et trasmitti ius primogeniturae ad filium suum. lege quod si. ff. de acquirendo rerum dominio. probatur iure naturali nam quae est ratio quare prae magis diligit filius et est certe philosophus septimo physicorum. quod pater habet in filio suo non est facit lege iste quod de membris causis. lege si. ff. de custodia furis. ergo cum nepos censeatur persona primogeniti habet iura primogeniturae ad lege si is qui ducenta. paragrapho ultimo. ff. de rebus damnatis. tertio in textu in feudis in capitulo primo de successione feudi. et in capitulo primo de gradibus successione in feudo. ubi nepos succedit in feudo. quarto quod is possessio non transferat ad heredes. lege cum heredes in principio ff. de acquirenda possessione in feudis traditio ad filium capitulo primo de feudis cognoscitur et ibi notatur in summa. quanto nam nepos ex filio utriusque punctu excludit patrum vel avunculum veterinum vel sanguineum tantum auctoritas. lege itaque. Codice de successione et in authentica de plantis. et veteri. fratris ergo eodem modo in casu nostro nepos excludit patrum. sexto facit quoniam nepos repraesentat personam patris primogeniti. lege ut tam in testamento. Codice de suis et legitimis in paragrapho cum filius isti de heredibus qui ab intestato deferuntur ergo excludit patrum ex persona primogeniti. septimo facit quoniam ea quae competunt filio ut filio non ut heredi transmittuntur ad descendentes et ut non pente suo. lege si quis. et lege si generis prioris Codice de his qui. et ibi vide baldum. sed ius primogeniturae competit filio ut filio primogenito ut dixi in dimidio in hoc opusculo ergo nepos excludit patrum. octavo boni facit textus in lege emancipatus paragrapho si. ff. de senatus. nono boni facit textus in lege aristotiles. Codice res pignoris obligari. possunt lege prima. ff. qui potiores in pignore habeantur. ubi tertius creditor praefert secundum creditori quod tertius creditor habet iura cessa a primo creditore ita debet preferri nepos qui habet iura primogeniturae a patre suo primogenito. decimo facit. lege prima. paragrapho si quis duos ff. de administratione librorum ubi nepos excludit patrum. xj. facit lege si opaz ff. de operibus libertorum. 7. lege a duobus. ff. eodem titulo. ultimo boni facit quod ratio naturalis est ut filio eodemque nepote maxime qui ius primogeniturae venit a genere. lege cum Romae de bonis datus lege scripto ff. uniuersitate libro iij. ff. de interdicto et relegan. ¶ Item boni facit privilegium pro de regulis iuris in i. vj. ubi notatur quod privilegium cecidit non personae sed esse ut est ius primogeniturae trasmittitur ad heredes. lege non solum. ff. de in integrum restitutione. et boni facit. Codice de gradibus de super negotio per ela. et capitulo lege de voto ubi in subsidium admittitur patruus non existere nepote ergo existere nepote excludit patruus. propria quoto parte. f. per patruo allegat clementinam pastoralis de re iudicata adducit talis ratio nam quocunque iure primitiatis siue primogeniturae deferunt patruo excluso nepote textus est in lege prima liberis prior. paragrapho i. et in lege libertus quaestio. ff. octavo bonorum libertorum. ¶ Tertio quoniam illa regula quae vult quod nepos repraesentat personam patris habet locum quando tractatur de successione avi. patrui. vel avunculo alias praefert patruus nepoti textus est in authentica post fratres fratrumque Codice de legitimus heredibus sed ius primogeniturae non solum debet ex successione sed ex eius providentia divina. in capitulo primo. paragrapho nunc vero coram duobus qui feudis dare possunt ergo nepos in casu isto non repraesentat personam patris sui. ¶ Quarto quod si duae est ceterioris additio filius qua nepos. lege si viva. Codice de bonis maternis. ergo prae quicunque est filius respectu avi excludet nepote. ¶ Quinto quod ea quae competit ratione etatis non trasmittuntur ad heredes. lege ea quae. Codice de temporibus in integrum restitutione petentibus sed ius primogeniturae est ratione etatis ergo non trasmittit ad nepote. ¶ Sexto quod incerta non trasmittunt

<column-break/>

lege unica. paragrapho finali autem. Codice de caducis tollendis sed quis sit primogenitus tempore mortis est incertum ergo non transmittit ad heredes. ¶ Septimo quia regula est quod potior est in gradu prior est in successione. lege post sanguineos. paragrapho primum de suis et legitimis et dicta authentica post fratres sed patruus est in potiori gradu quam nepos. lege iurisconsultus. ff. de gradibus. ergo etc. ¶ Octauo quia fundamentum iure primogeniturae est etas maior cui defertur honos. lege finali Codice de fide consuetudinis et dixi supra ergo cum patruus sit maior etate excludet nepotes a iure primogeniturae attenta mente consuetudinis argumento eorum quae notatur Dionysius in capitulo finali de regulis iuris libro sexto et Bartolus in lege non dubium. Codice de legibus. ¶ Nono facit quod cessant verba consuetudinis in nepote et vendicat sibi locum in patruo qui est primogenitissimus tempore mortis ergo nepos excludetur a patruo. lege ille aut ille. paragrapho cum in verbis ff. de legatis tertio lege hos accusari. paragrapho omnibus. ff. de accusationibus ¶ Decimo quia si consideramus etiam ius civile uocatur patruus ad successionem ex regula comuni quia prior in gradu sed nepos ex filio praedefuncto venit ad successionem cum patruo ex quodam privilegio iure singulari quia repraesentat personam patris ut in paragrapho cum filius institutionibus de heredibus quae ab intestato deferuntur sed firmius et robustius est ius patrui quod venit ex iure comuni quam ius nepotis quod venit ex quadam equitate et privilegio argumento lege eius militis. paragrapho militiae missus. ff. de militari testamento. ex quibus concluditur patruum excludere nepotem a iure primogeniture. ¶ Nunc proficiscoz ad decisionem huius dubij sedem distinctionis maiores nostros posse tenus concordando. Igitur aut constat quod consuetudine quod nepos excludat patruum vel econtra et standum est consuetudini. ff. de legibus minime in capitulo finali de consuetudine et ibi notatur aut non constat de aliqua consuetudine et tunc si constat de mente acedetis ex verbis vel aliter quod nepos excludat patruum vel est standum verbis mentis. capitulo si papa de privilegiis in sexto et qualiter colligatur mens traditur per Lyram in lege voluntatis. Codice de fideicommissis et in lege si servus plurium. paragrapho finali de legibus prima aut non constat de mente et tunc aut habet consuetudinis vel constitutionis loquuntur de potiori in gradu puta quod solus potior in gradu succedat in regno et tunc patruus qui est potior in gradu succedet. dicta lege iurisconsultus iuncta dicta authentica post fratres et est de mente Baldi in dicta lege ut in testato. Codice de suis et legitimis aut verba consuetudinis locuntur de iure primogeniturae tunc si prior fuerit natus patruus quam nepos patruus excludit nepote. si vero nepos prius fuerit natus quam patruus tunc nepos excludit patruum ratio quia tunc est primogenitus. capitulo esau de verborum significatione et est de mente Baldi in dicta lege ut intestato. aut non constat quis prior etate sit an patruus vel nepos et tunc patrem utrunque succederet secundum notata Baldi in authentica ex testamento in vltima columna Codice de collationibus. ¶ Sed pulchrum est videre quid si hoc casu quando nepos et patruus sunt eiusdem etatis alter decedat an superuiuens habeat partem ius non decrescendi loco. Respondeo quod sic secundum Baldum in lege unica in vltima columna Codice quando non petentes partes ¶ Et praedicta omnia sunt ubi regnum esset ita de uoluntatem ad preces istius nepotis quod tunc nepos excluderet patruum succedendo patri suo regi textus est in dicto capitulo primo et in dicto capitulo gradibus. ¶ Rursus quaerendum est quid si primogenitus sit a natura demens vel furiosus an progenitus excludet eum respondeo quod sic secundum Baldum in capitulo primo de successione feudi quod consuetudo debet intelligi de habili non autem de inhabili a natura a principio secus si efficiat ex postfacto prodigus vel demens postquam regnum fuit in persona sua radicatum quae tunc daretur curator dicto capitulo gradibus secundum Baldum in dicto capitulo primo de successione feudi. ¶ Circa articulum patrui et nepotis que examinavi addit auctor Ioannes de ymo quas refert et sequitur dominus de sancto geminiano in dicto capitulo gradibus usque quo ad nepote extra patruum. paragrapho filio. sexagesimo quarto ultra aliud consilium oldradi. centesimo nonagesimo tertio secundum vnam cotam vel facit aliam ducentesimo septuagesimo secundo. ¶ Quero nunquid esau potuit accusare fratrem suum iacob de suppolita ut ita dixerim partu glossa et Angelus tenent quod sic

For the sake of the country, I will not be sparing of myself in giving you
honor and glory at all times among those of the interior.
Finally, I beg you to forgive my mistakes
and my poor performance, for the reason that it is not often without mistake
when one is a beginner. I wrote this
on the way to Holland.

---

Given in the town of Kleve, which
is Clavenburg, where I stayed for some days in the care of the Baron
of W. et cetera, and the local prefect et cetera, on the eleventh of February, 1631.

->Joannes Elichman, Silesian<-
->Doctor of Medicine, by his own hand<-

## TH. IX.

*Per nimium somnum atque vitam sedentariam, sanguinis ventilatio atque insensibilis transpiratio impeditur, unde partes heterogeneae quae alias per insensibilem transpirationem evocari solent, Massae Sanguinis immixtae manent, unde obstructiones, et exinde sanguinis non parum inficitur, ex quo postmodum oritur intemperies acris. Dum motus et vigiliae limites excedunt depauperantur spiritus, partes spirituosiores per cutis poros qua data porta avolant, remanentibus solis crassioribus ad motum minus aptis; dum, quod excerni debebat, retinetur, et vice versa quod retineri debuisset, excernitur, malum est: plus tamen est periculi in excernendorum retentione, quam in retinendorum retentione, animi pathemata dum excedunt varias fluidis inferre alterationes, et in hoc effectu producendo multum habere efficaciae, nemo inficias ibit, non opus est ergo ut de illis prolixius agam, cum ipsorum operandi et affligendi modus jam in vulgus notus sit.*

## TH. X.

Perlustratis hujus affectus Causis, in conspectum venit agmen symptomatum, ad signa diagnostica igitur progredior, etsi ex definitione morbi jam innotuerint, hic latius ea tradam, phænomena quæ in hoc effectu occurrunt, explicaturus. Verum videor audire quosdam susurrantes illam doctrinam de signis carere fundamento, partemque semioticam esse merè conjecturalem: Ultro concedam, Medicum non posse, certitudine, uti dicitur, Metaphysica, morborum eventum prædicere, eorundemque exitum definire, sufficit tamen rem ita posse fieri ut concipitur, quod si aliter contingat, id dico fieri per accidens, qui enim œconomiam animalem, naturamque fluidorum perspectam benè sibi reddidit, nonne poterit instantis tempestatis indicia dare, nec non prædicere quomodo terminabitur morbus.

## TH. XI.

Humores excreti jam examinandi veniunt, cujus illi sint indolis, lympha, quæ è glandulis intestinalibus extillat in cavitatem intestinorum, cum muco, parietibus ipsorum, adhærente, excernuntur; an autem talis mucus detur non amplius dubito qui rem sæpius vidi cum Celeberrimus vir Dominus Dorstenius Anatomicas dissectiones institueret: Huic lymphæ, immixtæ sunt partes sanguineæ, ut & frustula intestinorum, frequens est excretio, quippe illud sal acre de quo supra dictum, tunicas intestinales, ita vellicat, ut fibris inflatis atque constrictis, necesse sit, ut si quæ sint quæ excerni debeant, excernantur, ad sitque ejerendi desiderium, quod Tenesmus dicitur.

I have seen more than once in the country that grape-gatherers were seized by dysentery from the excessive drinking of must and the swallowing of grapes. This happens especially in foul air, for such effervescence occurs in the veins and arteries that they not infrequently rupture at the extremities, a fact which travelers who suffer from nosebleeds also experience quite often for the reason given before.

### TH. VII.

These things being premised, it is clear how far the Ancients strayed from the goal while, in explaining the causes of diseases, they fled to an innate spirit being irritated, and asserted that a certain, I know not what, expulsive and retentive faculty was damaged. Of them, as the most celebrated Svicerus says (though in a different subject), *confusing the spiritual with the corporeal, they betray their own obscure concepts with an inept name.* Those who accuse an intemperance of the viscera speak no less obscurely; for what else do the viscera contribute except space, like a pot? Therefore, every fault that happens to the viscera is not from the solid parts, but from the fluids.

### TH. VIII.

The *six so-called non-natural things* contribute much to the production of this disease. Concerning each, what shall we note? First, air presents itself, which, if it is not temperate in motion and mixture, but impregnated with salts of various kinds, acrid ones, and others, will produce fevers, tumors, ulcerations, and other evils. That this is so is easily proved *a posteriori*, for we very often experience the ulceration of the lips, which arises from no other cause than from such a Sun <note>symbol for the Sun</note>, emulating the nature of nitric acid. Next to air, food and drink claim the place for themselves, from the fault of which two famous [types] arise.

Space, Self, and Mind—these five substances, although permanent, cannot produce effects. The treatise itself explicitly states that, among the qualities, those that "have ability" are said to be able to obtain effects. Those ten that are generally permanent, as well as qualities that can also produce effects, are categorized accordingly. Action <term>karma</term>, although it produces effects, is impermanent in its essence; it is not what is being discussed here. "Non-existence" <term>abhava</term>, although it is also permanent, cannot produce effects because it is not a fundamental entity. What is being analyzed here is solely what is required by Consciousness-Only. As for the other various topics, such as how many qualities are required to be called "having qualities," and so on, and how many are "objects of knowledge," these are not the requirements of this text. I will briefly omit them and not describe them in detail. They are as stated in the ten categories <note>referring to the system of categories in Vaisheshika</note>.

The categories of Substance and so on, as maintained by the Vaisheshika school, are mostly considered to have real existence and are obtained through direct perception.

There are three parts to the refutation: first, stating their doctrine; second, correctly refuting it; and third, concluding the error. This is the first part. Now, the statement consists of two points: first, stating they believe these are really existent; second, stating they believe they are obtained through direct perception. If stating they are "really existent," this refutes all six categories <note>Substance, Quality, Action, Commonality, Particularity, and Inherence</note>, as all six are considered real. Chronica 21.* et invocavit Dominum (David) et exaudivit eum per ignem de cælo, et *2. Paralipomenon 7. versus 1.* Cum finivisset Salomo orare et ignis descendebat de cælo; quod nos incitare debet ad diligenter orandum, sic enim **DEUS** cælestem ignem Spiritum Sanctum in sacrificia labiorum ac cordis nostri immittit, eaque ignita reddet.

*Causa finalis sive finis*, est vel *Physicus* vel *Theologicus*: iste est sacrificiorum consumptio, hic excitatio fidei in sacrificantibus et testificatio specialis providentiæ ac gratiosæ præsentiæ.

### IX.

Adjuncta sunt 1. *Tempus* quod certo modo extraordinarium est, ut cum in dedicatione Levitici cultus, in confirmatione promissæ liberationis, in Templi Salomonæi inauguratione, ac in probatione veri cultus ac falsi confutatione, à **DEO** demissus est ignis. Ordinarium etiam quodammodò videtur tempus observatum, quando nimirum sacrificandi vespertinum huic actui legitur determinatum. Quod de primo sacrificio Aaronis, et dedicatione templi Salomonæi ex lege certum est, de sacrificio autem Eliæ expressis verbis dicitur.

### X.

2. *Locus* qui certus non fuit sed pro re nata, vel *extraordinarius et profanus*, vel *ordinarius et sacer*. *Extraordinarius et profanus* fuisse videtur locus quo Abel sacrificavit, et petra Gideonis, et Arca Arasnæ Jebusæi, de quo postremo loco notandum mediante hoc sacrificio quodammodo sanctificatum et futuræ templi ædificationi destinatum. *Ordinarius et Sacer* fuit tum Tabernaculum conventus, tum ipsum templum, ut in primo Sacrificio Aaronis, ac Regis Salomonis quo ista loca consecrata sunt cultui divino.

### XI.

*Cognata* sunt cæteri ignes cœlitus delapsi ac demissi, ut ignis quo Elias in cœlum raptus, ignis Sinaiticus, ignis fœderalis Abrahami etc.

### XII.

Ex hisce hactenus prælibatis, hanc eruimus sistimusque ignis sacrificialis cœlestis definitionem *vel potius descriptionem. Ignis sacrificialis est flamma quædam supernaturalis ac typica, à DEO creata, cœlitusque accensa sæpè ac visibiliter demissa, idque propter nominis sui gloriam omniumque hominum ac Judæorum præcipuè salutem, nec non ad subitam et solam holocaustorum consumptionem, Christumque vel totam Sanctissimam Trinitatem typicè præfigurandam.*

## QUÆSTIONES.

1. Quaestio. *An Sacrificium Abelis etiam huc spectet?*

seed: fifty, by which the captains of fifty, along with their fifty soldiers, were consumed. *2 Kings 1:10, 11.* The fire that fell upon the herds of Job, *Job 1*; the fire of the covenant of Abraham, *Genesis 15:17*; the majestic fire in the burning bush, *Exodus 3*; the fire appearing on Mount Sinai, *Exodus 19*; and at times seen in prophetic visions around **God**. Compare *Ezekiel 1:10, 11.* We call it sacrificial because it was extraordinarily ordained by **God** the Best and Greatest to consume sacrifices of every kind. For in the sacrifice of Abel, it consumed a sheep; in the sacrifice of Aaron, which is described in *Leviticus 9:24* as consuming sacrifices of every kind (as noted by <term>Aben-Esra</term>); in the sacrifice of Gideon, *Judges 6:20, 21*, it consumed meat, cakes, and a libation; and finally, in the sacrifice of Elijah, it is read to have consumed an ox. Therefore, it is rightly called sacrificial fire.

### II. Quæstio. An motus ignis cœlitus delapsi sive evibrati fuerit naturalis an verò præternaturalis & violentus?

Affirmative Posterius; descendere enim de cœlo contrarium est naturæ ignis, utpote qui naturaliter sursum fertur.

### III. Quæstio. An fuerit ejusdem naturæ cum igne elementari?

Hyparxis autem eius erat esse vn'omnia. Huius ergo vn'omnia, fue geniture dedit.videlicet, vnitas esset & omnia. Sed cur, illum patrem, vnum dicimus, genitum vero vnitatem appellamus? (iuxta doctrinam, & Procli, & Damascij Platonicorum, quamqua Theologi uerissime teneant omnia contineri in Deo, & non in filio distincto a Patre, & Spiritu sancto, excellentissimo modo) Apud Zoroastrem, quidem & Hermetem, etiam unum illud, monas appellatur. nobis uero doctrine clarioris gratia melius uisum, vnum illud, hanc uocare vnitatem. Vnum quidem, quia tantum vnum, & independens. Vnitas uero, & dependet inde, & multitudinem respicit: in illo quidem vn'omnia, multitudo est, vniter uero, & simplicissima. In vnitate uero multitudo est iam distincta, & in numerum effusa. Vnum, supra omnem se fe rapuit relationem, & supra omnem transcendit multitudinis respectum. Vnitas uero numerum respicit, & ad multitudinem refertur. Vnitas ergo hec primaria, ab vno primo est. Multitudo uero, que in hac est vnitate, ab illius prouenit, vt, ita dicam, omnitate. Sed qua de causa, Vnum illud omnia, vnitatem hanc omnia, de se protulit? Cur pater ille, filium hunc genuit? Qui alijs omnibus fecunditatem tribuit, sterilis ne esse debuit? Nec debuit, nec potuit. Debuit, quia bonus erat, & est. Potuit, quia omnipotens fuit, & est. Producere ergo habuit necessitatem, voluntatem fecit producendo. Voluntas, fecit necessitatem. Voluntatem enim Dei, necessitas sequitur, inquit Hermes. Ergo omnia ex ipso, & per ipsum. Qui rectissime quoque dixit.

Et hoc ei opus est, patrem esse. Huius essentia est vtero ferre omnia, & facere.

Omnia enim, quæcunque sunt, in Deo sunt, & a Deo facta, & inde dependentia.
Deus ergo & pater omnium genitorum est & factor. At quo modo ea genuit, aut fecit? Per potentiam scilicet quam habuit, ea faciendo. Deus enim, pater entium & genitor est. Entia uero ab eo facta sunt, & genita. Inter hæc duo media est potentia, per quam genitor producit: genita producuntur. Nisi enim ille

<column-break/>

Ergo potentia hæc primissima, supereffentialis est. Est enim ante essentiam, quando inter vnum, & effentiam est media. Et entia præcedit, & prima est ipsius Vnius genitura. Et ideo recte a Zoroastre celebrata. Potentia patris: & ab Hermete patris filius, vt paulo post uidebimus. Redeamus ad modum. Si per vnius potentiam ab vno, tranfitus fit in ens. & quasi per vnius egressionem & progressionem. Ergo per motum quendam, ab uno gignitur essentia. Necesse enim est, aut per motum id fieri, aut per statum, aut utroque modo, aut neutro. Si neutro, neque utroque. Si nó utroque, saltem alterutro. At statu ne, an motu? Ait Hermes.
> Τὸ ἓν μένον ἕστηκε, καὶ οὐ κινεῖται.
Vnum uero, manens stat, & non mouetur. Quod autem manet, non progreditur. Et contra, quod progreditur, non manet. At vnum ipsum, manet. Non ergo progreditur. Progressio motus quidam est. Motus autem actio. Actio uero omnis aut in essentia, aut ex essentia. Inessentia quidem, non uidetur progressionis, & productionis fieri motus. Neque enim entia, per eum motum inde exifsent. Ergo ut exirent, motu ex essentia eguerunt. Seu potius ex vnius hyparxi. Hyparxis enim ei est, id, quod entibns essentia. Quid ergo exitu entium ex vnius hyparxi, vnum, entibus exinanitur? Absit. Non enim mouetur. Ergo statu prodierunt. At neque stat. Neque enim habet in quo stet alio, quàm in se ipso. Neque quo moueatur. Est enim ubique. Ait enim Hermes uerissime.
> Καὶ οὗ δ' αὐτοῦ οὐ δέν ἐκτὸς, οὐδ' αὐτὸς οὐδενός.
> Et extra ipsum, quidquam. & ipsum extra quidquam. Sed quo modo tandem secunda produxit entia? Suo forte statu, ex se ea deprompit. Illa uero ab eo sunt dimota, ipso manente? At depromptio, actio quædam est. Actio uero, motio. Ergo etiam mouetur. Motum ergo & statum in se habet? Statum ne prius? motum postea? Redit ergo in idem quæstio? Nequaquam. Sed in eo, status mouetur, & motus stat. Et quod in eo mouetur, aut ab eo, stabiliter mouetur, & quod stat, mobiliter stat. Nempe manet ipsum. Manentque fecunditate sua de se omnia extrahens, & extra se proferens. promit de se ipso, manens ipsum quod erat prius. Quo enim modo, minus fiat, quàm vnum? Aut quo res, quas de se promit, extra ipsum abeant, cum ipsum fit ubique. Et producta omnia, adhuc in se contineat? Neque ergo exinanitur suis primis illis: neque se euacuat, vt minus fiat quàm vnum, aut minus, quàm omnia.

Ignis proinit de se calorem, non tamen minorem quàm prius, imo eundem sibi retinet. Ita Primum, ita Principium, ita Vnum, ita Bonum, ita Deus, nihil diminuta, aut prinitate, aut principitate, aut vnitate, aut Bonitate, aut Deitate sua, produxit omnia, nulla materia coadiuuante. Imo ex se, deprompsit ipsam etiam, & extra se protulit. Protulit autem, quia vnum: vt inde multitudo rerum gignere-tur. Protulit ob bonitatem, vt multitudo, & numerus is, entia esset. & non entia, nequaquam esset. Nam hæc in se retinuit, vt quando vollet, proferat, & quando noluerit non proferat. Itaque vnum, in rerum secundarum productione, non progreditur se, neque mouetur. Sed dum illas profert, & illæ de eo progrediuntur, ipsum manet in se ipso. Illæ uero actione ex hyparxili-lius prodeunt, & emanant. non aliter, atque aqua e fuo emanat fonte, ipso quidem immo-to; sed aquam proferente: aqua uero mota, & inde scaturiente. Quid ergo, si immotu est, & in se ipso manet, producere non videtur? Productio, actio: & actio, motio est. Vel & mouetur, & non mouetur? Et producit, & non producit? & efficit res, & non efficit, modis suis: scilicet ineffabilibus. Non efficit quidem, quia iam in se existentes, a se tantum discernit. Efficit uero, quia eas de se profert, & ipsæ ab eo profluunt. Videtur ergo prior quæstio redi-re? Per se ne ipsæ, ab vno prodeunt? An causa aliam fuæ proditionis habent? Cérte, vel a se ipsis, uel ab alio, uel ab vno ipso producuntur. Ab alio quidem, minime dicendum. Quid enim vnius prius? aut vni par? Non a se ipsis, nisi quatenus producenti non resistunt. & assensum fuæ productioni pandunt. Vnum tamen eas de se profert: bonitatis suæ necessitate ad actum. simul alteras a se, & a sua omnitate efficiens, vt non identitatis horum cum illis, sed alteritatis harum ab illis, causa fieret. Quæ causa nulla alia fuit, quàm ipsa rerum ab eo progressio, & proditio. Omnis enim proditio, seu promanatio, cum secretione est. Omnis autem secretio, ab vno, multitudinis est causa. Et quando in vno incipit multitudo, tum proditio succedit. Sed si vnum, non est id, quod secretionem faciat, a qua multiplicatio fiat, & ab hac proditio quidnam, id fuerit? Bonum ergo ipsum non qua vnum, sed qua bonum, secretionis rerum fecundarum ab vn'omnia, a primis, primissima est causa. Secretio uero est causa multiplicationis. Multiplicatio progressionis. Exemplo id fiat manifestum. Centrum circuli, vnum & indiuisibile est. In eo vno termini sunt linearum omnium ab eo prodeuntium, inter se in ipso, minime distincti. Ab eo lineæ prodeunt innumera, inter se iam distinctæ, ad circumferentiam vsque, quæ in centro indiferetæ erant omnes. Dum tamé a centro fecernuntur, multiplicantur: & dum multiplicantur, prodeunt ab vno; prodeunt tes, ab eo discedunt. Discessus hic, post centrum est. Eiusque causa, centrum non est. Sed ex illo fluxus quidam, quo lineæ ab illo, & fecernuntur, & multiplicantur, & prodeunt, & discedunt. Neque discessus istius, ipsum causa est. Neque ipsum a se discedit, neque exinanitur; vt se fe in lineas multiplicet. Sed post ipsarum discessum, centrum adhuc permanet. Neque ob linearum abitum, ipsum diminuitur, aut quicquam patitur: Lineæ tamen ab eo exeuntes, ac prodeuntes, non amplius id sunt, quod in iplo erant. Sed sunt, & ab eo, & inter se distinctæ. Habent tamen ab eo id quod sunt, ipsumque illis, esse tribuit. Neque ab eo diuelluntur; sed ab eo pendent. Manet enim omnis proditionis causa. Et quod prodit in proprietate, & terminis fuæ causæ manet. Ita, vt quod prodit, uideatur & in eadem causa esse, in qua fuerat, & inde etiam discessisse. Hoc fano modo, (si nefas non sit hac uitia similitudine) ab vno omnia indiscrete, fecernuntur, & multiplicantur discreta prodeuntia omnia. Quid uero, in ea ab vno progressione, aliquid ipsa, de ono ferunt secum? An uero ipsum, eis aliquid largitur? Vel & ipsum bonitate sua ea largitur: & ipsa, bonitate illa gaudentia, secum libentia ferunt ea, quibus ueluti sunt donata. At quænam ea sunt, quæ donata secum ferunt? Vnum profecto se-cundum, ab uno primo, cuique in portionem datum, per quod & una sunt singula, & per quod etiam sunt multa. Et per quod etiam sunt entia. Neque enim esse possent entia, nisi una essent. Neque possent esse multa, nisi uenirent ab uno. Hæc itaque ab uno secreta, post unum omnia, sunt una simul, & multa. Et post principium, quæ fuerat quarta principii, conditio. Et ab uno sunt, & a principio quæ con-ditio eius fuerat tertia. Neque enim hæc, aut ante unum sunt, aut cum uno, sed ab uno. each. And so the question would proceed into infinity. If things were not from many, nor could they be from both. Therefore, it is necessary that all things were from the One. For that is the most true principle of beings, without which beings neither could have been, nor can they be, and which bestows [being] upon all; that, however, is the One, without whose participation all beings would rush into nothingness. Because for all beings, it is best to be one. And the greatest of evils for the same is not to be one. But also for another reason, all multitude is from the One. For if multitude were said to be from another, it would be necessary that this be either one, or not one, or nothing. But that nothing can be the cause of anything has already been shown several times. If, however, it is not one, it is already a multitude. And thus, a multitude would give birth to a multitude. And one could ask about this birthing one: from whom was it born? From a multitude, or from the One? And again, it would be sought into infinity. Therefore, it is left of necessity that all multitude has been, and is, from the One. Therefore, all multitude was first in the One. Therefore, the One would have brought forth the multitude from itself, unless it had pre-existed in it: for no one gives what he does not have. The multitude of beings, therefore, was from that One, namely, the very first, which we have called <term>unomnia</term> <gloss>the One-all</gloss>. The multitude, I say, of beings, of which we distinguished two kinds: incorruptible and corruptible. But which of these is from that One? For those beings, which we said were all in Him, whether they are different from these two kinds of beings, or whether they are the same, seems to be in great doubt. For if these are those, the One is exhausted by them. And thus rendered imperfect, and not sufficient, and not good. But if these are different from those, in what way was it truly said that all beings were in the One? Or perhaps both are true, that they are the same and not the same. They are the same, in that way in which cause and effect are the same. They are not the same, however, in another way, in which cause and effect are different among themselves. For we say it thus. Those beings which both were in the One, and still are, have been and still are the cause of these other beings. These, however, are the effects of those. But because these two other kinds are very different from each other, are both of them effects of those first ones in the One? Or are some of these prior effects, and others posterior? But which is prior? Which is posterior? As the discourse proceeds, this will be opened up, if first the manner is opened, by which these second ones proceeded from those first. And for what reason, and by what degrees, and in what order, and also in what time. For all these things are necessary for this perfect science, in contemplation. Therefore, about the manner first. Which offers itself as twofold: either by the proper powers of the One, these second ones are
<column-break/>
brought forth from It, or they themselves flew out from the One by their own powers. Or even by both. If we say that beings proceeded from thence by themselves; and that they flew out by their own powers as if doves from a dovecote, then the One, acting as nothing to perfect them, would have been the least of principles, or the principle of nothing. For what honor of goodness would there be for It, if It provided nothing else than to have contained the beings in itself before, and then to have allowed them to fly out? If this is absurd, because It would not have been omnipotent, it is necessary that the One produced all beings by its own [powers], by no powers of the beings themselves. But I shall ask, what did It produce? Did it produce all beings? Those which it had in itself? Or others from these? If those which it had in itself, it no longer has them. And it is exhausted, and rendered imperfect and insufficient. But this is far more absurd. Therefore, it produced others from them. Therefore, beings here open themselves as threefold. The first, which were and are in the One, and the two second kinds, eternal and corruptible. Of these two, the former are shown to be eternal, and deservedly will be called second; the mortal shall be called third. They are also from the One, but derived through the second means, by the manners which will be opened later. Now let us proceed about the seconds, and let us finish.

The second beings, therefore, flowed from the first. The first, it was said, were those which already for a long time we assert to have been all in the One, in the One-all, unitively, in a unified way, and most simply. All those things are the multitude itself, but most simple, and unified, and unbegotten, and unproduced, and first, and supreme. Which was and is sempiternally in the One-all, and neither ever proceeded nor will proceed from It: nor did it come into It from elsewhere. But it is so one with It, that nothing can be more one. From this most first and supreme multitude which is in the One-all, and which is the One-all, let us derive the second. Because the One is the One-all, it is one, and all things, and each of those all, and the one is everything. And this is because the One is everywhere, and while it is everywhere, it is in itself. And it fills itself and all things in itself, by itself. But these things, as has been said often, are ineffable, and transcend every concept of human reasoning: since the Father snatched himself away, and covered himself in the abyss of his light, so that we might indeed recognize Him through his lights, but know Him not at all. But however much we may conceive it, we say the second multitude of beings came from the One-all through emanation. This emanation is nothing other than a certain secretion and issuance from that One-all. It is necessary, therefore, because the One both is and makes all things, that the One likewise brings forth from itself, through this emanation, the One and all things. Na una essentia, multas in se uires producit, & extra se multas actiones. Vnum totu, partes multas. Non totum corporeum inqua, nec corporeas partes. Sed incorporea omnia. Et quæcumque fiunt, uno fiunt, & uno, entia omnia seruantur. Et si uno careant, in proprium ruunt, ut diximus, interitum. Sut-que omnia entia mista, ex uno, & multis. Et mistio hæc, ex uno, & multitudine, quam, non unum, præbet entibus, communio quædam, & unio est entium. Ens ergo, & unum, non unu, nullius alterius entibus est causa, quam ut fint una. Omnia ergo, & fecunda, & tertia, quæcumque entia dicuntur, sunt ab uno, primo vt a causa. Et vno proprio in sua essentia consistunt. Hoc autem vnum etiam primum rerum omnium esse ostendimus. ### XXXVIII.

Potest demonstratio propter quid ab omni caussarum genere procedere ; præcipuè tamen à caussâ formali ; et hinc quod dici solet à quibusdam , potissimum demonstrationis medium esse, ipsius subiecti definitionem, intellige formalem.

### XXXIX.

Neque negandum existimo, quin probari possit, idque demonstratiuè, huiusmodi definitionem formalem subiecto suo conuenire ; verùm non tanquam ipsius definitionem ; neque etiam per caussam formalem ; sed vel à materiâ, vel à fine, vel ab ipsius caussâ efficiente ; definitionis enim formalis non datur in eodem genere alia definitio.

### XL.

At quando propria passio per caussam ipsius passionis formalem de subiecto suo demonstratur, tunc etiam, quin definitio formalis per caussam formalem, hoc est, definitionem subiecti, demonstratione identidem probetur, nihil est quod prohibet.

### XLI.

Concludendo igitur, neque subiecti definitionem, neque definitionem passionis, sed utramque simul coniunctam, utpote quæ in se omnes conclusionis caussas continet, tanquam medium demonstrationis potissimum, merito constituimus.

### XXXII.

Among these, just as the universal is more excellent than the particular, so the affirmative precedes the negative: just as also the ostensive, even if it were negative, precedes that which leads to the impossible.

### XXXIII.

That demonstration is therefore the most excellent of all which is simultaneously universal, affirmative, and ostensive; and it can be constructed only in the first mode of the first figure.

### XXXIV.

Although in a negative demonstration not all things which were said above can be kept entirely, it suffices, however, in such a demonstration, that the premises be necessary and immediate: which happens when two highest genera are denied of each other; or two definitions, or ultimate divisive differences of the same are mutually removed from each other.

### XXXV.

Just as also among affirmatives some are more excellent than others, so also among negative demonstrations; for that is said to be the most powerful, in whose conclusion a proper property is denied of that which is not its proper subject, or which does not express the cause, in the way that the proper definition of the subject does.

### XXXVI.

Such a demonstration is constructed in the second figure, and only in its second mode. For if it were made in the first figure, the disposition of the matter would be changed at the same time as the form; nor would it be a negative demonstration, at least the most powerful one.

labor Aristoteles. frustra. Quarto. in principio de celo inquit. (nam. constantia. bec quoque sunt corpora et magnitudines. hec autem erit corpus et magnitudine. hec autem per se vitium sunt) et omnes exponunt: et simpliciter ibidem quod corpora habentia corpus et magnitudinem sunt mixta: que habent elementa. non solum qualitates in mixto sunt: sed elementa. Quinto principaliter. stante hac positione: tunc complexio esset per mixtionem: quod est contra eos. et probatur. nam per est qualitas inquantum qualitas: quod inquantum instrumentum substantiae. nam esse instrumentum est accidens qualitati inquantum qualitas: et accidens est posterius eo: cui accidit. ergo nexus ex qualitatibus inquantum qualitates per nexus ex inquantum instrumenta: et sic complexio erit per mixtionem. Sexto. instrumentum magis debet esse sic: sed qualitates prime sunt instrumenta formarum elementorum. ergo forme et qualitates debent esse simul: et sic omnes actu in mixto erunt. Septimo. una forma simplex non potest esse duarum formarum specie omnino instrumentum: sed quaelibet mixti est instrumentum forme mixti. ergo non forme elementarie. Octavo. Aristoteles ostendit. secundo de generatione. quattuor esse corpora in mundo: quod quattuor sunt combinationes poles. Tunc arguo. in mixto quattuor sunt poles coniugationes. ergo ibi actu sunt quattuor elementa: aliter ratio Aristoteles nulla: et maxime quod ibidem Aristoteles ait aqua esse coagulationem frigidi et humidi. Igne vero arsionem calidi et sicci. Sed in mixto sunt de bonis hoc. ergo de finita. Plato etiam ait hominem esse microcosmon: quod in eo quattuor elementa spectant: atque quattuor qualitates: quod etiam Plotinus affirmat. Ex quibus concludemus non posse esse in mixto qualitates: nisi sint ibi forme elementarie.

### Caput. VIII.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Ornamental woodcut initial D</image-desc>
Dixerunt elementa non ad esse mixto: nec quod ad formas substantificas: nec quod ad qualitates. sed tamen: quod mixtus potest exercere opera eorum: et sic saluari secundum virtutes. Sed quod hoc possibile sit impossibile ostendamus. Nam vel elementa sunt in mixto: quod formas et qualitates mitti potest exercere effectum: et tunc eorum: vel quod in mixto sunt non quidem qualitates eiusdem speciei cum qualitatibus elementorum: sed propter virtutes alterius rationis: distincte formas et qualitates mixti. Primo destruamus primam partem. et refellemus secundam. Si ergo est (ut dicit prope) tunc celum esset mixtum ex qualitatibus primis: et ex formis quattuor corporum: quod Aristoteles falsum esse probat in libro celi. Et ducit enthimema. nam lux solis potest exercere omnia opera elementorum. ut demonstrat averroes in secundo celi. secundo 42. Exercet preterea in autumno siccitatem: in hyeme frigiditatem: in vere humorem: in estate calorem. ergo qualitates quattuor virtute continentur in luce. ergo lux esset complexio solis: quemadmodum qualitas mixti est complexio mixti. Adhuc sol producit sui presentia ignem: sui absentia aqua: sua media dispositione media elementa. ergo sol continet quattuor elementa: et propter consimilem actionem: et propter nobilitatem. ergo propter sui substantiam continebit elementarias formas: et propter sui lucem qualitates. ergo mixtum temperatum: quemadmodum mixtum generabile. Rursum tunc aurum esset ex metallis mixtum. nam aurum propter nobilitatem et propter convenientiam in operando continet omnia metalla. ut dicunt alchimiste. ergo non tantum erunt quattuor corpora simplicia. Amplius. tunc rationalis anima esset mixtum ex formis quattuor elementorum naturali anima: et quia potest uti operibus earum: et quia nobilior. Hec autem non dum vidimus in aliquo librorum Aristotelis. Nunc contra secundum membrum arguamus. Primo. quia si solae possint in mixto: tunc non qualitates: nec formas. tunc non poterunt in actum operativum devenire ex propria eius modi. Amplius. sicut res se habet ad esse: ita ad operari: sed ens in potentia non est ens perfectum. ergo non potest agere. Rursum semper extimat species movens. ut in nono tradit philosophie. et tertio auscultationis physice: cum igitur elementa non sunt ibidem in actu: nec possunt agere: nisi recurramus ad formam mixti: et sic erit primum membrum. Sed quoniam haec positio (utcumque intelligat) sit contra Aristoteles arguo verbis eius. Inquit ipse in fine primi de generatione concludens...

dens quid sit mixtio ἡ δὲ μίξις · τῶν μικτῶν ἀλλοιωθέντων ἕνωσίς. id est mixtio vero mixtorum: que alteraverunt unio. Nec valet dicere (ut quidam aiunt) (Philosophus alteratorum) vel alteraverunt) supple se: sit preteritus. nam verbum illud (mixtorum.) dicit actuale quod: etiam eorum est mixtio: que se alteraverunt. ut dicit textus. Sed nec virtutes: nec posse alteraverunt. quia non est mixtio. Adhuc ibidem ait. Cum gutta vini mille milibus amphoris aque non misceretur. solvitur. enim species: et transmutatur in totam aquam. ergo miscibile in actu aliquid ex parte manere. Rursum ostendit que sunt facilia divisione: cuius sunt humida. Si ergo miscibilia solum virtute: vel potentia essent in mixto: ad quid tantopere laboraret ostendens facilia et difficilia mixtu. Si quis profecto consideret verba omnia libri de generatione: inveniet fere omnia contra hanc sectam: licet ipsi valde glorientur in verbis Aristotelis. faciunt etiam contra hec verba Aristoteles adducta in proximo capite et alios: et inducemus postmodum in opinione Averrois alia multa: et rationes eius erigemus. Hec de positione latinorum dicta satis.

->Auerroys positio et verba. Caput. IX.<-

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Ornamental woodcut initial M</image-desc>
Movet hanc questionem auerroes in tertio de celo et mundo. commento. 47. usque verbis. Et querendum est quod de virtutibus non remanent forme elementorum in actu. scilicet in mixtis deferentes alias formas. scilicet mixtorum: quas recipiunt: est ergo questio eorum cur forme elementales sub esse perfecto accepte non sunt dispositiones materiae ad recipiendum alias mixtorum formas: et arguit quod debeat esse. dicitur cum iam posuistis quod non sunt materiae propter quibusdam formis nisi propter suas formas: quod si sic arguar. forme quibus materiae proprie efficiuntur proprie materiae mixtis: sunt dispositiones: mediantibus quibus recipiunt in materia formas mixtorum. Sed forme elementarie sunt: quibus materia proprie efficit propria mixto. ergo mediantibus formis elementariis recipiunt formas mixtorum. Et sic forme elementarie erunt actu in mixtis omnibus. Deinde soluit questionem: et primo probat quod forme elementarie sub esse perfecto non recipiunt in materia: ita ut mediantibus eis recipiant formas mixtorum: et inquit. dicamus igitur quod si esset ita ut diximus: quod. scilicet preciperent sub esse perfecto: necesse esset ut nullum ens generaret ab eis. hoc est ut nullum ens reciperet in materia mediantibus eis: quod esset diversum in formis substantialis: sed tamen esset accidens. quod dicitur si forme elementarie primo essent recepte in prima materia: tunc omne adveniens materiae: et receptum in ea illis mediantibus: esset accidens. Enthimema hic non deducit: sed in pluribus locis auscultationis physice: et prima philosophie deduxit: et in libello de substantia orbis. Nam omne adveniens enti in actu perfecto: et specifico est accidens. Hec est differentia inter formas accidentales et substanciales. ut idem declaravit in secundo de anima. Secundo principaliter probat formas elementarias corrumpi hoc est remitti. Ad hoc ut materia mediantibus illis recipiat formas mixtorum. et inquit. et ideo necesse est cum ex eis generatur una forma. ut corrumpant formas eorum secundum medietatem: hoc est secundum partem. quod dicitur quod si materia mediantibus eis debet recipere formam mixti: ille remittuntur secundum earum substantias aliquid ex parte. Deinde tertio probat quod non corrumpuntur ex omni parte: ita ut materia nuda recipiat formas mixtorum: et inquit: quoniam si corrumperentur secundum totum: tunc prima materia reciperet per se essentialiter omnes formas.

Secundo sequeretur quod non recipet formas mixtorum mediantibus istis corporibus. Ex iis potest capi formas elementarias non recipi sub esse intenso: sed remisso in parte: non in toto: sed quomodo valeat haec ratio: dicemus in difficultatibus. Mouet auerroes statim questionem contra se et inquit. si igitur aliquis dixerit sequitur ex hoc quod forme substantiales elementorum recipiant magis et minus: quod falsum est. Nam haec dispositio est accidentium non formarum substantialium. et arguit: quia omnem est in multis locis. ut in predicamentis: quod forme substantiales non recipiant magis et minus. Ex his duobus videtur dictum illud falsum. Respondet et dicit. primo quod substantiales elementorum sunt diminutive respectu formarum substantialium perfectorum. secundo dicit: quod suum esse est medium inter formas substantiales et accidentia. Deinde removet errorem Avicennae. et primo narrat eum et dicit primo quod haec determinatio latuit avicennam. dicit secundo quod ipse concessit formas substantiales non recipere magis et minus. et ideo conclusit elementa non misceri nisi secundum qualitates et non secundum substantias: quoniam mixtio est unio refractorum. Modo solum qualitates refranguntur: propterea solum earum erit mixtio. Contra arguit primo: quia tunc mixtum habebit plures formas elementorum perfectas et in actu. hoc autem est falsum: quia tunc mixtum non esset unus: quia vel propter unam formam: et hoc non: quia adsunt quattuor perfectae: aut propter contactum: quo modo continua vel contigua sunt unum: et hoc minime: quia tunc mixtum esset unus contactu et non vera unione. Secundo mixtum est unum per se: vel propter unam formam substantialem: vel propter unam formam accidentalem: non propter accidens: quia tunc non esset unus per se. si est unus propter formam substantialem: ergo sic non sunt quattuor formae perfectae in uno mixto. Tertio arguit: quia tunc quilibet esset distincta hoc est in alia parte materiae ab alia. nam uni punctum materiae habere duas formas perfectas est impossibile: et sic non quaelibet pars mixti est mixta. Quarto arguit. si remanent formae elementariae in mixto sub esse perfecto: vel qualitates etiam remanent sub esse perfecto: vel solae qualitates remittuntur. Si primum: tunc in mixto erunt quattuor elementa perfecta. ut ignis. nam ignis non est nisi compositio calidi et sicci. Si vero formae remanent et qualitates remittuntur: tunc possibile esset totam formam esse absque tota sua qualitate. nam tota qualitas et pars sunt unius rationis. quod si potest forma esse sine parte: et sine tota etiam esse poterit. Tunc de Avicenna ita scribit. paucitas vero exercitationis istius viri in naturalibus et bona confidentia in proprio ingenio induxit illum ad istos errores. Sed contra averroem arguet quod: quia tunc figurae elementorum recipiunt magis et minus. Secundo. recipiens debet esse denudatum a natura recepti. quod materia stans sub forma elementi non poterit recipere formam mixti: quia sunt eiusdem generis. Ad primam respondet quod figura sortitur conditiones formae perfectae quantum ad recipere magis et minus. Ad secundam autem recipiens debere denudari a specie recepti non a toto genere. Et si dicas contra: quia sic materia sub forma aquae existens posset recipere formam ignis. Respondet in fine commenti: quod omnes formae elementariae sunt eiusdem ordinis in substantialitate. sic autem non sunt formae elementariae cum formis mixtorum. debet ergo maior sic intelligi: quod recipiens debet denudari ab omni forma eiusdem ordinis ad hoc quod aliquam illarum recipiat: sic non opus ut denudetur ab omni forma alterius ordinis. unde dicit quod non oportet recipiens denudari a toto genere eius: quod debet recipere: sed tantum ab eis quae sunt eiusdem generis proximi: non autem remoti. et ideo non potest materia manente forma unius elementi et tunc quicunque remissi recipere aliam formam elementarem: quia tunc non esset mixtio. vult ergo quod materia debet denudari ab omni forma eiusdem generis proximi: et eiusdem ordinis. si debeat aliquod eorum recipere. hic sunt formae elementariae inter se: non in comparatione ad mixtum. Haec crasso modo est positio averrois. Haec de positione eius.

### Declaratio positionis Auerrois. Caput. X.

Sed haec sint ita. Adhuc restat in huius viri doctrina inquirere. Primo quid sit forma mixtionis. Secundo

<column-break/>

quid mixtio. Tertio quid complexio. Quarto quomodo mixtio est per complexionem: et an mixtio et complexio posteriores sint ultima forma mixtionis: an altera forma per eis. Quinto. quomodo se habent inter se mixtio et complexio: et quomodo ad formam. Sexto. quae fuit necessitas mixtionis in composito: et cur non suffecerunt qualitates tantum. Haec enim non satis ipse expressit. Quantu ad primam videtur averroes ex verbis hic acceptis velle formam mixtionis esse congregatum ex quattuor formis substantialibus: quemadmodum color medius apud eum est congregatum ex extremis confractis. Ex alio videtur contrarium. nam per formam mixti reponitur mixtum in specie. modo per illud congregatum non videtur reponi mixtum in specie. Videtur quibus mihi salvo meliori iudicio: quod forma mixti est duplex. disponens materiam ad ulteriorem formam: et perficiens materiam atque constituens compositum in certa specie. Forma mixti disponens est medius quoddam formarum: quod est congregatum illud disponens ad ultimam formam. ut dicit. forma mixti perficiens est forma ultima constituens totum in certa specie. nam rationalis anima in homine apud averroem una finem rem est forma mixti et rationalis: sub alia tamen ratione. Inquantum enim reponit hominem in genere et sequitur mixturam dicitur forma mixti. Inquantum vero dat esse homini: dicitur specifica et rationalis sic possunt verba eius glosari. Quantu ad secundum dicendum: quod mixtio est unio formarum elementariarum. Sed quoniam in omni unione opus aliquid est ut actus: et aliquod ut potentia: opus in mixtione aliqua forma esse ut actum: aliqua ut potentia. forma autem quae est ut actus est dominans et vincens. forma ut potentia est victa et superata. ex quibus constituit mixtio una: et hoc in pluribus locis declaravit averroes. Ulterius quid complexio. dicamus quod est qualitate unio iterum quibusdam vincentibus: et aliis victis. Ex his sequitur quod mixtio est natura per complexionem. nam sicut formae posteriores qualitatibus: ita mixtio per complexionem. Nam si sunt in eodem instanti ambae: tamen una est secundum rationem et naturam posterior. Ulterius dicendum quod complexio et mixtio ut indeterminatae et in potentia praecedunt formam. ut terminatae et actu sequuntur eam. nam ut indeterminatae sunt dispositiones reducibiles ad genus causae materialis. ut terminatae sunt dispositae per formam. Et quoniam posterius naturae est posterius causae. ut dicit averroes in libro de substantia orbis. ideo mixtio est per complexionem prioritate materiae ad formam: et mixtio et complexio posteriores forma prioritate materiae ad formam: et contra forma posterior est posteritate formae ad materiam. Tunc remanet declarare. unde fuerunt necessariae formae elementariae: et videtur quod fuerunt primo necessariae propter ordinem naturalem. nam sunt medie inter primam materiam et ultimam formam. Secundo. quod instrumenta non possunt esse absque causis principalibus: et quia qualitates sunt instrumenta: formae principales causae. ideo fuit necessarium formas praeesse. Tertio propter naturam mixti. aliter enim mixtum non esset mixtum. nam ex qualitatibus sit tantum complexio. Haec igitur erant declaranda.

Auerroes contra Avicennam arguit quod si ibi essent formae perfectae: omne adveniens esset accidens: tamen ponendo eas imperfectas et remissas non sequitur. Contra primo unus subiectum habere plus una forma est impossibile. ut dicit in libro de substantia orbis. Secundo tota forma et pars formae sunt unius rationis. ut ipse sumit contra Avicennam. et tota forma elementaria et pars eius sunt eiusdem speciei. si non repugnat formae imperfectae stare cum alia doctrina. nec formae perfectae. Et econtra. si repugnat formae perfectae et imperfectae: quia sunt unius rationis. Tertio

produce their works, such as to heat, to moisten, to dry, and to refrigerate. Therefore, the elements are contained in virtue within the form of the mixture, and the qualities within the complexion; and thus, the elements are not parts of the mixture, nor the qualities [parts of the] complexions, but they are contained in them by virtue of their power. From these things, it is clear that they remain in the mixture neither as to their substances nor as to their specific qualities, but only as to their powers. For the form of the mixture can proceed into the powers of the forms of the elements, and the quality of the mixture into the powers of the four qualities. Thus, the elements are contained in the form of the mixture, and the qualities in the complexion, only to that extent and by that power. This is the view of the author and many of his followers.

### The Arguments for the First Position of the Latins. Chapter IV.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial P</note> The first position differs from the second (as has been seen) only in this: the first posits that the qualities of the mixture and of the elements are of the same species, and that they are made from them by tempering, and the form of the mixture by complexion, insofar as they are qualities. Furthermore, it follows from these that their virtues are produced by mixture. The second, however, posits that the elements remain neither as to their qualities nor as to their essences, but only as to their virtues, insofar as the form of the mixture, due to suitability and nobility, contains the forms of the elements—namely, due to the complexion, the qualities. Thus, the qualities of the mixture are distinguished in species from the qualities of the elements, and the form from the forms. For the first position, the proponents are accustomed to adduce many reasons. First, because the heat of the mixture is of the same kind as the heat of the essence; therefore, they are of the same species. Second, the heat of mixtures sometimes generates the heat of the elements; therefore, they are of the same species, which is clear to the mind, for metal heated by impact sometimes generates heat and fire in tinder. Third, touch does not distinguish between the heat of the mixture and that of the elements; therefore, they are the same in species, since no touch is a judge of this kind of touch, just as no sight is of the visible. Fourth, the gravity or levity of the mixture is of the same species as the gravity and levity of the elements; therefore, and for other reasons clear to the mind. For as Aristotle writes in the fourth book of *On the Heavens* and the fourth of the *Meteorology*, oil is above earth as levity, and this is also of the nature of air. This is confirmed because some mixture is heavier than another in air, since it is not so in water; therefore, the gravity of mixtures is of the same species as that of the element. Fifth, all [elements] move to the center, or are light from the center, or heavy by simple elemental gravity. This is clear in the first book of *On the Heavens*; but the mixture strives to be carried either from the center or to the center; therefore, it is heavy or light by elemental gravity. From these things, the first position is clear, namely that the qualities of the mixture are not only virtually present like the qualities of the elements, but are formal and of the same species. Moreover, the total active quality of the mixture is composed of real heat and real cold, and the passive quality of real moisture and real dryness, and from these, the complexion of the mixture is made.

### The Arguments for the Second Position. Chapter V.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial Q</note> That the quality of the mixture is not of the same species as the elemental quality: First, because every opinion concludes the form, but the opinion of a mixed quality is really not of the same species, as all testify; therefore, neither are the qualities. Second, then in every point of the mixture there would be opposite qualities, such as hot and cold. Third, no mixture can have in the same [point] diverse second qualities, such as various flavors; therefore, neither the first qualities. Fourth, any quality denotes the substance in which it is; therefore, if all four qualities were in the mixture, then one and the same mixture would be hot by reason of heat, and cold by reason of cold, and thus [it would be] hot and cold. Fifth, where it is actually such, it is superfluous to be formally such. But the complexion is actually all the qualities of the elements; therefore, they are superfluous if they were there in act.

### Arguments against the First Sect. Chapter VI.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial C</note> The elements do not agree to be in the mixture as to the existence of their forms, but only by virtue and power. This is first proven from the words of Aristotle in the first book of *On Generation*. Solving the question of how the miscible elements are in the mixture, he writes: "neither the one" (namely, being corrupted) "nor both" (are corrupted). "For they are preserved..." From these it is clear that the virtue of a thing is not the form of the thing, but the virtue of the miscibles is saved, because their form is not. Furthermore, in the same place he shows that barley is not mixed with wheat, and this is because their forms remain. Therefore, even when their forms remain, mixture does not occur. Moreover, Halienus <note>referring to Averroes, often cited as the Commentator</note> in the first book of the *Prior Analytics* says: Aristotle thought that the elements were confused only by their qualities; therefore, this dogma is to be chosen because of its certainty, in that it preserves [the argument] from the inconvenient. There are many reasons for this, which we shall state, for we shall argue with Averroes. These are the positions and arguments of the Latins stated thus far.

### Arguments against the Second Sect. Chapter VII.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial P</note> The first sect (as has been seen) concedes that the qualities of the elements remain in the mixture, and that they are of the same species, asserting these are facts, not merely in being. But this is wonderful for many reasons. First, because Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* shows from his own intention that hard bodies cannot touch one another unless air or water intervenes; and surely by this reason: the surfaces of hard bodies are moist; therefore, water intervenes. He proves this, saying: "The moist is not without a body, nor is the moistened; but it is necessary that it be water or have water." The force of the argument, therefore, is that the surfaces of two bodies placed in water are moist; therefore, water intervenes, because the moist cannot be without water or air. In the same way I argue: in the mixture there is heat; therefore, there is fire. There is moisture; therefore, air. There is coldness; therefore, water. There is dryness; therefore, earth. These consequences hold by the force of Aristotle's reason that no quality is without its proper body. To whom Simplicius, a very serious man, says: Why did Aristotle say "but it is necessary that it be water or have water"? He answers: "To the moist, which is water; but it is referred to the moistened, [which] has it." And thus he means that every simple moist thing is aqueous, and everything moistened has water. But the mixture is moistened; therefore, it is necessary for it to have water. Themistius in the same place writes thus: "And it is manifest to you that [regarding] bodies, some moisture is always surrounding and adhering, not so that it can be [the case] that two solid bodies touch each other by chance in water." The force of the argument is therefore: hard bodies are well moistened; therefore, water intervenes, because it cannot happen well in anything without water. From these it is clear that there cannot be a formally elemental moisture in anything unless water is formally there. It is more necessary, however, to say according to Alexander of Aphrodisias, who in the second book of *On Sense* plainly writes that the first qualities are the substantial forms of the elements. Wherefore, if there are four qualities in a mixture, it is that there are four elemental forms there, which (as he says) are in the mixture like burning embers. Second, principally Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens* says: "Since of bodies, some are simple, others are composite, and those..." and he does not speak about virtues according to qualities or virtues, which he clarifies in the fifth [book]: "I call simple those which have the first movement according to nature." As if explaining more, he writes: "such as fire and earth and their species and things related to them." Behold how he posits that mixtures are formally composed from these; and he clarifies this more by what he writes underneath: "For it is necessary to be moved; these [are] simple, but these [are] mixed in some way. Of the simple, simple [movements]; but of the mixed, composite [movements]." Now there cannot be a mixture of movements unless there is a mixture of the principle of movements. If, therefore, the mixture moves with a mixed movement, then the principle of movement will also be mixed; and what he will say more: if the principle will be mixed, then it would be no more the movement of one than the other, and thus the mixture would not move naturally downward more than upward. He answers that the movement is mixed from upward and downward motion (but to be moved according to the predominant). He says that that movement is mixed from the predominance [and] leans toward the place of the element predominant in the mixture. From these it is clear that the elements are in the mixture by some act. Otherwise, these things would have been superfluous; if he wanted to explain otherwise, it would not be what he explains with all his strength. Third, principally, the gravity of the mixture is of the same species as the gravity of the element; therefore, in the mixture is the substantial form of the heavy element. Aristotle concedes [this], for he proves [it]; for gravity concludes the form of the element. Otherwise, Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens* would not conclude [the existence of] the four simple bodies. For we would say there is something heavy, not because of a simple body, for he does not grant a simple heavy [body]...
