Auerroes in primo auscultationis physice. comento. 69. ex propria intentione sumit omne adveniens enti in actu esse accidens: quod si intelligis perfecto: non habet intentum contra quicunque. nam forma corporis est in potentia confusa et valde imperfecta. Lirca has dictiones debes scire quod forma substantialis potest dupliciter considerari: vel in ratione disponentis: vel in ratione perficientis. Dispositio disponens ad ulteriorem formam est vel confusa et generica. ut forma corporis: vel remissa ut forma elementaria. Similiter omnis forma perficiens: vel est perfecta: vel intensa: ut forme elementarie intense. Ex quo sequitur primo contra auicennam: quod si forme elementarie non remittuntur in mixto. tunc omne adveniens est accidens. nam si non remittuntur: non sunt specifice. sed perficientes: et omne adveniens post esse perfectum est accidens. Sequitur secundo quod si in mixto sunt remisse: sunt ibi ut dispositiones non ut perficientes: sicque non omne adveniens erit accidens. Secundo debes scire: quod ista forma: et pars forme sint eiusdem rationis inter se separate: non tamen respectu tertii. Nam quantum ad esse disponens habent vel perficiens habent diversas rationes: et sic respectu tertii differunt ratione. Nam si capiatur substantia esse perfecto perficiere sub ratione una. Si sub esse disponens sortiatur rationem aliam: et sic differunt ratione. Sic non potest dici de qualitate respectu forme elementarie. nam qualitas est vel essentialis propria elementi: vel proprium accidens: modo in eis que sunt eiusdem essentialitatis: quicquid competit uni competit et reliquo. ita enim est tota qualitas essentialis toti forme: sicut pars parti: ut auerroes docet. secundo de anima. Quare si potest forma esse sine parte propria: et sine toto esse poterit: cum totus et pars sint eque essentiales forme. Modo forma perfecta elementaria: et pars eius non sunt eiusdem essentialitatis respectu materie: et propterea non oportet si materia per partem disponatur: quod per totam formam etiam disponatur: sed quo modo valeat ratio auerrois contra quicunque: posterius dicemus. Nunc vero satis sit tollere in dictis eius contradictionem. Per hoc ablate sunt repugnantie: cum nam dicit Auerroes unum sub non posse habere nisi unam formam: intelligit de perficiente: cum vero dicebat parte forme et totam esse eiusdem rationis: iam diximus verum esse: eis consideratis inter se non respectu materie. Et diximus non esse ita in qualitatibus elementariis. Cum etiam adducebatur verbum eius in primo auscultationis physice: iam diximus illud verbum esse intelligendum post adventum forme perficientis: secus autem est post adventum forme disponentis: et hoc modo possunt solui omnes auctoritates Aristotelis. et Auerrois alibi. si infinite essent. Ex his perspicua est differentia inter formas accidentales et substantiales. Nam substantialis recipitur in materia prima subiective: is dispositio possit recipi etiam in ente in actu. accidentalis vero recipit solum in ente in actu perfecto. secundo perspicuum quomodo generatio est transmutatio totius in totus nullo sensibili remanente. ut primo perygeneseos scribit Aristoteles. hoc enim. (ut Auerroes scribit ibidem in paraphrasi eiusdem verbi. comento. 24.) verum erit pro quanto nihil remanet in materia: quod sit subiectum essentialiter ei in quod est transmutatio: et principaliter materia est subiectum generationis. subiective autem aliarum transmutationum non est materia nisi remote. Intellige ergo nullo sensibili remanente. ut subiecto principali: sed remanente ut dispositione nihil prohibet. sicque ablate sint difficultates auerroys ex eius dictis.

Secunda etiam non valet. nam natura in fieri et transmutari servat ordinem: sed in perfici et facto non servat ordinem. Quando igitur natura ex elementis facit mixtum servat ordinem in transmutatione. non autem in perficiendo. Nam forma mixti potest ita imediate perficere materiam; sicut forma elementi: si non sit in fieri et transmutari. secunda ratio nulla. Sed viri stoicizantes (pace eorum) non recte revolverunt volumina Aristotelis. Nam ista definitio quinti metaphysice competat materie: competit etiam omni cause materiali: etiam elemento: et partibus: et ceteris. ut materia acceptis. Et quod ita sit: lege verba Aristotelis 3. celi: quicunque inquit. Sit itaque elementum corporum ad

<margin>

</margin>

quod alia corpora dividuntur intus existens potentia aut actu. hoc enim vero modo: adhuc dubitabile. ipsum autem individuibile in altera specie. tale autem est elementum omne. In his verbis unum habemus perspicuum. scilicet. elementum manere in re: et per consequens quod definitio elementi competit quattuor corporibus. Alterum dubium utrum maneat actu vel potentia: nec Auerroys per illud primum argumentum intendit probare elementa remanere in mixto. ut quidam male sentiunt: immo vult quod per corruptionem figure non corrumpatur penitus: ita ut nec actu: nec potentia maneat: quia sic perderet rationem materie et elementi. Per illud igitur argumentum Auerroes non vult probare: nisi quod elementum penitus non corrumpatur: quia saltem debeat remanere. ut sit pars mixti actu: vel potentia: et hoc non tantum dicit Auerroes. sed aristoteles. errant ergo in primo: quia credunt Auerroem per illud probare elementa remanere in actu: et non est ita. Circa secundam Auerroes supponit duo quod fieri essentialiter ordinatur ad factum: et transmutari ad mutatum esse: et hec est intentio Aristotelis. sexto physice auscultationis. Ponunt secundo fieri et factum ita se habere: quod quicquid est de essentia: et essentialiale uni: et essentiale debeat esse alteri. Nam si fieri est de essentia facti: et omne essentiale ipsi fieri erit essentiale facto. his duobus acceptis: ratio Auerroys tenet. Nam si natura essentialiter servat ordinem in fieri: cum fieri sit propter factum: et in facto debet servare ordinem: quare si elementa sunt partes factionis: erunt partes facti esse. Secundo potest hec ratio Auerroys confirmari. Nam fieri est factum incompletum. motus enim et terminus motus sunt unius speciei: et non differunt nisi penes perfectum et imperfectum. ut traditur quinto physice auscultationis. comento nono. ergo quicquid est essentiale uni est alteri non repugnans et essentiale. ergo si ordo est de essentia transmutationis. erit etiam de essentia perfectionis. Tertio dispositiones fuerunt inducte propter factum: tanquam propter ultimum finem: sed adveniente fine ultimo: non debent corrumpi media: que fuerunt propter illum finem: immo perficiuntur. aliter conarentur ad terminum non in futurum peruenturum. ergo frustra. Multe alie possunt esse rationes confirmantes rationem Auerroys. sed hec satis sunt. Nec de rationibus eius.

## §. VII.

No less weighty are those reasons which are brought forward for the negative side of our problem, and which suggest that the crimes of the intoxicated should rather be punished more severely and harshly than those of the sober. And to begin, no one of sound mind will dispute that drunkenness is the foulest of all vices, inasmuch as it is seriously forbidden by divine law as the tinder of all evils, which is apparent from Isaiah 5:11, Hosea 4:11, Sirach 19:2, Luke 21:34, Ephesians 5:18, and very many other places in Holy Scripture. Doctorum communiter suffragio ex modo considerandi prodit, quod subjectum scientiae adequetur, & una scientia ab alijs distinguatur: scientiae autem quae communem accipiunt denominationem, communem etiam considerandi modum habeant necesse est.

*1° (Cum Astronomia, omnium recte sentientium calculo Mathematica dicatur, ut pote Geometriae subalternata, sicut rem consideratam, ita & considerandi modum nisi Mathematicum nequit habere.*

*2 Quare motum circa medium qua tale, a propria contemplatione Astronomica excludendum tuemur: & quae de eo ab Astronomo dicuntur, a Physico omnia mutuari affirmamus.*

*3 Nihil igitur nostro judicio inconsulto magis dici potest, quam asserere corpus caeleste mobile circa medium qua tale, vel motum ut mensurabilis est, vel denique magnitudinem ut mobilis est circa medium, subjectum esse Astronomiae; quandoquidem sic dicentes, vel in re considerata, vel in modo considerandi, vel in utroque, errorem errant manifestum.*

*4 Quinetiam penitius conditionem & naturam scientiae subalternatae intro-spicientes, dicamus subjectum Astronomiae, esse magnitudinem mobilem circa medium, qua magnitudo est.*

*5 Quare motus tantum ut accidens sensile rei considerata adjectum considerabitur; interim putamus totam Astronomiae considerationem propriam, ad solius quantitatis cognitionem referri.*

*6 Considerabit igitur Astronomus motum, magnitudinem, & figuram, quae sunt affectiones & termini corporum naturalium, verum tantum ut in ijs rationes quaedam Mathematicae (ut est ratio majoris minoris, aequalis inaequalis, distantis propinqui, proportionalitatis & ejusmodi) reperiuntur; cum Physicus omnia referat ad naturam unde fluere intelliguntur.*

*7 Ut non sit mirum pro hac diversitate, nonnunquam (ut 2. Phys. cap. 2.) dixisse Philosophum Astrologiam a motu abstrahere, nonnunquam vero (1. Metaphys. text. 19.) cum motu, imo etiam ipsum motum considerare.*

4 Cum una eademque linea recta ex minore circulo majorem portionem auferat; ex majore vero minorem; sequitur idem vas majorem copiam aque in inferiore loco, quam in superiore recipere. 17 It is the property of the tactile organ to be constituted in the middle and temperament of its proper object. 2. <italic>On the Soul</italic>, text 118.
1 It perceives only excesses and defects. Ibidem.
2 Similarly, the tempered cannot be perceived by touch. Ibid.
3 Is there, then, no tangible thing that cannot be touched?

18 The temperament is diverse not only in diverse bodies, but also in the parts of the same body, indeed even of the same part at a different time.
1 Hence it is that the same tepid water is felt differently by different men at the same time, or by the same person differently affected but at distinct times, and is felt as both hot and cold.
2 There is no tangible thing given that cannot be touched simply: if not by one part, then by another of the same body: if by none of one body, then by some other of another by necessity.

19 The illumination of the agent intellect is the formal reason of the object as intelligible in actuality, just as light is the reason of the visible in actuality.
1 It does not act on the patient <note>passive recipient</note> by itself, but as it is joined with the phantasm.
2 Therefore, there is no action of the agent intellect on the patient (if we speak of its illumination) that is different from the action of the illuminated phantasm on the same. Just as there is no other action of light as it is the act of color than the action of color on the eye.
3 It is not poorly said by some that the agent intellect does not act so much as an intelligent being, but as an intelligible one.
4 The proper action of the agent intellect will therefore be nothing other than to effect, for the benefit of its illumination, that the phantasms of various things which it encompasses in itself impress various species upon the patient intellect, and thus render the potentially intelligible things intelligible in actuality.
5 Its action is therefore twofold: one improperly so called with respect to the phantasm, which it perfects as a habit; the other more proper with respect to the patient intellect, on which it acts together with the phantasm, as an object in actuality acts on a knowing faculty.

20 The mere illumination of the phantasm does not make something be understood in actuality, but besides that, a judgment of the phantasm by the intellect is required.
1 The agent intellect not only illuminates, but also judges the received species.
2 So that this third is a certain action of its own perfecting intellection, through which it is said to act in itself through an immanent action, by judging the reception of the species in itself as its own proper receptacle.
3 From this it appears that all those who think the patient intellect is sufficient in itself to judge are commonly mistaken: for although this may be true as regards the substance, which is one of the agent and patient, yet as regards the office, it cannot be true.

Sepulchers are not called <term>בתי מתים</term> <gloss>houses of the dead</gloss>, but <term>בתי חיים</term> <gloss>houses of the living</gloss>, because namely the Bodies of the Pious in the Sepulchers, as if in their own little beds and couches, rest not dead, but given to sleep.

## EPILOGUE.

§. XIIX. Nothing now remains, unless we demonstrate that the Rite, concerning which we have hitherto dealt, also left some trace of itself in *Antiquity & Ecclesiastical History*, which Calixtus the Elder denies *L. on the Resurrection of the Flesh, p. 55.* We presuppose, however, that that *Rite* was not *universal*, or of *all Christian Churches*; but only *particular, of one or another Church*, for example the Corinthian; and it was not at *all times*, but *in the time of Paul*, and finally not in *every administration of Baptism*, but *observed peculiarly by at least some Pious ones*. Therefore it ought to seem a wonder to no one that the writers of *Ecclesiastical History* did not mention this *Rite* completely. For then without a doubt that custom of baptizing over the dead came into *desuetude*. Yet it is certain from *Antiquity* that, since it was not permitted to the first Worshipers of the Christian Faith, on account of the immense and continuous persecutions of the enemies of the Church, such as the *Neronian* [persecution] in the time of Paul, to have *Sacred Buildings* where they could administer their *Sacred Rites*, they were accustomed to gather in *Cemeteries*, which Onuphrius shows in a more detailed manner in his own book on *Cemeteries*. For the *use of Cemeteries* (says Baronius, *Volume II. Annals to the Year of Christ 130*) *was not only useful for burying the bodies of the deceased, from which also the name was given, but also in the time of persecution, for the hiding-places of Christians.* And the Magdeburgensians, *Century IV, c. 6. on Rites and Ceremonies, folio 407*, record it thus: *But if it was not permitted for Christians to frequent Temples either on account of persecutions, or they were abandoned for some other necessary reason, they gathered in Cemeteries, and places outside the cities: just as they did in the persecution under Valens at Antioch, where Christians held meetings outside the city walls at the roots of the mountains.* Theodoret *Lib. IV. c. 24.* And *in the persecution under George at Alexandria, where when the Adversaries, prevailing in piety, held the Temples, and Christians were forced to flee their company, they gathered in Cemeteries for prayer*, Theodoret *Lib. XXI. c. 14.* What is more, Lord Chrysostom says in *Homily XL to the People*: *that some lived in Monuments and Sepulchers*.

§. XIIX. Nil jam restat, nisi ut demonstremus etiam, Ritum, de quo hactenus egimus, in *Antiquitate & Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ* vestigium aliquod sui reliquisse, quod negat Calixtus Senior *L. de Resurrect. Carn. p. 55.* Praesupponimus verò, *Ritum* illum non fuisse *universalem*, seu *omnium Ecclesiarum Christianarum*; sed duntaxat *particularem, unius vel alterius Ecclesiae*, verbi gratia Corinthiacae; neque fuisse *omnibus temporibus*, sed *tempore Pauli*, nec denique in quâvis *Baptismi administratione*, sed *à quibusdam saltim Piis peculiariter observatum*.. Mirum ergò cui videri non debet, *Historiae Ecclesiasticae* Scriptores hujusce *Ritûs* ex asse non meminisse.. Tum enim procul dubio in *desuetudinem* venit mos ille super mortuis baptizandi. Id tamen ex *Antiquitate* constat, quod, cùm primis Fidei Christianae Cultoribus ob immanes continuasque hostium Ecclesiae persecutiones, qualis erat tempore Pauli *Neroniana*, non liceret *Aedes Sacras* habere, ubi *Sacra* administrare sua possent, in *Caemeteriis* convenire fuerint soliti, quod prolixioribus ostendit Onuphrius, proprio de *Caemeteriis* Libello. *Caemeteriorum* namque *usus* (inquit Baronius *Tomus II. Annal. ad Ann. Chr. 130.*) *non modò inserviebat humandis defunctorum corporibus, ex quo & nomen est inditum, sed & persecutionis tempore, ad latebras Christianorum.* Et Magdeburgenses *Centuria IV. c. 6. de Ritibus & Ceremoniis folio 407.* ita recensent : *Quod si Templa aut propter persecutiones frequentare Christianis non liceret, aut aliâ quâdam necessariâ ratione desererentur, in Caemeteriis, & Locis extra urbes conveniebant : quemadmodum fecerunt in persecutione sub Valente Antiochiae, ubi extra urbis moenia ad radices montium Christiani conventus agebant.* Theodoretus *Lib. IV. c. 24.* Et *persecutione sub Georgio Alexandriae, ubi cùm Adversarii, pietatem praevalentes, Templa obtinerent, eorumque conjunctionem Christiani fugere cogerentur, in Caemeteriis ad orationem conveniebant*, Theodoretus *Lib. XXI. c. 14.* Quid quod Dominus Chrysostomus *Homil. XL. ad Populum* dicat : *quosdam in Monumentis & Sepulcris habitasse*.

Extrema quod spectat liberalitatis, in excessu opposi-

## XI.

**Avaritia** (ab aveo dicta, quia avarus æris est avidus,) contra vitium est, quo in nimium accipiendo retinendoque modum excedimus, nullâ habita ratione justitiæ aut honestatis, vel (ut *Philosophus* vult) malum est insanabile et inextinguibilis pecuniarum sitis. Furto etenim, rapina, usura, fraude, perjurio, mendacio, aliisque sexcentis injustis modis rapit et corradit, quæ rapere et corradere modò potest. Quare ut vix ullum avaritiâ deterius est vitium; ita avaro nihil est scelestius. Sed et hæc à nonnullis Ethicis in *simplicem* distingui solet et *compositam*. *Simplex* est, quæ dando deficit, sine αὐξήσει excessu, vel quæ accipiendo excedit sine δόσει defectu. *Composita*, quæ et dando deficit et accipiendo modum excedit. Hæc omnium audit pessima. Ad priorem pertinere dicitur φειδωλία nimia parsimonia: ad posteriorem ars furandi, lenonia, fœneratoria, aleatoria, et omnis illa quæ aliis indebito surripit modo, *Vide Adrianum Heereboord Collegium Ethicum pagina 94..*

## XII.

Cæterùm **Prodigalitatem** minus esse vitiosam magisque adversari liberalitati quàm avaritiam, diversis ex Philosophorum rationibus probant auctores; Avarorum quidem nostro hoc seculo plena sunt omnia, qui ne nummulum quidem conferant, si vel captum in Turcia fratrem liberare eodem possent. Nec desunt prodigi, qui ad explendas libidines vel montes profunderent Persicos, qui toti sunt aurei. Nullus horum meretur laudem, sive enim illud sive hoc fiat, à recto virtutis disceditur tramite, et mediocritas, de qua in definitione dictum, violatur. Instituta tamen collatione inter prodigum et avarum, hunc prodigo esse deteriorem manifestè apparebit. Etenim tenacius

To these must be added all those who, struggling to reach the pinnacle of honor through benefits or largesse, render themselves unworthy of the title of liberal men. Indeed, benefits are not to be given merely so that we may be freed from the importunity of those who ask; such things do not shine as a benefit, but are sullied by vice.

### IIX.

But the giver, studious in maintaining proper methods, should not pour out gifts rashly or without judgment, nor should they cast benefits indiscriminately upon the unworthy or the worthy. Benefits, if you remove judgment, cease to be benefits and fall under some other name, says Seneca in the first book of *On Benefits* <note>original: "De Beneficiis"</note>. Therefore, to avoid rashness, let the giver consider both his own condition and that of the recipient. Once equipped with the ability to give, let him confer the benefit without annoyance and with a certain joy of spirit; for that which is done from virtue is removed from pain and distress. Let him give with a ready mind and in a timely manner, where help can be provided; for to give quickly increases a benefit, whereas giving slowly diminishes it. Let him give only as much as his resources can bear. For liberality is to be estimated not by the size of the gift, but by the readiness of the giver. The liberal person should not give in a place where he might show himself off while the other is put to shame, nor in the presence of those who might reproach the recipient or insult the giver. For in this way, a benefit is rendered unwelcome. Finally, he should also have care for the recipient, so that he does not cast pearls before swine without discrimination. Yet, where he encounters the wicked who are in extreme need, and whom he hopes will return to a better life, he should not entirely close the doors of liberality, but should consider giving to the humanity and not to the man <term>τρόπῳ ἀλλὰ ἀνθρώπῳ</term> <gloss>not to the character [of the individual], but to the human [being]</gloss>, since extreme poverty compensates for the dignity of the needy person.

Sed Modi servandi studiosus dator, non temerè aut absqve judicio munera effundat & promiscue in indignos dignosvé beneficia projiciat. Habilitate instructus ad dandum, absque molestia & cum animi quadam jucunditate beneficium conferat; ex virtute enim quod fit à dolore remotum est & molestia. Animo det promto & tempestivè, ubi succurri potest; citò namque dare beneficium auget, tardè minuit. Det tantum, quantum ferre facultates possunt. Liberalitas qvippe non doni magnitudine, sed donantis æstimanda promtitudine. Non det liberalis loco quo ipse se ostentet, alter pudefiat, nec coram illis qui accipienti exprobrent aut danti insultent. Sic enim ingratum redditur beneficium. Denique accipientis etiam habeat curam, ne gemmas sine discrimine porcis objiciat. And in his seals he bears not the double-headed eagle but the simple one (Freherus in *Notes to Peter de Andlo*, treatise *on the Roman Empire*, book 2, chapter 5).

### XXI.

That is called into controversy: If three have elected a fourth from the number of Electors, can the elected consent to his own election, and increase the number with his own vote? And the affirmative opinion is founded on the § at the end here, in law 4, *Digest: What of each university* by name, chapter 33, *extra de Electione*. The reason is because he is not elected by himself, but by his co-electors, and while he increases the number, he follows not his own judgment but that of his colleagues (Cavalcanti, book 1, *Decision* 40, number 23). Thus, Louis the Bavarian is deservedly to be excused, who did not keep the faith given to Frederick, Duke of Austria, in his own election (Cuspinianus, *On the Division of the Empire between two competitors*), because in a promise the person of the speaker is understood to be exempted, since ordered charity begins from oneself (final chapter, *Distinction* 86, law 6, *Code on Servitudes and Water*).

### XXII.

Clearly, if the power of electing is committed to one, with six Electors conferring it upon that one man—as happened in the election of Adolph of Nassau, where the Archbishop of Mainz obtained all the votes by marvelous cunning (Cuspinianus in the life of Adolph)—or if that power falls to him while the others are emanating, he cannot elect himself (final chapter, *extra on Institutions* by argument of the § at the end here, where it is required that if anyone wishes to consent to his own Election, three must elect him). And indeed, such an election would be ambitious (Innocent in the said chapter 33, number 1, *extra de Electione*; Cavalcanti, said *Decision* 40, number 8). For while he thinks himself worthy of the Empire by domestic praise, he betrays a disease of the mind, by which he considers himself more excellent than all. To covet the primacy of honor is vanity, for they desire him who flees, they burden him who desires; and Innocent rightly says in the said chapter 33, he ought to presume others to be good, but in himself acknowledge blame where there is no blame (final chapter at the end, *Distinction* 5, final chapter *extra on Presumption*).

### XXI.

Illud in controversiam vocatur: Si tres elegerint quartum à numero Electorum, an electus in sui electionem consentire, & sua voce numerum augere possit? Et Affirmativa sententia fundatur in §. fine hic, in lege 4. Digestum Quod cujusque universitate nomine capite 33. extra de Electione. Ratio est, quia non eligitur à se, sed coelectoribus, dumque numerum auget, non suum sed Collegarum sequitur judicium, Cavalcanti libro 1. Decisione 40. numero 4. Ut meritò excusandus sit Ludovicus Bavarus, qui fidem Friderico Austriæ Duci datam, in sui ipsius electione non servavit, Cuspinianus de Divisione Imperii inter duos competitores. quia in promissione persona loquentis exempta intelligitur, cum ordinata charitas à seipsa incipiat. capite finale Distinctione 86. lege 6. Codice de Servitutibus & Aqua.

### XXII.

Plane si uni commissa est eligendi potestas, sex Electoribus eam in unum illum conferentibus, ut factum in electione Adolphi Nassoviensis, ubi miro astu omnia vota consecutus est Moguntinus. Cuspinianus in vita Adolphi. aut si ea potestas in illum cæteris emanentibus recidat, is seipsum eligere nequit. capite finale extra de Institutionibus argumento §. fine hic, ubi requiritur, ut si quis velit in sui Electionem consentire, tres ipsum elegerint. Et sanè ambitiosa esset electio, Innocentius in dicto capite 33. numero 1. extra de Electione. Cavalcanti dicto Decisione 40. numero 8. Dum enim te Imperio dignum domestico elogio existimat, animi morbum, quo se cunctis præstantiorem existimat, prodit. Primatus honoris concupiscere vanitas est, fugientem enim se desiderant, desiderantem onerant, & rectè ait Innocentius in dicto capite 33. alios præsumere debet esse bonos, in se verò culpam agnoscere, ubi non est culpa, capite finale in fine Distinctione 5. capite finale extra de Presumtione.

### XXIII.

62. X. Visûs imbecillitas hîc accidit humoribus et spiritibus visioni dicatis permixtis cum vaporibus elevatis: tùm exsiccatione propter vacuationem nimiam.

63. XI. Convulsio, huic malo satis familiaris, sed præ reliquis omnibus maximè extimescenda, hîc oboritur partim propter purgantis venenatam qualitatem; partim ob vellicationem nervosi et musculosi generis, ab humoribus acribus, corruptis, malignis, agitatione in vaporem et flatum resolutis.

64. XII. Febris accenditur tùm ratione medicamenti inflammantis, tùm separatione frigidorum humorum; tùm etiam ob continuas vigilias, animi affectus, dolores, et cetera huic malo supervenientes.

65. XIII. Imbecillitas tandem atque lassitudo totius corporis, utilium humorum nimiam profusionem, spirituum et virium resolutionem sequitur.

66. His omnibus malis communes sunt errores rerum non naturalium tempore purgationis commissi, de quibus *Mesue libro citato.*

67. Signa causarum omnia eo recensere ordine, quo ipsas tractavimus causas, supervacaneum, et propter tautologiam odiosum foret; cùm in genere omnes ad ipsam purgantis rationem, corporis singularem dispositionem, et humorum conditionem reduci queant: duo quidem priora relatione ægri et Medici (si errorem fateri velit) patefiunt; humores autem cùm excernuntur, semetipsos produnt odore, colore, substantiâ, mordicatione, calfactione, et cetera in exitu.

68. *Partis generantis et mittentis vitia noscuntur propriis signis. Totum si*

36. In quantity; for the sake of which the action of the medicines is protracted, but humors create greater molestation for the body due to their abundance and weight. See Galen *3 on Natural Faculties, 13*; Mesue *Canon, Intention 3, chapter 3*. They become copious for the stated causes; but most of all because they are retained against the order of nature.

37. And such superpurgations, which are made by the nature of the humors' abundance and depraved quality rather than by the irritated force of the medicine, and are as it were certain critical evacuations, if especially Diarrhea is in the offing, it is very probable that they happen more often even with a light medicine given: and we have as a witness of this thing Fernelius, who in *book 3 of the Method of Healing, chapter 10*, writes thus: A copious humor, and as it were stagnating, as in the obese, and in those who have gorged themselves with gluttony, or for any reason have collected a flood of humors, is poured out by a light medicine with usually a great disturbance of the belly. For with the veins opened, the abundance flows out spontaneously as if from a perforated cask, not by the unbridled force of the medicine, but by the strength of Nature unloading itself, which sometimes without any irritation, but by its own impetus, deposits and throws off that burden.

38. Finally, as an adjuvant cause, one may add the sense of the part, whether by nature or by ulceration, Galen *3 on the Causes of Symptoms, 2*, whether it be such absolutely, or relatively to the body, which is easily purged, and an unproportionate object.

39. The other cause, for which the retentive faculty of the vessels is damaged by accident, is traction. It happens in four ways. I. By heat. Galen *On the Faculties of Simples, 5, chapter 17*. II. By pain. *Book 2 on the Differences of Fevers, chapter 11*. III. By the property of the purgative. IV. By flight of a vacuum or by the manner of succession. Galen *3 on Natural Faculties, chapter 15*. For with those humors that are in the offing flowing out first, the rest are carried to the emptied places by a certain following.

40. The causes of heat and pain, which indeed have a place here, can be gathered from what has been said. But that each of the purgatives attracts a humor familiar to itself, which although Hippocrates does not approve of in many places, as one who has not prophesied, with Galen thinking in *2 on Elements, 3* that there would be some Physician who would deny this: yet Galen himself, both elsewhere and in this place, demonstrates against Asclepiades with certain arguments: primarily, however, in the whole book *On the Faculties of Purgatives* and *book 5 on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, chapter 17*.

41. We omit other more remote causes, as they are also commonly known, by design. Mesue in the *Canon, Intention 3, chapter 3*, reduces all the stated causes to three; namely the condition of the medicine, of the patient, and of the non-naturals, which can be seen there.

<margin>Affected location.</margin>
42. From the explanation of these causes, the primarily affected location is easily detected. Indeed, it is manifest that the vessels, especially those which are around the mesentery and intestines, are subject to these actions for the greatest part according to their extremities, and Galen teaches that such an affection exists in the veins, *book 3 on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, chapter 27*.

<margin>Difference.</margin>
43. Thus far concerning the causes of superpurgation. We shall touch upon some differences at least. And first indeed by reason of form, or of discharge, which can be greater or lesser; swifter or slower; shorter or longer; because of the causes mentioned, whether more intense or remiss, the superpurgation itself also varies.

44. II. By reason of the excreted humors, certain degrees are as it were constituted, so that one <term>hyperkatharsis</term> <gloss>excessive purgation</gloss> is perfect, which according to Fallopius in the cited place leads to death on account of the profusion of blood, which even Hippocrates and Galen in the cited place seem to have proposed for asserting the quaternary number of Elements and humors: another is imperfect, which is of only one or another humor drawn out beyond the due quantity: and of this or that species, in the order which we stated above.

Ut quoque, qui late dominantur in orbe potentes,
    Quorum maiestas regia pondus habet.
Haud quicquam contra facientem tale loquentur,
    Audentes se non opposuisse Deo.
Sed potius posita frontis grauitate superbæ,
    Submittent famulo corda superba meo.
Agnoscentque humili venientem pectore CHRISTVM
    Præstantes animo non simulante fidem.
At non Iudæa populus de stirpe superstes,
    Solus cum sancta tam pietate colet.
Quin etiam quæ regna colunt exotica Gentes,
    Eius adorantes numina laude ferent.
Et fuit ante minus coeli quocunque sub axe
    Cognitus, aut verbi cultus amore sui.
Afficietur ibi solidæ pietatis honore.
    Quis sit, & ex verbo conspiciendus erit.
Namque nihil quarum de tantis venit ad aures,
    Ad quas non aliquis nuncius ista tulit.
Quæ virtute potens fauet meus omnia seruus,
    Consilij eximia dexteritate sui.
Accipiant animis hilares, lætique videbunt
    Gloria fit serui quanta futura mei.
Sed quis erit, faciles qui nobis præbeat aures,
    Et notum cupiat robur habere DEI?
Quos apud hæc unquam de tantis concio rebus,
    Quæso parem potuit promeruisse fidem?

When they come, they all seek the royal halls.
Behold, the father Suevus sat in the middle of the hall,
A yellow crown adorned his sacred head.
He held the royal scepters, the sign of empire,
Of which the Lemnian <note>Vulcan, the smith-god who worked on Lemnos</note> fire-master was the author.
Around him stood the rivers and the fountain deities,
To whom he uttered divine sounds from his mouth.
"Accept, O sons, you who hold the fish-filled rivers with me,
What chattering rumor brings to us.
Margrave Johann, the first progeny of Joachim the second,
Wounded by the arrow of Venus, is in love.
And now he desires, by destiny, to join to himself a bride
With the bond of marriage, a daughter of a magnanimous prince.
Therefore, act, O swift Nymphs, lead the Marchian kings
In purple, each in his own order.
So that the bridegroom, warned by the illustrious image, may follow
The deeds of the leaders who earned glory for us.
Meanwhile, rivers, with gathered gems,
Prepare golden gifts for the new bridegroom.
Such precious metal as the Ganges sends,
Or which the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia, said to have golden sands</note> carries as shining gifts."
The King of rivers, Spree, had scarcely spoken these words, when the Nymphs
Equipped with garments set about the work.
They take wools dyed in purple shellfish,
And add golden threads as an ornament to the gems.
They move their ready arms, taught the texture by Pallas <note>Athena, goddess of weaving</note>,
They weave with their fingers the Marchian lineage.

Sigismund, the Caesar to whom the Marchian scepters were given as a gift,
The first to whom they were given, worthy rewards for such a great Duke.
His virtue and the glory of war brought this to him,
While he was the famous governor of the city of Noridos <note>Likely a reference to Nuremberg</note>.

An undivided comrade, skillful Prudence,
May she serve your every future use in life:
Just as Tritonia <note>Minerva</note> was always present to great Achilles,
The same had clung to Tydides <note>Diomedes</note>, and through the waves and all

For prudence alone rescues great men from perils,
And repels threatening fates with her shield.
Prudence alone is the watchful ruler of all honor,
And the same is always the most faithful guardian of scepters.
If you can descend into the studies and customs of the people,
You will win every point; the people are fastidious and hateful,
They fall ill, they sometimes rage, but often they are burdened
By unjust bundles <note>fasces, symbols of magisterial power</note>, grieving under an unfair weight.

Let your first care be to inquire into the causes of the disease,

And you will easily manage it, nor will anything deceive you,
If you are gentle in your speech, and drink in the complaints
Of the praying people with an easy ear, nor with an unfair mind,

Augustine, in Epistle 86 to Cassulanus, is asked about a certain urbanite who taught that Saturday must be fasted by Apostolic tradition which the Romans observe. He condemns him because he had torn the entire Church from the rising of the sun to its setting, and sighing, he exclaims: Alas, the Roman Church today observes too much that the Apostles did not hand down. The same [author], in Epistle 119 to Januarius, says that the Christian religion, which the mercy of God wished to be free with very few and most manifest celebrations of the sacraments, is so pressed by servile burdens that the condition of the Jews, who were subject to the ceremonies of Moses and human laws, would be more tolerable than that of Christians now is. And Saint Thomas repeats this complaint on chapter 23 of the Gospel of Matthew and adds: O most holy father, if you were living now, what would you say? signifying that many traditions have been added after the times of Augustine. From these [facts] it is manifest that the perpetual consensus of the Church is not placed in unwritten traditions.

### THEOREMA IV.
#### De termino extrinseco infiniti.

Expendimus præcipuas proprietates illius infiniti consistentis in quantitate, vel in numero, quas omnes Recentior ille acutissimus Infiniti scrutator tota quæstione prima undecim articulis examinavit : quare tantùm obiter indicavimus, quæ ille prius fusius detexit; sed quia iis, quæ in rem suam faciunt tantùm, contenti non sumus, distinguamus amplioribus verbis duplicem infiniti terminum, unum intrinsecum, alterum extrinsecum.

Conclusio 1. Terminus intrinsecus est, qui pertinet ad ipsam infiniti constitutionem, ita ut quocunque termino sublato, ipsum infinitum non remaneret; talis verò terminus intrinsecus ex utraque parte repugnat infinito propter absurdas, quas secum trahit sequelas.

Conclusio 2. Terminus extrinsecus est, quo scilicet, et quocunque termino sublato, adhuc remaneret infinitum : hujusmodi terminus est verbi gratia visio beatifica, cùm enim sint possibiles plures et plures creaturæ sine fine, ea cognitio erit perfectior, quæ plures aut pauciores creaturas repræsentabit, ergo sunt possibiles cognitiones perfectiores et perfectiores, quæ versentur circa plures creaturas, nulla tamen ex istis cognitionibus æquabit perfectionem visionis beatificæ; ergo in illa collectione infinitarum cognitionum perfectiorum et perfectiorum visio beatifica erit terminus extrinsecus, illâ enim subtractâ adhuc illa collectio retinet infinitatem. Et pariter subtractis omnibus aliis terminis ex illa parte, si enim velis assignari posse post visionem beatificam immediate aliam cognitionem perfectissimam reliquarum, et sic deinceps adhuc sublatis omnibus terminis istis, remanet infinita illa collectio, quæ complectitur solas cognitiones tendentes in individua creaturarum finita plura et plura sine termino, inter has enim

<column-break/>

cognitiones non datur suprema et ultima, ergo semper est invenire aliquam infinitatem, ad cujus complementum non sint necessarii omnes illi termini ex parte superiori. Et sic possunt dici termini extrinseci, et non intrinseci in constitutione Infiniti, quà Infinitum est. Hinc solvitur argumentum illorum, quo cum Durando evincere se posse existimabant, repugnantiam specierum creaturarum perfectiorum et perfectiorum in infinitum. Non enim (ut ipsi supponunt) inter illas species daretur ultima, penultima, et cetera haberet equidem terminum extrinsecum, nempe Deum, non autem terminum intrinsecum in sensu superius explicato.

Hoc Theorema de infinito capaci termini extrinseci, sed non intrinseci, non obiter tantum animadvertendum est, cùm ex eo pendeat tota quæstio de quantitate, et multa ex eo dilucidiùs explanentur, et faciliùs percipiantur. Hinc enim solvitur argumentum, alioquin difficile, quod fieri solet contra infinitum, seu actuale seu objectivum in mente Dei, supposita infinita divisibilitate ipsius quantitatis et est hujusmodi.

Objection: First: Those things would not be absurd, namely, that infinite men having eaten enough would not, however, count more hairs than heads: Second: that if each of those men had one gold coin, and all the coins were thrown into one heap, then any of those men could take ten gold coins from that heap: for all these things would arise from the admirable property of the infinite: that each infinite can correspond to infinite other infinities: but they seem to make the opinion concerning the infinite ridiculous: therefore, etc. Answer: I grant the consequence of the major premise with the absurdity excluded: which Vasquez, <term>Compt.</term> <gloss>probably referring to a commentator or contemporary scholar</gloss>, Arriaga, and others deny less consequently, and as far as that case regarding the gold coins is concerned, and consequently to other similar ones which could be fabricated, it is necessary that this be granted by all in another equivalent case: for God could create one man every single year, and one gold coin throughout all eternity: in which case every man would be seen as having to have only one gold coin from God, and no more.

But indeed, could God create those same gold coins in such a way that in every year He would produce ten gold coins from those gold coins? Certainly, since those gold coins are infinite, they also contain infinite sets of ten gold coins, which sets of ten, produced successively, would correspond to the individual years of eternity. Imagine, then: that God assigns to each of those men being created through individual years, individual sets of ten gold coins, which sets of ten are created simultaneously with the men themselves. Then God will see that those same gold coins, which in the first distribution fell individually to individual men, could in the second distribution be taken away from each of those same men, with no addition having been made to the gold coins, or subtraction from the men.

we do not tolerate Timones among philosophers at all: just as we do not tolerate those who can be in all places at once: which Aelian writes that Pythagoras was able to do in his *Various Histories*. And although Cicero in Book 1 of *Duties* criticizes philosophers, whom Plato in Book 7 of the *Republic* says are just because they despise and account for nothing those things that most people vehemently seek and over which they are accustomed to fight among themselves, along with Plato: yet if we wish to judge truly, Plato spoke excellently and wisely. For an official who builds some structure does not deserve better of the Republic than a learned man who explains the doctrine of Religion, who shows what is just, what is shameful, what is useful, what is not, who reveals the nature of things, and shows the necessary remedies to men. Nay, Cicero himself in the same book grants leisure and vacation from managing the Republic to outstanding philosophers: which the laws also do: as is to be seen in Book 4, section 30, of the Digest *On Vacations and Excuses of Duties*. And he praises the practice of severe and grave men (who, when they could bear neither the vices of princes nor of subjects, withdrew into the fields) for the reasons by which they were impelled to do so. For poets write that justice, having left the cities, migrated first into the fields, and then, when it had been driven out from here as well, into heaven. Thus just men migrated to the fields, because they thought there were fewer bad examples and fewer vices there. And yet these solitary men did not cast off the care of their domestic affairs, as monks did.

Vtrique igitur obediendum est: quandiu scilicet magistratus tanquam inferior Dominus, non repugnat suis edictis superiori Domino Deo. Huc tota spectat obedientia Magistratui debita. Sic Heluetia, Deo fic inftigante, impium magistratum ex-cuffit. Vincentia quoque in Venetorum poteftatem venit, quòd Respub. in fcortatores non animaduerteret. Roma eiecti hac occafione Reges & Respub. mutata fuit in liberu ftatum. Rara dixi illa exempla, nec facilè imitanda, nifi Deo inftigante. <header>COMMENT. ON ACTS OF THE APOSTLES</header>

the patron of the cause from the assembly of the enemies, so that the adversaries can effect nothing more fatal. Christ rightly said in Matthew 28, "I will be with you even to the end of the world." And in Luke 12, "Do not fear, little flock." He describes a bright example of this matter here.

<margin>Proposition.</margin>
Proposition. That they were divinely liberated from a grave danger in an unusual way. We call the danger grave because it was brought by the greatest men, and those of the highest power; add that it looked toward death. Yet the manner <note>of their release</note> did not stand thus. Above in chapter 4, they were dismissed with threats added, and the leaders themselves hesitated, lifeless, as to what they should decide about them.

But here a liberating Angel is present divinely, so much so that the guards do not feel this, and having been dragged back to the assembly, they soon have Gamaliel as a defender. How these things eventually turn out, the matter itself will declare.

The whole history embraces almost these chapters: First, the double captivity. 2. The double liberation as well. 3. The remarkable defense of Peter, which indeed looks to the whole cause; but primarily to the death and resurrection of the Lord. 4. What Gamaliel does in this cause, and in what manner the Apostles are eventually dismissed.

We will weigh the captivity at present, and specifically these things: First, the imprisonment. 2. The miraculous liberation. 3. The attempts of the enemies before the matter was more fully known. 4. The perseverance of the enemies after the matter was known. We will treat these briefly.

<margin>Imprisonment of the Apostles</margin>
1. The imprisonment is grave, which can be recognized from this: First, from the authors. 2. From the driving cause. 3. From the act. The authors of the danger are the High Priest, whether he was Caiaphas, or Annas, or another, such as John, Alexander, and the like. These, while Christ was living among men, were capital enemies of sound doctrine; the same <note>men</note> also opposed the Apostles most atrociously everywhere. Therefore it is dangerous to join oneself to these, and it is to be feared lest, in whatever direction they urge dangers, there the true Church and piety might be. I say this is probable, because we see that this has happened for the most part. Therefore, let men fortify themselves not only with the protection of human authority, but of Divine scripture. For if they are severed, the pontificate remains an empty hypocrisy and an enemy of God.

To the high priest approach all who were with him, that is, the primary men, not unlike him in profession, authority, life, and morals; what kind they were, learn from this: it was the sect of the Sadducees. The reason why it opposed itself to Christ primarily was that they deny the resurrection, but the Apostles teach it, and produce the example of Christ. Concerning this sect, see Epiphanius.

<margin>What zeal signifies.</margin>
2. But from where did the cause of that counsel proceed? He indicates the matter thus: They were filled with zeal, that is, with anger, envy, a certain sinister emulation. Zeal sometimes signifies the just indignation of a good man, as in John 2: "Zeal for your house has consumed me," concerning Christ cleansing the temple. This anger is just; concerning which David <note>said</note>, "Be angry and do not sin." Otherwise <note>it signifies</note> a sinister emulation for a thing which we love to defend. Thus the Jews defended Moses and the law, although it had been abolished by Christ. Thus Paul to the Romans testifies that they have a zeal, but not according to knowledge. This zeal is called bitter by James in chapter 3. Otherwise it is simply called envy. 1 Corinthians 3: "When there is emulation among you, are you not carnal?" That anger is joined to it. The meaning therefore here is: Anger, and a certain envy against the Apostles, <note>held by</note> the learned Jews out of devotion to the Mosaic law.

<margin>Whence the envy of the High Priests toward the Apostles</margin>
Hence what is said <note>in Greek</note>, it boils, and physicians say that anger is a boiling over. Below in chapter 13, the Jews are seized with the same counsel.

They envy the new doctrine and the miracles, and they grieve that the law is being abolished and despised; for from this their trafficking also is diminished; hence those tears. Thus Herod is moved against Christ, Pharaoh against the children of Israel, Sennacherib against Jerusalem, because the contention is about leadership and the sum of things, for glory and dignity.

Hence that <note>expression</note>: For they did not sit until then; but he wishes to say that they were moved with the greatest zeal and effort to harm the Apostles.

3. The act: They lay hands <note>on them</note>; then they put them in public custody. Those who prevail over those whom they bring into their own power are said to lay hands on them. But the reason they are handed over to prison is that nothing was accomplished by threats above in chapter 4. Nothing <note>was accomplished</note> even by exclusion. They resort, therefore, to what is safer. Once imprisoned, they will not be able to teach. Below in chapters 12 and 16 you have the family <note>of the accounts</note>.

But why is the public prison chosen? The reason is that there they are either held more safely, or if any sedition arises from this among the faithful, it might look like a public sedition, so that they might be able to invoke the Roman garrison against them, which otherwise neglected causes of religion. They think, therefore, the Apostles are safer there, or if the crowd adhering to them attempts anything, it will look toward sedition. Hence Pilate will take note of them as seditious.

<margin>Liberation of the Apostles by an Angel.</margin>
II. Liberation follows. First consider here by whom they are liberated: By an Angel of the Lord. You see an unusual manner of liberation. Above they were liberated by another means, and below they will often be liberated by other means. An Angel serves them here. Matthew 4: they ministered to Christ. Luke 16: they carry the soul of Lazarus into the bosom of Abraham. Matthew 14: they are present to infants. Tobias has an Angel as a guide and guardian. Jacob likewise.

Hence it is said to the Hebrews 1 that they are ministering spirits, which is taken from Psalm 104. And otherwise also concerning the Angels.

Authores periculi sunt Pontifex, sive is Caiaphas fuerit, sive Annas, aut alius, qualis Ioannes Alexander, & similes. Periculum igitur est hisce sese coniungere, ac metuendum ne in quam partem illi urgent pericula, illic fit vera & Ecclesia & pietas. Probabile hoc dico, quia videmus ut plurimum id contigisse. Itaque muniane se homines non solùm praesidio humanae authoritatis: sed scripturae Divinae. Nam si dirimantur, pontificatus inanis manet hypocrisis & Dei hostis.

Pontifici accedunt omnes qui cum ipso erant, hoc est, viri primarij, non dissimiles ei professione, authoritate, vita & moribus: qui quales fuerint, hinc disce. Secta Sadducaeorum fuit. Cur illa se opposuerit Christo, imprimis ratio fuit, quòd hi negent resurrectionem, Apostoli autem eam doceant, & Christi exemplum producant. De hac secta vide Epiph.

<margin>Zelus quid significet.</margin>
2. Causa verò illius consilij, unde profecta est? Hac rem sic indicat. Repleti sunt zelo, hoc est, ira, invidia, sinistra quadam aemulatione. Zelus significat interdum boni viri iustam indignationem, vt Ioan. 2. Zelus domus tuae comedit me: de Christo repurgante templum. Haec ira iusta est: de qua David, Irascimini & nolite peccare. Alias sinistram aemulationem, pro re, quam amanater defendimus. Sic Iudaei defendebat Mosem, & legem, quamquam a Christo deleta esset. Sic Paulus ad Romanos. Testatur illos habere zelum, sed non secundum notitiam. Hic zelus dicitur amarus a Iacob. cap. 3. Alias simpliciter invidia dicitur. 1. Cor. 3. Cùm fit inter vos aemulatio, nonne carnales estis? Coniuncta est illa ira. Sensus igitur hic est, Ira, & quadam invidia contra Apostolos, doctos Iudaeos studio Mosaicae legis.

<margin>Vnde invidia Pōtificum in Apostolos</margin>
Hinc quod dicitur a, ebullio, & medici dicunt iram esse ebullitionem. Infra 13. eodem consilio rapiuntur Iudaei.

Inuident nouae doctrinae & miraculis, & dolent legem deleri, contemni: nam hinc illorum quoque nundinatio imminuitur: hinc illae lachrimae. Sic Herodes commouetur contra Christum, Pharao contra filios Israel, Sennacherib contra Ierolymam, quia contentio est de principatu, & rerum summa, pro gloria & dignitate.

Hinc illud a, Non enim fedit hactenus: sed dicere vult, summo studio & conatu laedendi Apostolos commotos esse.

3. Factum, Iniiciunt manus: deinde ponunt in publicam custodiam. Manus iniicere dicuntur qui praevalent his quos in suam redigunt potestatem. Quòd autem carceri mancipat hinc est, quòd minis nihil est effectum sup. 4. Nihil etiam exclusione. Confugiunt igitur ad tutius. Incarcerati non poterunt docere. Infra 12. & 16. familia habes.

Sed cur publicus deligitur carcer? Ratio est, quòd illic vel tutius detinentur: vel siquid seditionis hinc oriatur a fidelibus, spectet ad publicam seditionem, vt contra eos possint inuocare praesidium Romanum, quod alioquin causas religionis negligebat. Cogitant igitur, Ifthic tutiores sunt Apostoli, vel siquid conetur turba illis adhaerens, spectabit ad seditionem. Hinc in eos, vt seditiosos aduertet Pilatus.

II. Liberatio sequitur. Primum hic confidera, a quo liberentur. Ab Angelo Domini. Vides insolitum liberationem modum. Sup. alio medio liberati sunt, & infra saepe aliis liberabuntur mediis. Angelus hic illis inferuit. Matt. 4. ministrarunt Christo. Luc. 16. deportant Lazari animam in sinum Abrahae. Matt. 14. adfunt infantibus. Tobias Angelum ductorem & custodem habet. Iacob similiter.

Hinc dicitur ad Heb. 1. ministratorios esse Spiritus, quòd sumptu est ex psal. 104. Et alias etiam de Angelis.

擇滅者謂不由擇力緣缺所顯即實教菩薩以如實觀觀諸法性本自寂滅以立此名不動無為者謂第四禪離前三定三災不至無喜樂等動搖身心得不動名即五那含定受想滅無為者無所有處想受不行名受想滅無盡定此與不動皆屬二乘真如無為者理非倒妄不妄不變名為真如以遠離依他偏計此正唯識所證十種真如若依起信正是八識體中本覺及真如門乃對生滅之真如未盡一心故是相宗之極則此上百法乃總答云何一切法也下答云何為無我

言無我者略有二種一補特伽羅無我二法無我此二無我直顯一心之源也蓋我法二執有麤有細麤者名分別我法二執細者名俱生我法二執此二種執始從凡夫外道二乘歷三賢十聖直至等覺方纔破盡此二執即一心名為佛今此二無我則麤細皆在此中補特伽羅云數取趣謂諸有情數數起惑造業名為能取當來五趣名為所取此蓋就凡夫所執分別五蘊假我及

外道所執之神我以取分段生死之苦者而言也其實二乘所執蘊即離我及涅槃我與地上菩薩未破藏識七地已前俱未離俱生我以取變易生死之微苦者今論中但說凡夫分別之我未及聖人蓋就相宗一往所談其實佛意以聖教量之法皆破之方極大乘之義也法無我者謂我所執之法也凡夫法執身心世界六塵所執外道所執妄想涅槃二乘所執偏空涅槃菩薩所執真如論云現前立物謂是唯識性以有所得故非實住唯識以有證得是為微細法執所謂向起貪著是謂微細法執此執未空故未盡異熟倘屬因果直至金剛道後異熟空時即入果海即起信云菩薩地盡覺心初起心無初相遠離微細念故得見心性究竟是則按此百法前九十四乃凡夫所執人法二我六種無為乃二乘菩薩所執人法二我以雖證真如猶屬迷悟對待總屬生滅邊故今生滅情忘聖凡不立極一心之源故

...because sleep as a mind-factor can make the body and mind dull and heavy; but it is not fixed as good or evil. "Investigation" and "reflection" are the minds that do good or evil. When one is about to act, one must return to ask the mind; thoughts and speech and other measures are turned to "investigation," and entering the subtle is "reflection." What is called "coarse and subtle is speech." Speech is indeterminate. For example, praising the Buddha and bodhisattvas, first investigation and then reflection, only then can one obtain wonderful words. Like people in a lawsuit, it is also from investigation to reflection that one can obtain a calculation; therefore, these two are indeterminate.

As for the fifty-one mind-factors, they are the factors "possessed by the mind." However, they correspond with the mind, so they arise at the same time. These mind-factor dharmas are also called "mind-numbers," also called "mind-traces," also called "mind-paths," and collectively called "false thoughts." There is also this dust; they are also called "defilements," and they are also called "defilements" because they are disturbing. Having these mind-factors disturb the mind, the mind is originally pure; in the mind, there is originally no such thing. It is like clear, cold water: if you throw sand and earth into it, the earth is lost, and the water is gone; cleanliness is natural, and turbidity is called "defilement." Today, practitioners specifically need to sever these defilements; only then is it true cultivation. The *Shurangama Sutra* says: "It is like clarifying turbid water; the sand and earth settle by themselves, and the clear water appears before you, named the 'initial taming of guest-dust.' Defilements go, and the mud becomes pure water; this is named 'inheritance of severing the fundamental ignorance.' Therefore, practitioners, even if they obtain Chan concentration, if they have not severed defilements, they are only called 'clear water appearing before you,' while the sand and earth are settled at the bottom; if you stir it, it is turbid again. How much more so if one has not obtained Chan concentration and yet claims to be awakened to the path?" Like Ananda, who received the Buddha's revelation of the storehouse nature, which was thoroughly clear, and he described what he realized, but only said, "The mind traces are perfect and bright," because all previous uses were false thoughts; he did not know it, did not see it, and today he sees it; this is only then that the defilement is perfectly bright. Today, people take false thoughts as the awakened mind; is this not being self-inverted? However, this mind-factor name, although it is the school of characteristics, requires people to see through these false thoughts. Characteristics are then easy to wonder at and awaken to the originally possessed true mind. How can one just count names and characteristics?

Above, although the kings and factors are divided, they all belong to the "seeing part" of the eight consciousnesses.

The eleven form-dharmas: these are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—the five roots—and color, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma—the six dusts. These five roots are what the eight consciousnesses gather from the four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind) to form. The inner body is the root upon which consciousness relies. The five dusts are also the four great elements; they are the objects created for use. The dharma-dust is the falling shadow of the five outer dusts, belonging to what the six consciousnesses transform; half belongs to the mind, and half belongs to the object. These eleven dharmas all belong to the "object part" of the eight consciousnesses, because they are manifested only by consciousness.

Question: "These five root-bodies are the inner bodies of sentient beings, said to be formed by gathering the four great elements. What does this mean?"
Answer: The *Shurangama Sutra* says: "Delusion and falsity have empty space; based on emptiness, the world is established. Thoughts clarify and become countries; knowledge and perception are sentient beings." This says that because of delusion, the one mind is transformed into the <term>alaya-vijnana</term>; then the spiritually bright true emptiness is transformed into stubborn emptiness. In the stubborn emptiness, ignorance condenses and forms the four great elements and false colors. Therefore, it says: "Based on emptiness, the world is established." It is the country formed by the clarifying and condensing of false thoughts.

眠爲心所者能令身心昏重之用。但非一定善惡。耳。言尋伺者。乃作善作惡之心。將作之時。必返求於心。意言等量。龐轉爲尋。入細爲伺。所謂龐細發言言不定者。如讚佛菩薩。初尋後伺。方得妙辭。如刀訟之人。亦由尋入伺。方得成算。故此二法。爲不定耳。如上五十一法。心所者。乃心家所有之法也。然與心相應。故同時起耳。此心所法。又名心數。亦名心迹。亦名心路。總名妄想。又有此塵。又名染。又名煩惱者。擾亂也。有此心所擾亂。心然淸淨。心中本無此事。如淸冷水。投以沙土。則土失。留水亡。淸潔自然。渾濁名煩惱。濁。今修行人。專要斷此煩惱。方爲眞修。楞嚴經云。如澄濁水。沙土自沉。淸水現前。名爲初伏客塵。煩惱去。泥純水。名爲承斷根本。無明故。修行人。縱得禪定。未斷煩惱。但名淸水現前。而沙土沉底。攪之又濁。況未得禪定。而便自爲悟道乎。如阿難蒙佛開示。如來藏性。徹底分明。而自述所悟。但曰。心

迹圓明。以向來都是妄想用事。全不知。不見。今日乃見。此是煩惱方得圓明了。耳。今人以妄想爲悟心。豈非自顚耶。然此心所名。雖相宗。要人識破此妄想。相則容易。易妙悟。本有眞心。矣。豈直專數名相而已哉。

已上雖分王所。總屬八識之見分。
十一色法者。謂眼耳鼻舌身。五根。色聲香味觸法。六塵。此五根。乃八識。攬地水火風。四大所成。內身爲識所依之根。五塵。亦是四大。能所八法。所造爲所受用境。其法塵。乃外五塵。落謝影子。屬六識所變。一半屬心。一半屬境。此十一法。通屬八識相分。境。以唯識所現故。

問曰。此五根身。乃衆生之內身。言攬四大所成。此義云何。
答曰。楞嚴經云。迷妄有虛空。依空立世界。想澄成國土。知覺乃衆生。此言因迷。一心轉成阿賴耶識。則靈明眞空。變爲頑空。於頑空中。無明凝結。成四大。妄色。故云。依空立世界。乃妄想澄凝。所成之國。

And receive the Latin realms into your peaceful lap.
Yet may Umbria be a matter of the greatest concern to you,
Than which there is nothing more beautiful in all great Italy.
Umbria, the fatherland of the Roman Callimachus, whose
Cynthia became famous through his charming poems.
Umbria, which has not been conquered by poured-out rains, and than which
There is no fatherland more pleasing to the god Bromius <note>original: "Bromius" (Bacchus)</note>.
Here I have my father, exhausted by long age,
And here the sweet air holds my mother.
Here are my grandmother, here my brothers, here the dear pledges of my grandchildren,
And here, dearer than all to my eyes, is Panthea.
O if it might be granted to at least see your deeds,
Which leaders you have conquered by piety and by hand.
I myself also desire to be sent into the midst of the enemies,
And to stir men to war with a rousing trumpet.
Neither would the iron with its gleaming spear-point terrify me,
Nor the harsh lance sent into my side,
Nor the sad terrors through the wounds of cold death.
For this is only to be feared by timid men.
I will not be able to do this: I will at least be able to tell of your deeds,
And Calliope will hear our prayers.
Now farewell, soft Elegies; farewell, loves;
And farewell, our too-celebrated Panthea.
And may a greater spirit fill my mind, so that I may now
Sing of the deeds of Caesar in lofty song.

The effect of meteors is the health and utility of men. For through these, lifted smokes are consumed, which otherwise would ruin everything with their rot, the use of which evaporation is also observed and noted in the human body.

The matter in which, or the object in which meteors remain and are generated, are the air and the earth, which place some call the belly of the earth, others the concavity and caverns of the earth.

# ON THE NATURE AND
## PROPERTIES OF THE PELICAN.

<note>A decorative initial T begins the text.</note>
The land lies near the rebellious African peoples,
it claims for itself a name derived from Egypt,
it is noble for its many fruit-bearing fields;
countless crops arise again from that soil,
it produces health-giving, medicinal herbs,
through it descend the muddy streams of the Nile,
it also brings forth this species of brute creature and a thousand forms,
the same land continually produces monstrous beasts.
In these regions is also born the bird, the Pelican,
to which the learned Latins have given the name <term>Plateae</term> <gloss>broad-billed birds</gloss>.
Not far from the waters of the sevenfold Nile it dwells,
it inhabits vast places where it builds its nests for itself,
and hatches its young in cavities, from which,
when departing from them, it conceals them with great skill.
When the shepherds see this with prying eyes,
without delay, when they perceive the mother departing far from the chicks,
they do not fear to prepare cruel losses,
but soon attempt to kill them with tricks.
For they wrap the featherless Pelicans in the dry dung
of bulls, and by casting in a gleaming flame,
they make them suffer their final fate.

Which send [forth] great things, hay, wine, and the grove,
Barley, and then they offer life to men and the rest.
For on one side it is surrounded by a high vineyard,
Which, after the dawn has put the stars to flight from the sky,
And fiery Titan <note>the sun</note> extends its rays with light,
Giving back its clear lights through the oblique world,
It touches this first, with which light they rejoice.
If winter is indeed about to come, here it immediately adapts
This land for the farmers, who praise the gifts of Phoebus <note>the sun</note>.
If it is flower-bearing spring, if it is a most honeyed year,
Then, then Phoebus loves to lie down in the tender grass,
And from here he sees the hills giving back shadowy leaves,
And he rejoices then in the well-arranged vines.
When he first sees this grassy land with his seeds,
He nods with happy omens, and gives hope of birth. But indeed, when summer is first born,
And he sees the fruits gradually growing in the earth,
And although they are tender in the immature heat,
Phoebus leads the fragrant work (wonderful to say):
While he wishes to be otherwise, and is hidden by the high sky.
Then the star-powerful God <note>the sun</note> sends down rains to the generous vines
In a peaceful fall, with sweet ones falling.
This greatest hill, leaning forward on a sloping path,
Receives the dew falling from the sky as the dawn first comes,
And then he adapts it to the vines first.
It hardly receives the cloud-filled rains in a rapid fall.
For this hill stands in the way of the rains coming from the high sky,
Since they come as if pacified.

Facile erat ei inconuerso dicere, <foreign xml:lang="greek">ἄπηκτα</foreign>, scilicet, concretilia, aut vt Chymici Philosophi loquuntur, incoagulabilia esse, quae nec calore, nec frigore concretionem patiantur; sed cum materiae dispositio & natura certa substernenda fit, maluit hanc potius attingere, inque ea causam non con-crescendi designare, cum actus agentium sint patientium, nec agere quid possit <foreign xml:lang="greek">τὸ ἐνεργητικόν</foreign>, nisi ei astipuletur patiens. Negat ergo, oleum, argentum viuum, mel, picem, &c. concrefcere calore aut frigore, ob dictam materiae indispositionem. Sed, quanquam non iam superstitiose scruter, fitne calor & frigus solitarium accipiendum, <foreign xml:lang="greek">καθ' αὑτὸ</foreign>, non autem aliquod aliud principium formale, & proprietate quadam naturae, tanquam Medusae aspectu concretionem procurans, qualiter Zuingerus de sale Orionio seu Gorgonio; tu vero non ita pridem de Mercurio in sublime acto, ille quidem ratione olei, tu argenti vini refertis: mirabile tamen id videtur pronuntiatum, cum constet, & oleum, & hydrargyrum cum re-liquis, quae proposuit, concretionem sustinere, etiam a frigore solo. Experimur nimirum, id in oleo ex oliuis expresso frigoribus hybernis. De hydrargyro non ita vulgaris est experientia. Vidi tamen vel mediocri frigore (his enim diebus, quibus haec scribo, mollior folito fuit aer, adeo vt medio Decembri nondum viderimus niuem iustam) Mercurium Philosophorum, quem in geranio feruo, in pastillum solidum a folo frigore compactum, idque etiam superiori anno aliquoties animaduerti, qui hypocausto illatus, continuo ad priorem reuerfus est liquorem: Quin & obseruatum est, & me-diis vndis mercurialibus existere radios, instar crystallorum pyramidalium, qui sunt illi veri crystalli, & quibus solo calore resolutis conficitur illa aqua perennis phosphorica; argenteae facie absque perspicuitate resplendentes, vt egregie doceant in fe esse <foreign xml:lang="greek">δύναμιν</foreign> illam coagulandi, quam tam anxie perquisierunt Philosophi. Si concrefcit itaque hydrargyrus talis solo frigore, perinde vt & de metallorum generatione idem differuerat Philosophus: & resoluitur calore; qui fit, vt inconcretilem scribat? Non autem leui vtitur argumento. Aerem in eo excellere ait, idque verum esse, Philosophi Chymici.

<margin>Anni 1596.</margin>

# De Azotho & aqua permanente.

Chymici non ignorant, qui ideo & volatocum & spirituosum, quin & spiritu nuncuparunt, & ob eius no fixi praesentiam, metalla quadamtenus statuerunt fugacia. Aet nec calore nec frigore cogitur: quod testatur serenitas hyberna vel frigidissima, sicut & aestiua aestuissima in partibus Lybiae, Aegypti, & similium regionum. Nec dici potest exprimi ex eo vi frigoris aerem. Non enim rediret priori statui fi in igni, vel fugiat. Si etiam frigus exprimere aerem portionem posset, multo magis calor. Tuam de hac quaestione sententiam expectabo, & interim de illo Mercurii genere, quem Azoth Arabum & Chaldaeorum, vt volunt, ore appellant, cuiusque aliquod specimen coagulatum mihi superiori aestate dono misisti, atque vna etiam de aqua permanente tecum colloqvar; vnde simul hunc reportabimus fructum, vt ad veram Mercurii philosophici notitiam perueniamus.

Appellatio Azothi dicitur esse Chaldaica, & Arabica [Hispanis hydrargyrus Azogue dici fertur, fors à Saracenis accepta voce vt fit pro azog] significare; idem quod Latinis Chymicis mercurius, vel argentum viuum. Propriane fit <unclear>ἀννυλα</unclear>, an modificata, gnaris earum linguarum discutendum relinquo. Bellunensis interpretans vocabulum Afad, lilii quandam speciem esse dicit. Iam autem ex Lullio, aliisque Philosophis, etiam Paracelso referente Quercetano & Dornæo, scimus Lilii vocem adhibitam esse ad designandum philosophorum arcanam materiam, ex qua postea conficitur tinctura. Perinde itaque fit iam, siue Azoth, (aliis Azoc) siue Afad, siue lilium nominemus, modo aliarum significationum nulla obstet. Quantum autem in scriptis philosophorum sum versatus, atque etiam in Paracelsi deliramentis legi, quinque rebus nomen Azoth potissimum accommodatur. Paracelso est mediceina quadam opponenda incantamentis magicis, atque etiam ipsi Diabolo, quod adeo fortis fit, vt in hoc pellendo ipsi confidere possimus, D. Paulo longe aliam monstrante aduersus istum spiritum amaturam, nec Paracelso consuetae impietates & medacia sunt curanda. Alio in libro quem Azoth, seu de ligno vitae inscripsit, totam videtur hominis, & creationem & lapsum, & restitutionem designare. Sed neque hic vllam meretur autoritatem, cum ille liber sit vt maxime in Deum in pius, ita pestilentissimus, & horribilium mendaciorum profanationumque; diuinorum operum plenissimus, adeo vt si sphema Galenus ob impiam de Deo vocem fit damnandus, Paracelsus longe grauioris criminis & blasphemiae reus, nullo calculo veniat absoluendus. Vix quicquam fani, quod quidem ipse de suo, praeter medicas quasdam praeparationes & compositiones, protulerit, est apud Paracelsum. Eo ergo omisso Philosophorum pauca auscultemus. Apud hos initio nil differt à mercurio philosophorum, & prima materia. Deinde profert sana, etiam aliquid absolutus significat, quod sequitur secunda perfectione Elixyris animati constitutionem. Tertio est analoga quaedam hydrargyri per septenam sublimationem exaltatio, cui mihi tua praeparatio videtur respondere. Primi Azothi nomina etiam sunt alia, Appellant enim mercurium philosophorum, primam materiam, Leonem viridem, aquam permanentem, Draconem, aquam vitae, aqua philosophicam, vas Hermetis, & c. Mercurium Philosophorum esse arguit eadem materia, & apparatus idem, eademque proprietates & attributa.

<margin>Quid veteres et auripigmento vocat. Vnde aqua lilii Archelas fit ex auripigmento. Dornæus ex tibio facit, &c. Azoth quintuplex. Delirameta Paracelsi.</margin>

Mercurius philosophorum est ille (inquit quidam Philof.) quem natura paululum operata est, & in metalli formam conformauit, sed imperfectum reliquit: quod est, in perfectis corporibus natura confecit illum mercurium, sed nondum ad tincturam perduxit. Itaque arte est extrahendus & ad gradum absolutio. nis fuae adducendus: Esse enim eum in corporibus perfectis, & inde eliciendum arte, indicat hoc axioma: Tres partes habet Philosophia scilicet Solem, Lunam, & Mercurium, ex quibus conjunctis pater HERMES scivit conficere tincturam. Et: Verus Mercurius extractus est de duobus corporibus, estq; bene lotus & digestus: & juro per Deum, quod nullus alius mercurius est in via vniuersali, nisi jam declaratus, à quo pendet tota philosophia. Qui aliter dicit falsum dicit. Iterum: Materia lapidis philosophici est aqua: & intelligitur de aqua illorum trium, Solis, Lunae, & Mercurii, nec debent esse plura, nec pauciora. Sol est mas: Luna est foemina, Mercurius est sperma. Alius: Corpora submersa in Mercurium per conuenientem putrefactionem revertuntur in argentum viuum, quod ante fuerunt. Alia alibi adduxi: Et aperte Rosarium philosophorum ait: Lapis noster apud omnes Philosophos nominatur Mercurius, qui non est natus, vt multi putant, sed de corpore extractus Lapis philosophorum est ex tribus, scilicet Sole, Luna, & Mercurio, id est fac Mercurium ex Sole & Luna in suo esse fine Mercurio vulgi, sed per viam philosophicam. Haec ibi. Vbi notandum latibulum vltimis verbis comprehensum. Non fit per vulgatum hydrargyrum; & tame fit per hydrargyrum actu existentem. Nam quod in potentia est, non venit ad actum sua sponte; sed per actum similem; & alii philosophi saepe dicunt non posse vllo alio medio extrahi; sicut & in eodem Rosario negatur quinta essentia extrahi posse sine aqua, quam alibi appellat spiritum & mercurium, quia mercurio vulgi distat sola praeparatione. Et manifesta sunt haec: Si per juvamen argenti vivi, crudi frigidi, huius & ejus beneficio extrahitur sulphureitas calida sicca, & munda, & c. remanet mercurius purus, & c. Ite: Fac mercurium per mercurium, & c. Quae a. fit via philosophica qua extrahatur ex perfectis, saepe dicitur in modo refoluendi ad primam materiam per putrefactionem in fimo philosophorum, hoc est, Mercurio. Esse vero hunc ipsum mercurium tum aquam permanentem, tum Azoth, descriptio horum ostendit. Ita enim est apud Rosarium: Argentum viuum e corporibus extractum à primordio, est aqua pmanens philosophorum, quae fit post putrefactionem & separationem elementorum. Item: Aqua permanens fue perennis, siue vinum ardens dicitur aqua corporis, id est, quando corpus redactum est in mercurium: quae verba de nulla alia re possunt accipi, quam de mercurio philosophico. Appellatur autem permanens, quia constanter manet, non tantum in vnione partium homogenea, adeo vt nulla arte possit diuidi in portiones constituentes; sed & ex duabus aquis constat, nullo ingenio vnquam fegregandis, sicut non potest aqua aquae confusa denuo ab ea separari: Praeterea quia cum perfecta est, euasitque tinctura, constantissime corporibus tingendo adhaeret, vna cum ipsis natura facta. Non alia de Azoth passim scribuntur. Dictum enim illud, quod Azoth & ignis sufficiant: tu ipse mihi es confessus. Rosarius minor ait: Si scis regimen ignis, sufficit mercurius.

<margin>Mercurius Philosophorum quis. Mercurius Philosophorum ex quib. Nota: quod corpora perfecta dirigat quid mercurium: sed die prima ex aliunde vel arte ex argeto viuo extractum vel ex metallo immaturo in quo potes videre paruo negotio omnes colores elegantes. Est res vils, inuenitur, in omni pharmacopolio integro. Nota: Sine mercurio vulgi. Aqua permanens qua.</margin>

<margin>Whitening, imbibition, and fermentation. White stone, or white elixir.</margin>
VI. Take an ounce of black earth ground on marble. Add half an ounce of mercury extracted from the moon <note>silver</note>, and mix by grinding on the stone. Digest the mixture in a sealed glass in ashes with an equal heat for eight days, until the humidity has been dried out. Remove it prudently, and grind on the stone, and mix in another half ounce again, and digest, and repeat this four times, until two ounces have been imbibed, and the matter has emerged white. This is white sulfur, and foliated earth; likewise, the vivification of the body, conjunction, and fermentation. If you dissolve the stone four times, one part dyes a hundred parts of sublimated and rectified mercury; if five times, it dyes a thousand parts; if six times, a hundred thousand, etc.

Take one part of this king, add two parts of the water of the solution of the lime of Sol <note>gold</note> (in which three parts of gold have been dissolved into mercury), mix by grinding, and imbibe. Digest into a deep red stone. This imbibition can be done as many times as you please. One part of the first confection dyes one hundred parts of Luna <note>silver</note> dissolved into mercury, which mercury ought to have been washed previously by strong brine and heated in a crucible.

<margin>Isaac also increases it three times, or thereabouts, because there is a fear lest it fly off due to excessive subtlety.</margin>
Concerning the ferment, note that it ought to be the lime of Sol or Luna, made by *aqua regia* or *aqua fortis*, the former red, the latter white: and it is called the soul, because it gives life by means of the corporal mercury, so that you take one part of the lime and two of the corporal mercury, and join the mixture once made to the red king. The tincture is increased if one part of it is joined to three, or one and a half, of the mercury of the body; and this augmentation must be done three times, so that the first degree is thus completed, by which one part dyes one hundred. The second degree will be if it is dissolved again by the mercury of the solar body, and it dyes a thousand parts, and so it is increased into infinity.
