<margin>Azoth est a-curius & ignis. Azoth ergo mercurius est & aqua, cum hæ voces pro eodé usurpentur. Et ne accipias aliú qua perma- per philosophicum; Arnoldus inquit: Oportet vt in solutione sublimatione & subtiliatione folis & lunæ labores. nens, seu Hæc enim duo corpora sufficiunt. Alius, aqua & ignis sufficiunt, & aqua fortior est igni, quia facit de corpore solis merū mercurius.</margin>
<margin>Azothi vox spiritū, quod ignis nequit. Hæc quidem de igni externo: Sed & internus intelligendus, iuxta axioma: Nihil attribuitur, aliud adhæret metallis nec consungitur, nisi quod ex ipsis est. Sulphur ergo & mercurius sunt materia lapidis que potest nostri, vbi per sulphur, Rosario philosophorum interprete accipitur ignis internus. Moneo autem, in esse fexta si- his dictis interdum vocem Azothi etiam aquæ soluenti tribui, quanquam non fit Azoth, nisi in poten- gnificatio. tia. Hac ratione etiam Leo viridis appellatur, qui solem deuorat. Arnoldi hoc est: Aquam septies destilla- Liber arca- tam seruata ad partem. Ipsa enim est mercurius philosophorum solutius faciens matrimonium, & aqua vitæ abluens norū ex Bern- Latonem. Vbi vides de aqua illa dici eadem, quæ de Azotho. Vnde alius: Azoth est prima materia, & vo- hardo & a- catur leo viridis, Negat tamen liber arcanorum, qui Gebro ascribitur, licet falso, Azoth esse simplex ar- liis no fat in- gentum viuum, quod extrahitur ex minera, quia fit illud quod extrahitur ex corporibus solutis per tellectis Ge- mercurium; neque prioribus, dum hoc dicit, repugnat, eo nempe sensu, quem dixi. Porro de Azo- bro astriptus tho etiam frequenter dicitur, quod Latonem est, terram nigram & impuram abluat, & albedinem falso. Abluere La- in eo procuret, sed adminiculo ignis. Hoc intelligitur non in vno duntaxat opere, sed in quolibet. Ita- tonem.</margin>
<margin>Azoth est a- que & differentia hinc erit ipsius Azothi. Sed quid sibi velit catholicum illud effatum, videamus. Si que, cōfistē- terra non fat alba est, inquit quidam, tere eam cum aqua, & calcina. Azoth enim, id est, aqua, & ignis seu calor, sia & cado- abluunt Latonem seu terram impuram. Sed illa tritio non fit manibus, sicut nec ablutio, quæ nihil aliud est, quam ex ru argenti.</margin>
<margin>Gutta Sapo- nigredine albedinis productio, interuentu imbibitionis seu nutritionis per lac virgineum, & ignis calorem. Nec vlla alia nis est, by- res potest è nigro facere album. Apparet ergo iterum ex hoc effectu, quid sit Azoth. Rosarium hoc habet drargyri, ita dictum: Hermes ait, Azoth & ignis abluunt Latonem, & nigredinem ab eo auferunt. Iungite ergo siccum humido, ob ablutionē seu terram nigram cum aqua sua, & coquite donec albetur: Ablutio est nigredinis terminatio vel mudatio, donec vocati, quo- album fiat perfecte album, &c. Non est obscurum hic signari progressum ex nigro in album, per aquæ it- modo ob cor- rorationem & ignem: Idem vero enunciatur de Mercurio philosophorum. Ita enim quidam. Aqua fe- rosionē voca- pties destillata, est mercurius philosophorum solutius, faciens matrimonium, & aqua vitæ abluens Latonem. Simili- tur acetū, fal, ter de aqua permanente loquuntur vt: Oportet vt Sol & Luna sint in tinctura, & fermentum ipsius spiritus; & &c.</margin>
<margin>Bernhardi aqua permanentis argenti viui, & per illam aquam illæ naturæ debent fixari, & nutriri cum naturali calore, tam diu, Azoth qui quovsque habeant suam fixationem: quæ verba idem volunt ac Azoth & ignis abluentia Latonē, & nutrien- est philosophi tia: & cum aqua philosophorum fit aqua permanens, & pmanens esse no potest fine suo corpore, cū quo ces secundus.</margin>
<margin>Rebis. soluta est; seu ex quo per solutionem facta, & cum quo vnita, necesse est Azoth, aquamque permanen- Elixyr. tem etiam hoc nomine esse vnum & idem. Præterea de Azotho dicitur, quod fit humidus, seu fluidus Tinctura. actu, quodque initio candidus, postea euadat niger. Inde & aqua vocatur, & mercurii candor intelli- Rebis tamen gitur: Et paulo ante, philosophi sententia fuit, iungendum esse siccum humido. De candore vero etiam veteri quida hoc dictum attendendum est: Conceptio est, (inquit Philosophus) cum terra in nigrum pulverem soluitur, & dixerunt fan- incipit aliquantum de Mercurio fecum retinere. Tunc enim agit masculus in fæminam, id est, Azoth in terram. Licet guinem esse, Azoth appareat in prima mistione seu conjunctione albus, pro eo quod fæmina vincit suo colore: nihilominus in putre- quida crinē: factione per ignis beneficium, denigrantur ambo per ignem agentem in humido. Non autem credas in se denigrari il- alis stercus, lam abluam: quæ candida manet, sed apparet nigra ob innatantem spiritum seu sulphur nigrum, quo separato redit quos secutus candor natiuus, qui postea etiam causa est, cum igni, vt illa quoque terra debetur. In Rosario minore dicitur, me- Parac. qui lior inceratio fieri cum Azoth viuo (non cum occiso) & gutta Saponis, & melior etiam imbibitio, qua fit cum Mer- vocat vrinā. curio, folus perfectius nominatur, & solus philosophorum mercurius. Quanquam autem fatis superque ex di- Spiritus mi- ctis patet, debere illum Azothum confici ex auro & argento per mercurium destillatum septies, eum- neralis cru- que, continere mercurium corporum perfectorum, esse liquidum, candidum materiam lapidis, aquam dus. Nota permanentem, qua fit imbibitio, & c. tamen eadem etiam luculenter exposuit in secundo significatu modū extra- Bernhardus. Non enim differt secundus Azoth à primo, nisi perfectionis gradu, sicut descriptio eius ctionis, Eli- habet. Eam, si libet, paucis contemplemur. Azoth, inquit, fit ex Elixyre. Elixyr non est aliud quam corpus in a- xyr ita Pe- xyr pars secunda in opere philosophorum. Rebis est pars prima, Elixyr secunda, Tinctura tertia. Azoth non requiri- nottes: opor- tur ad Elixyr, quia Elixyr precedit vt aqua oleum, & Spiritus animam. Ex Elixyre extrahitur Azoth tanquam ex a- tet ex are no- qua oleum. Spiritus mineralis crudus tanquam aqua conjungitur cum corpore suo, vt ipsum prima coctione soluat. Hinc stro accipere nominatur REBIS. Ex istis duobus simul dissolutis componitur Elixyr; id est, aqua tincta. Ex Elixyre fit Azoth ha- partē vna & bens naturam sui corporis calidam & virtutem, id est, oleofam naturam calidam humidam. Est enim ignis & aer actu. naturæ, non abolita spiritus & Elixyris essentia, (quæ perfecta cum est Azoth vocatur) oportet nos di- cta in.</margin>

# Imperial Commissioned Explanation of the Classic of Filial Piety

The minister [I, the author] submits: The meaning of this chapter is generally consistent with what Zhu Xi says in the *Chapter and Sentence of the Doctrine of the Mean*: "Respecting high ministers means trust is focused, so small-minded officials cannot drive a wedge between them; therefore, one is not confused when facing affairs." This is also an interpretation of the meaning of the *Doctrine of the Mean*. The word "respect" is the heart-method of emperors. Extending from the respect shown to one's kin, the *Book of Documents* says: "If virtue is abundant, do not be over-familiar or insulting." If one is over-familiar or insulting toward gentlemen, one cannot exhaust human hearts; if one is over-familiar or insulting toward small-minded men, one cannot exhaust their strength. Toward both gentlemen and small-minded men, there is truly nothing that should not be respected. Yet, within this state of total respect, there are those who *ought* to be respected in particular; this involves more than just the abundance of rituals and manners. Therefore, I believe this is precisely an interpretation of the *Doctrine of the Mean*.

Apostles, it remains entirely uncertain. **Lorinus and Mariana** believe the name of Matthias was inscribed on one tablet, the name of Joseph on another, and that both were placed into an urn, with the agreement that whoever’s name was drawn first would be the Apostle; they hold that the name of Matthias was drawn first. Truly, as Scripture is silent, we choose to <term>ἐπέχειν</term> <gloss>withhold judgment</gloss>, since we know there were various methods of drawing lots at that time: for according to *Proverbs 16*, small tablets, dice, pebbles, or little stones were cast into the fold of a garment; among Homer in the *Iliad 7*, into a helmet; among Plautus in *Casina*, into a water jar; among Cicero in *book 4 of the Verrines*, into a hydria; among Virgil in *Aeneid 6*, into an urn. Nevertheless, it is certain that GOD, by directing the lot, declared Matthias.

### §. 12.

That the Apostles used a form of lot-casting without sin could be argued against **Thomas** 2. question 95, Article 8, and those from whom he drew here—Jerome, Chrysostom, and Bede—who believe that the Apostles, being as yet unrefined and inexperienced, did this according to the custom of the Fathers of the Old Testament before they had received the Holy Spirit. But let those words of **Dr. Walther** in his *Biblical Harmony, page 999*, suffice for us now, where he forcefully states: *The Apostles used the lot on this occasion, which they are not read to have used thereafter, because this present calling was not intended to be simply mediated, but Apostolic: and therefore they did not rashly rush into divination.* Nor should it be thought that GOD preferred Matthias, a stranger to Joseph, in the Apostolate merely because of consanguinity: for many recount that this man was the brother of James the Less, Simon, and Jude, the Apostles, and the son of Alphaeus and Mary—called Barsabas from an oath, but named the Just from his notable Justice and Holiness. Therefore, Christ rejected him, both so that He might not seem to prefer so many of His own kinsmen to outsiders, and so that four brothers would not be in the college of the twelve Apostles at once. Truly, we find many subtleties here, but meanwhile fewer Truths: we acknowledge GOD alone as the <term>Καρδιογνώστην</term> <gloss>Knower of Hearts</gloss>, who alone could show whom He willed, which was Matthias, whom He declared by lot. And the Eleven received him, once declared; which Luke expressed quite emphatically with these words: <term>καὶ συγκατεψηφίσθη μετὰ τῶν ἕνδεκα Ἀποστόλων</term> <gloss>and he was numbered with the eleven apostles</gloss>.

Declaratum verò Undecim receperunt; quod Lucas satis emphaticè his quoque verbis expressit: καὶ συγκατεψηφίσθη μετὰ τῶν ἕνδεκα Ἀποστόλων.

Ac hisce duobus exemplis sunt et annumeranda illa: **RATIO** facit, ut a duobus petam hereditatem, sed **Pegasi** sententia **UTILIOR** est. **RATIO** facit, ut duobus teneatur, sed teneri **INIQUUM**. **Labeonis** sententia **RATIONEM** habet, sed **HOC JURE** utimur. Subtili **RATIONE** non fiet, **BENIGNIUS** tamen dicetur. Stricta **RATIONE** non liberantur, sed **UTILIUS** est; et id genus alia trecenta. Eaque (ut puto) est, lex non omnium Digestis de legibus, vera sententia.

->XXXIV.<-

Quae caeteroquin viri docti, de mente legis non omnium disseruerunt, parum mihi liquet, an probare debeamus. Nam, ut glossarum quasdam opiniones mittam, quae ipsa temporis diuturnitate extabuerunt, vulgaris persuasio est, (sive eam primus attulerit, ut sibi videtur, **Zasius**, sive, (ut **Menochio**,) **Lacellotus Politus**, esse quidem legum omnium rationes. ### XXX.

If the action of loan should concur with the <term>Aquilian</term> law, and the action of loan was brought first, <term>Ulpian</term> says it is most equitable that by bringing the action of loan, one remits the <term>Aquilian</term> [action]; yet he seems to have a reason if one says it is competent to bring the <term>Aquilian</term> [action] for the surplus. Whence it is sharply questioned, and not yet sufficiently defined, whether <term>Ulpian</term> approved the former or the latter opinion. After the gloss, <term>Bartolus</term> and <term>Paulus Castrensis</term> waver. The latter, however, writes that <term>Ulpian</term> was more inclined to the former. <term>Cujacius</term>, on the contrary, [inclined] to the latter, along with <term>Cabotius</term> and (as far as I know) all recent [commentators]. What then? My reasoning is thus: that which <term>Castrensis</term> desired can be defended most strongly. But with new reasons. And that place of <term>Ulpian</term> contains a certain law received against reason on account of some equity, and as if a lamp of the law *On not all things* lighting from its own light.

Consistent with this is that the script of Law 34, section last, *On Origin and Actions* is entirely erroneous, and for "but it is truer that it remains," with a negation added: "but it is truer that it does NOT remain" should be read. Thus, as we can attest it stands clearly in a very old manuscript codex, which we inspected through the kindness of the honorable <term>Valerius Guilielmus Forsterus</term>. <term>Bartolus</term>, the ancient critic, also testifies expressly that he found this in other codices besides <term>Accursius</term>, when he says concerning the affirmative reading: "But that letter is not good, nor common." ### XXX.

Si commodati actio, cum Aquiliæ concurrat, & commodati fuerit actum prius, Ulpianus æquissimum esse dicit, ut commodati agendo Aquiliæ remittat: videri tamen rationem habere, si quis in superfluum Aquiliæ competere dixerit. Unde acriter quæsitum, nec dum satis definitum est, prioremnè, an posteriorem sententiam Ulpianus comprobarit? nutant post glossam Bartolus, Paulusque Castrensis. Hic tamen in priorem, procliviorem fuisse Ulpianum, scribit. Cujacius contrà, in posteriorem; cum Cabotio, ac recentioribus (quod sciam) omnibus. Quid ergò? mea sic ratio est, fortissimè defendi posse id, quod Castrensis voluit. Sed rationibus novis. Adeoque illum Ulpiani locum, jus quoddam contra rationem, propter aliquam æquitatem receptum, continere, legique non omnium quasi lumen de lumine suo accendere.

### XXXI.

Cui consentaneum est, omninò mendosam esse, l. 34. §. ult. de O. & A. scripturam, & pro: sed verius est remanere, adjecta negatione: sed verius est NON remanere legendum esse. Sic, quomodo in bene veteri codice manuscripto, perspicuè extare, contestari possumus, quem beneficio C. V. Valerii Guilielmi Forsteri, inspeximus. Quomodo etiam in alijs codicibus se reperisse, testatur expressè, præter Accursium, Bartolus, criticus antiquus, cum ait de lectione affirmante: Sed ista litera non est bona, nec communis. Qui potes hoc affirmare, lucerna juris, Bartole? quoniam patet (inquit) EX LIBRIS ANTIQUIS, quos AD HOC, sum PERSCRUTATUS.

*Scribit Ulpianus: perquam durum esse, hoc est, (aliter atque Salomonio placuit ac Bodino) iniquum, injustumque, ut ne eos quidem servos, quos in agris, vel in provinciis habuit mulier adultera, manumittere vel alienare possit. Cur perquam durum? Claudicant hic Iasonis, Verii, Altiati, Pruckmanni, aliorumque rationes. Igitur Donelli sententia aliquantulum immutata, has fere, duritiei ejus causas, dari posse putamus. 1. Quod servorum promiscue omnium libertas inhumane impeditur, si postea, ad quaestionem aliqui duntaxat vocantur. 2. Quod crudeliter, si inscii aeque atque scii, innocentes, atque nocentes vocantur. 3. Quod dominae adhuc, eripitur liberarum rerum suarum administratio et alienatio.*

*Quid ergo? an ideo in Iacobi de Arena sententiam imus, ac d. l. prospexit, spiritu, rationeve carere dicimus? aut concludimus cum Bern. §. 6. Tandem in citato versu, quæ quidem dubia sunt, adduntur hæcce: quicquid sit a *vite vini* **מחרצנים ועד זג**, quæ verti solent: *ab acinis usque ad corticem*. Quid **חרצן**, quid **זג** significet, eruditi certant & adhuc lis est sub judice. Cùm enim affirmante Aben Esra ad hoc loco **החרצנים אין לו ריע וכן זג**; tam vox **חרצן** tùm vox **זג** in Scripturis non amplius occurrant, ne mireris hinc, eruditos in his vocibus explicandis in diversas scindi partes & sententias, quas referre prolixum foret, quasdam vide à Matthaeo Polo in Synopsi Critica & à Bonfrerio in hoc loco allatas. Sufficiat jam rudi Minervâ pauca voces ipsas spectantia attulisse. Alii volunt per **חרצנים** denotari exterius sive exteriorem cutem sive corticem uvarum, per **זג** interius & ipsa granula in uvis: aliis contrarium placet. Illud vult Rabbi Jehuda: *hoc* Rabbi Jose, ceu verba eorum in Jalkut folio 209. columna 4. allata edocent: **החרצנים אלו החיצונים והזגין אלו הפנימיים דברי רבי יהודה, רבי יוסי אומר כדי שלא תטעה : כזוג של בהמה החיצון זוג הפנימי ענבל**; hoc est voluit Rabbi Jehuda, **חרצנים** esse *exterius acinorum sive cutes exteriores*, sed **זגים** esse *interius sive interiores vinaceos*. Verùm Rabbi Jose dixit: ne errorem committas: res sese habet ut in *tinnabulo pecudum*: ubi pars exterior dicitur **זוג**; interior verò **ענבל** id est *malleus sive clavus interior*. Hujus sententia clarius exponitur in Sepher Mitz-gad folio 73. columna 4. ubi ita: **רבי יוסי אומר החרצנים הם הפנימים והזוגין הן הקליפה החיצונה וגו'**: Rabbi Jose dixit, **חרצנים** esse *interius, quod seminare soleant*; sed **זג** esse *corticem exteriorem*. seed: of grapes: and that is indicated when someone soaks and moistens grapes in water, and thus the flavor of wine results therefrom. This meaning is also chosen by Jacob Bonfrerius on this passage, and others. The Syrian rendered it: "and all that is soaked from grapes," and "all secondary [wine] from grapes." There are those who interpret it as cooked drink, which Aben Ezra also cites in the first opinion quoted: "Every thing... grapes, and some say cooked beverage." The sense is: "Everything that is liquefied or macerated with grapes, and there are those who understand it as a cooked potion." Nor are there lacking those to whom it pleases to render it: "all remainder or residues of grapes," as if <term>mishrat</term> did not descend from <term>sharah</term>, but was written defectively and derived from <term>shear</term>, which meant "residue, remainder," for <term>meshearet</term>. And at first glance, the Chaldaic Paraphrase of Onkelos might seem to favor this opinion, which is thus: "All macerations of grapes," which some explain as the residues of grapes, as if it descended from <term>shear</term>, "it is a remainder." But since letters are not rarely changed when expressions are transferred from Hebraism into Chaldaism, it seems more correct to establish that this word is made from <term>sharah</term>, with the <term>shin</term> changed into <term>tav</term>, which change is very common; see Ludovicus de Dieu, *Grammar and Harmony*, book I, chapter 11, pages 9 and 12. As for that defective writing, it is asserted beyond necessity and beyond the use of the word: one should not descend to irregularities by the suffrage of scholars as long as any hope, which is given here, of defending the customary writing shines forth. The Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum seem to hint at every drink prepared from pressed and macerated grapes: the former has: "every liquid in which grapes have been macerated," the latter: "every liquor of grapes, etc." Add the version of the Septuagint: "whatever is produced from the grape," which is whatever is prepared from the grape. But what prevents us from combining what has been brought forward in a certain way and understanding by <term>mishrat anavim</term> both that which is macerated and dissolved in wine itself, and whatever later is pressed out of already-pressed grapes, either by being soaked in water or boiled, from the remaining liquid; for the Nazirites could eat or drink nothing of the sort, and thus neither the previous nor the latter abstinence allowed it, which for anyone who intends to weigh the matter more deeply

Nec deesse leges, quibus reddere placet: omne residuum sive reliquias uvarum: quasi משרת non à שרה descenderet, sed defectivè scriptum esset et deductum à שאר, residuum, reliquum fuit, pro משארת. Et primo intuitu pro hac sententia facere videri posset Chaldaica Paraph. Oncelica, quæ ita: כל משרות ענבין, quod quidam reliquias uvarum exponunt, ac si à שאר, reliquum est, descenderet. Sed cùm non rarò literæ immutentur, quando dictiones ex Hebraismo in Chaldaismum transferuntur, hinc rectius videtur statui, vocem hanc esse ex שרה factam, mutato ש in ת, quæ mutatio est usitatissima, vid. Lud. de Dieu Gram. Harm. l. I. c. 11. p. 9. et 12. Nequaquam enim Valet Consequentia à principio Quod, seu toto supposito ad principia Quibus, seu partes suppositi, ut & hactenus allata & adhuc afferenda exempla luce meridianâ clarius reddunt. Ita homo est tres ulnas longus, nec tamen anima est tres ulnas longa, sed corpus, etsi utrumque, & anima & corpus hominem constituant. Homo videlicet est principium Quod, corpus principium Quo, seu id, secundùm quod longitudo illa homini competit. Unde non sequitur: Homo est tres ulnas longus. Ergo & corpus ejus est tres ulnas longum, & anima est tres ulnas longa. Coronidis vicem liceat unicum tantùm exemplum ex Theologia apponere, suâ luce itidem clarissimum. Christus est infinitus, ut principium Quod, hoc est, Christus est totum suppositum, seu, persona illa, quæ infinita est ac denominatur. Principium autem Quo, seu, natura illa, secundum quam infinitum esse Christo competit, non est humana ejus natura, sed divina. Unde itidem non sequitur: Christus est infinitus. Ergo & divina ejus natura est infinita, & humana est infinita. Instituuntur videlicet ejusmodi collectiones ex principio isto: Quicquid principio, Quod seu, supposito competit, id omnibus quoque; partibus ejus competit; cujus falsitas nimium quantum jam apparuit.

and highly necessary distinction of a principle, whereby one is called a principle *that* <term>principium Quod</term> <gloss>principle that [which is]</gloss>, another a principle *by which* <term>principium Quo</term> <gloss>principle by which [something acts]</gloss>. The principle *that* is the whole suppositum <term>suppositum</term> <gloss>the acting subject/individual substance</gloss>, which is denominated either from some action which proceeds from that suppositum, or from some form, whether substantial or accidental, which is in that suppositum, or finally from some part of it. The principle *by which*, however, is some form, or that which behaves as a form, namely the nature and essence of the thing, or some part, or an instrument, insofar as either an operation is attributed to it, or the denomination of another thing from which the whole suppositum is denominated. Thus, a human being is the principle *that* understands (the human being, clearly, is the whole suppositum from which the action of understanding proceeds), but the principle *by which* is the mind of the human being, not the body. The same human being is endowed with learning and virtue as the principle *that*; the soul is the principle *by which*; the soul, clearly, is the form, or that according to which these things belong to the human being as a whole suppositum. An architect (the same logic holds for all other artisans) builds a house as the principle *that*; the principle *by which* is his art. Thus, a human being reads some writing as the principle *that*; the principles *by which*, or by whose benefit he performs this, are partly his sight, partly also his intellect; whence animals devoid of reason cannot read, because, although they do not lack sight, they are nevertheless devoid of reason.

XXI. We said this distinction is very useful and highly necessary, for by its benefit we can ensure that we do not confuse the most distinct things among themselves, and plunge ourselves into many false and absurd things in the cognition of things. It is certain that all actions which proceed from any suppositum are also attributed to it primarily, whence that trite saying in the schools of the philosophers: *Actions belong to supposita*. And not only actions, but all things from which the suppositum receives its denomination are for the most part and correctly attributed to it. §. 6. God, the best and greatest, demands from everyone an account of the things done in this life from the moment of death through a particular judgment <note>the assessment of an individual soul immediately after death</note>. Nothing is hidden there, for He is entirely an eye. He bestows heavenly rewards upon the pious after their departure, but sends the wicked to bear the torments of hell. Revelation, chapter 14, verse 13. Thus, Christ promises Paradise, that is, eternal happiness, to the thief hanging to his right from the moment of his death and without any interval. Hebrews, chapter 9, verse 27. The actions of each individual are examined as if by a balance. The supreme Judge rejects those who are found wanting, and He used this method against Belshazzar, Daniel, chapter 5, verse 27. Jerome in Joel, chapter 2: *Whatever will happen to everyone on the day of Judgment is fulfilled in individuals on the day of their death.* Lactantius, in *Divine Institutes*, book 7, chapter 21, denies this, contrary to the orthodoxy of the Church: *Let no one think that souls are judged immediately after death; all are detained in one common custody until the time arrives when the greatest Judge shall make an examination of merits.*

XIV. We find another point in Arnold, namely that the Ebionites opined that Christ was born only for the sake of the Jews, in the cited work of Origen, Book 4, <term>περὶ ἀρχῶν</term> <gloss>On First Principles</gloss>: For he says thus: > *Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor. 10:18). By which he signifies, indeed, that there is another Israel, who is not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, etc. Taught, therefore, by him, when the Savior says: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matt. 15:24), we do not understand it as these do, who savor earthly things, i.e., the Ebionites, who are also called poor by their very name, etc.*

From these words it is entirely clear, in Origen’s view, that the Ebionites supposed Christ was sent only to those called Israelites according to the flesh, who, after the destruction of the Samaritan kingdom, were all included under the name of Jews, regardless of which tribe they belonged to. The remaining words, which are contained in the definition, expressing *Efficient Cause, Subject, Matter, and End*, complete the differentia. The Efficient Cause is expressed by these words: *by those to whom such right belongs*. Sagittarius (29) separates those who have the power to establish stipends in this way: he makes some Ecclesiastical, who are distinguished either by the highest rank, as the Pontiff; or by a middle rank, as Bishops: others, however, he makes Lay; who in turn either manage affairs with absolute power in the Republic, as the Emperor, Kings, and Princes, who foster talents that will carry their memory with much praise into all posterity: or with restricted power, as Governors of provinces, Administrators, Magistrates, the Senate, and Colleges. But let not private persons finally neglect whatever pertains to the care and necessary cultivation of letters, since it concerns them no less (unless one thinks that what is done for the whole Republic does not touch the common people, as if they were another city inhabiting the same town) that both Republics be administered and preserved by the wisdom of Learned Men. Therefore, those who assist the poverty of students through legacies and stipends are held worthy of all praise, whether they leave something for pious causes on account of close kinship, or are held to the payment of such stipends by reason of power granted by the Laws. ### XII.
Actionis eductivae subiectum est ipsum illud, quod effectui in genere causae Materialis dat esse, et effectum hac ratione sustentat; quod subiectum, eductionis, sive sustentationis, sive inhaesionis dicas parum interest, nisi quod eductionis et sustentationis solam causalitatem causae materialis, inhaesionis verò ipsam etiam unionem formae ad subiectum innuere videatur, à qua unione ipsa actio eductiva quoque realiter differt, ut modus à modo, licet naturaliter necessario habeat actio eductiva formae absolutae connexam unionem, et ipsa actio eductiva in quantum eam coniunctam habere exigit, dici possit, unio radicaliter, non formaliter, aut entitativè. Actionis creativae subiectum adhaesionis est ipse terminus creatus, qui inhaesionis aut sustentationis subiectum esse nequit, quia actio creativa non est sustentatio, aut inhaesio, non enim est aliquid ea actio creativa, quo mediante aliud à termino creato, cui ipsa ea actio ut quo esse dat, distinctum causatur vel sustentatur: Actio verò eductiva est sustentatio et inhaesio, quia est id, quo mediante aliquid à subiecto distinctum causatur et sustentatur seu inhaeret. Quare sicut ipse terminus creatus per actionem creativam nec se nec aliud quidvis causat, ita nec ea actio in eo recepta dici potest esse causalitas eius termini ceu subiecti. è contrario verò sicut per actionem eductivam aliquid à subiecto, in quo ea recipitur et cui ipsa ea actio esse non dat, distinctum causatur et sustentatur; ita etiam ea actio dici potest esse causalitas eius subiecti in effectum à subiecto distinctum. dum autem terminus creatus dicitur subiectum adhaesionis, per id non significatur, terminum eum ab actione extrinsecè tantùm affici, (cum verè afficiatur ab eâ intrinsecè, non minus quam ab actione eductiva subiectum sustentationis) sed solum, quod ab ea non afficiatur intrinsecè, ut causa intrinseca à causalitate, sicut afficitur intrinsecè materia ab actione eductivâ, quâ mediante effectus generatur.

**X.** A Formal cause, as the received usage of philosophers names it, is that which intrinsically completes the being of a thing, by bestowing a certain being upon a subject that is of itself indifferent; this is either substantial, if the form be substantial and pertains to the first concept of the thing, or accidental, if the form itself is outside the first concept of the thing and is accidental. A formal cause, or formal principle, from which a thing has determined being, is constituted in the first act or in the being of an essential part capable of composing through the transcendental relation to the composite itself, as this denotes the subject and the possible union, just as matter is in the being of a possible part through the relation to the form and the possible union. The formal causality of the cause into the composite (which is the primary effect of this cause, not taken in a strict physical sense) is the union itself as it holds itself from the side of the form, and it is called information. Philosophers commonly assign as the negative secondary effect of the formal cause the expulsion of the prior form, which, according to the ordinary course of nature, accompanies every generation; and indeed, if the cessation of the prior form in the subject is accepted causally, so that it is on account of the introduction of the new form, then this (not as actually causing, but as potent to cause in its own way) is prior in nature to the expulsion of the prior form, though simultaneous in time. But if the cessation of the prior form is accepted precisely formally, then it is neither prior nor posterior in nature to the introduction of the new form, since in this way neither is the cause or effect of the other. The cause of the expulsion as such, in the way it is caused, is the cause itself ceasing to conserve, and the non-conservation is the causality of this negative effect. If, however, the expulsion is on account of the introduction of the new form, then the producer of the new form is also the cause of the expulsion, insofar as, according to the course of nature, it determines GOD to not conserve the prior form. Furthermore, every absolute and intrinsic formal cause, viewed in the first physical act, is prior to its effect or composite by a priority of both nature and origin. Not so every modal formal cause, which is not prior to its effect by a priority "in whom" really, but only "from whom." A formal cause that is extrinsic is neither always absolutely prior to its effect or specificated thing by a priority "from whom" nor "in whom," since it is not properly a cause but rather a terminus essentially terminating the relation of another to itself, and therefore in these a mutual specification does not imply [a contradiction].

**XI.** An Efficient cause, comparing it with other causes of a different genus, is the first principle in execution from which or by whom is movement or rest, not only negative but positive, or the conservation of a thing; or it is a principle influencing being into another by itself, precise of any intrinsic change of itself, as far as it is precisely from the reason of influence in the genus of efficient cause. Insofar as the same can simultaneously be a material cause and the subject of its own action, it can influence an effect distinct from itself with an intrinsic change of itself. It becomes actually causing through the actual production or action itself, which is its causality, and it is distinguished really and modally from the efficient cause itself (whether educing or creating) as well as from the produced terminus (producible by another cause or in another way), or as a modal entity from an absolute being. That entity of modal action is said, as are others of the same kind, to be such because their physical essence is to actually exercise that which they are, so that it is impossible for such a being to be placed in the nature of things as existing without it being intrinsic to some other and actually exercising what it is; so that if action exists, it cannot be without actually exercising the reason of action, and it is intrinsic to the terminus or to the subject alone if it is creative; or also to the subject if it is educative. Nisi in quibusdam ex speciali aliqua ratione implicet.

X. Formalis causa, vt Philosophorum receptus vsus, nominat, est quae intrinsece complet esse rei, subiecto scilicet de se indifferenti certum esse tribuens, vel substantiale, si forma sit substantialis, & de primo conceptu rei, vel accidentale, si ipsa forma sit extra primum rei conceptum & accidentalis. Constituitur causa formalis seu principium formale, a quo res habet determinatum esse, in actu primo seu in esse partis essentialis potentis componere per ipsam respectum transcendentalem ad compositum, vt hoc dicit subiectum & vnionem possibilem, sicut materia in esse partis possibilis per respectum ad formam & vnionem possibilem. Causalitas formalis causae in compositum (quod solum causae huius non in rigore physico sumptae, effectus primarius est) est ipsa unio vt se tenet ex parte formae & informatio dicitur. Secundarium effectum causae formalis negatiuum communiter assignant expulsionem formae prioris, quae iuxta cursum naturae ordinarium omnem generationem comitatur; & quidem si desitio formae prioris in subiecto accipiatur causaliter, vt sit propter introductionem formae nouae, tum haec non quidem vt actu causans, sed vt potens suo modo causare, expulsione formae prioris natura prior est, tempore vero simul, si vero ipsa desitio formae prioris accipiatur praecise formaliter, tum Introductione formae nouae nec prior est natura, nec posterior, cum vt sic neutra sit alterius causa, aut effectus. Expulsionis autem vt sic causa est, eo modo quo causatur, ipsa causa cessans conseruare, & non conseruatio effectus huius negatiui causalitas. Si vero expulsio sit propter introductionem formae nouae, tum ipsum quoque producens formam nouam Expulsionis causa est, in quantum iuxta cursum naturae DEVM determinat ad non conseruandam formam priorem. Ceterum omnis causa formalis absoluta & intrinseca, spectata in actu primo physico prior est effectu suo seu composito prioritate & naturae & originis. Non item omnis causa formalis modalis, quae non est prior suo effectu prioritate in quo reali sed a quo tantum. Causa vero formalis extrinseca neque semper absolute prior est effectu suo seu specificato prioritate a quo, neque in quo, cum nec proprie causa fit sed potius terminus alterius ad se habitudinem essentialiter terminans, & ideo in his specificatio mutua non implicat.

XI. Causa Efficiens comparando eam cum alijs causis diuersi generis, est primum principium in executione vnde seu a quo est motus vel quies non tantum negatiua sed positiua seu conseruatio rei, vel est principium per se influens esse in aliud, praecisam mutatione sui intrinsecam omni, quantum est praecise ex ratione influxus in genere causae efficientis, in quantum enim eadem simul potest esse causa materialis, & suae actionis subiectum, potest esse influere in effectum a se distinctum cum intrinsecam sui mutatione. Fit actu causans per ipsam actualem productionem seu actionem quae est eius causalitas, & tam ab ipsa causa efficiente, siue educente siue creante, quam a termino producto, ab alia causa vel alio modo producibili, distinguitur realiter modaliter; seu tanquam entitas modalis, ab ente absoluto. Dicitur autem entitas ea actionis modalis, vt & aliae eiusdem rationis, ex eo quod ipsa earum essentia physica sit, actu exercere id quod sunt, ita vt impossibile sit poni huiusmodi ens in rerum natura existens, quin alicui alteri sit intrinsecum & actu exerceat id quod est, ita vt si actio sit, esse non possit, quin actu rationem actionis exerceat, & sit intrinseca termino vel soli, si creatiua est; vel etiam subiecto, si est eductiua. Jesuitarum castris fervent, quorum hoc potissimùm sudorem ciet: Si DEUS est infinitus, nullum datur malum, nullum bonitatis gradus. Nam unius infinitas omne contrarium omnemque distantiarum à perfectione Divinâ inaequalitatem destruit. Nec non Necessitati Divinae Philosophorum libertas opponit hoc maximè ratiocinium: Quicquid intrinsecè aliquid adsciscit, intrinsecè mutatur. A. DEUS. E. quinimò instat et contra simplicitatem: Ubicunque datur unio ibi compositio. A. datur in DEO unio personarum ac naturarum. E. Hae omnia tamen speciosa magis quàm solida. Im. statim ex parte lubrico, ex parte falso nititur fulcimento: Nam nullam teneor possibilitatis aseitatem largiri ex eo, quia possibile semper aliud, potentiam puta, praesupponit, à quo producatur, et in quâ niduletur potentiâ. nec Chimera habet repugnantiam à se sed à DEO, non quidem ex illius impotentiâ qualis ipsi nulla est, sed perfectione summâ, quâ essentias confundere nauseat, potiusque sigillatim dispertiendo compossibilitatem iisdem denegat. Hostii telum flabello aeque facili potest averti: Quicquid Beati intuitivè vident per speciem realem comprehensivam id est finitum, ita negat Minorem. per intentionalem apprehensivam. Negat connexionem Majorem. Ipsis demùm Jesuiticis argutiis ipsius Moguntini Scholastici responsionem oppono: *Si DEVS est infinitus, nullum datur malum, nullum Bonitatis gradus.* scilicet in DEO, concedit extra, negat. Scrupulum Necessitati oggestum omissis G. Vasquez, A. Calov. et cetera responsionibus, ita expungo: Quicquid aliud intrinsecè adsciscit per modum subjecti quod antea non habuit. Ita negat Minorem. per modum termini. negat consequentiam. Argumentationem colophonis loco agmen claudentem ita annihilo: ubi datur unio subjectiva entalis stricta. ibi datur compositio. et negat Minorem.

### VII. DEVS ens est intrinsecè immensum ac aeternum.

Intrinsecè dico, cum DEO, cujus absoluta Infinitas aeternùm in se omnem colligit perfectionem, immensitas ac aeternitas competant independenter à coexistentiâ creaturarum nec non successivis extrinseci temporis vicibus, adeoque intrinsecè aequipollet immensitas perfectioni extensionis permanentis, successivae aeternitas. Siquidem immensitatis punctum omne ambit spatium, unumque ac indivisibile aeternitatis nunc, quemadmodum Sphaera maxima minores concentricas, omne claudit tempus. imò indivisibilis DEI immensitas

And they recognize the Emperor immediately by that name, and the rights annexed to their territories, which are called rights of superiority, or in German <term>Landts Obrigkeit</term> <gloss>territorial jurisdiction/authority</gloss>. For to whom the territory, properly understood, belongs, to him also belongs the jurisdiction, or the right inherent in the territory <note>Camillus Borellius, Consultation 70, number 34</note>. Therefore, the imperial cities indeed possess the rights of a prince, but the real rights of a prince, not personal rights. I say that imperial cities nonetheless possess the rights of a prince, because they have from the Emperor, in perpetuity, royal prerogatives <term>regalia</term> <gloss>sovereign rights</gloss> with both mixed and absolute jurisdiction <note>jurisdiction covering both minor and major civil and criminal matters</note>. They exercise these royal prerogatives in free and imperial cities by the right of the territory to which they are inherent, and not only those which are expressed in the chapter "Which are Royal Prerogatives," but also if there are others which, by received custom, are held as royal prerogatives. Although these flow from the Imperial Majesty in different ways and more powerfully into dukes, marquises, and princes than into cities, that greater or lesser degree does nothing to the substance, nor does it detract anything from the formal essence <note>Bartolus on the law "Infamem," Digest, Concerning Public Judgments; Gail, Book 2, Observation 57, number 7</note>.

*Princes, by virtue of this perpetual jurisdiction granted to them, exercise territorial right in their provinces just as the Emperor does in the entire Empire:*

Hence, princes seem to owe their principalities to the grace of God, which is witnessed in their rescripts, edicts, and letters as "We, by the grace of God." Formerly, not only princes and dukes, but even those inferior to them, used the same title, as testified by <note>Jean</note> Bodin, Book 1 of the Republic, chapter 10. For this reason, that law of Constantine was misunderstood by many, especially by Accursius, while he interprets "urban plebs," that is, Roman, arguing from the fact that that law was directed to Eusebius, Prefect of the City, when, however, it is directed to Eusebius, Governor of Lycia and Pamphylia, and speaks of the plebs of those cities. Accursius was deceived in the understanding of those abbreviations "V. P."; for he thought they were to be understood as "City Prefect," when, however, they are to be understood as "Praetorian Man." Which is also found everywhere and is proved by the reason that Eusebius, to whom Constantine writes, could not be Prefect of the City and Governor of Lycia and Pamphylia; he could indeed preside over those provinces, since he had previously been a Praetor somewhere; therefore, he was called so for the sake of honor. The same is indicated by similar abbreviations written in other places, "V. C.," which signify a Consular man, that is, one who had previously been a Consul. Contius also seems to have written very poorly on the rubric *On the capitation of citizens, etc.*, that is, *Roman*; because that law does not speak of Roman citizens living in Rome or elsewhere, but of the urban plebs in the Cities of Lycia and Pamphylia, and it is said, by the example of other Oriental provinces, that it is also to be exempted, namely, that those heads are not to be counted with the others. Thus also the title seems to be badly composed (whoever it may have been) since the title *On Citizens* is placed before a law speaking about the urban plebs; for that word, "Citizens," includes others also, besides the plebs, as everyone knows: And truly, their error can in no way be defended, because never from approved authors

Indeed, there is such robbery and sacrilege, and such a persecution of God and divine worship—by the faith of God and men—as no Christian would ever have hoped for. So much so that one can see that what Christ is believed to have said to the Jews selling and buying in the temple, according to the Evangelist, has superabounded in these people in every way. For they are so far from having made a house of prayer out of a house of negotiation that they have leveled even the most sumptuous temples to the ground and turned them into their own sacrilegious structures. Others, if they have not destroyed them, they have at least despoiled. From still others, finally, they establish stables for oxen and horses. <margin>Should the belly not be constipated?</margin>
¶ One should also take care that the body does not remain stopped up, but one must come to his aid with suppositories, with enemas, and in other ways, as is usually customary. Above all this, it is to be noted how one should proceed with the boils, which are, however, not of one kind. Since the humors are also of various kinds, the colors of the boils are generally uniform with the humors, and from this it is to be noted that not all kinds of boils are to be treated equally quickly.

<margin>The ulcer must be opened.</margin>
This, however, one must note: that one must not delay with the opening, but open them with all diligence, and in no way apply what might drive them back in. ושלמה ותרין עשר שבטין וכל נשמתין דשתין רבוא דישראל ורכל דלין עלאין ותתאין לא נעדר: לא חסר מנייהו חד מחשבנא כגוונא רצבא השמים: ועוד מרוב אונים ולא כהנא בהון כי אה אלהים ראה אלאה ראהאלאבשה בגבורה וברא עלמא במדח דהין: ובעינא איהו גבור אמיץ כח: איש לא נעדר לא יעקב דאמר ביה ויעקב איש תם (לשון כה) (3) מה דאמר בתלת אלין אתמר בתלת עלאין: ואתמר בתלת תתאין:

תקונא חמשים וחד וחמשים רפט טאעב דמחי צבי קד

תולדין דתהו דאתרמיז בראשי תיבין ולידת השמים והארץ תהו ואינון חמש משי דאתמר בהו כדאמר בראשי תיבין דאתמר בהו נפיליס דעסקין רפאים ובגין דא אתמר בהו דאתהדר בהו בגיניהון דאתהדר בגין דבהו בראם דלספקא לשכינתא והוה אתמר לה תהו בראת למיטב בגיניהון לשבת יצרה למעבד ישובא מנייהו. ובגין האי ה' אלה דאינון תלת אבהן וקרין להו תלת צלותין לגנתא בהון לקב"ה לספקא לשכינתא בהון דאיהי ה' זעירא דעמודא דאמצעיתא איהי גופא ותרין דרועין דיליה ימינא ושמאלא דבהון אחיד בר נש וגופא. ועל גופא דא אתמר דאיהי דאית ליה חמשיא במספר צבאות וכל ישראל דאינון שאין רבא מתיחסין בצבא דלעילא. לכלם בשם יקרא כלהו אתקריאו על שם צבא דלעילא: איש לא נעדר מחשבנא. ושכינתא בגלותא בגינא דאיהו מרחקא בעלה כלה מיה לזמנין אתפרנסת על ידי (ג) שליח לזמנין על ידי אברהם ולזמנין על ידי אימא: לזמנין לזמנין על ידי בני. לזמנין על ידי דצדיק. וכלא יהיב ליהא דאיהו לזמנין איהו בן אבא ואימא. בן יה' אבר איהו בין אבא ואימא נחת לה פרנסתא על ידי אבא ואימא וכי דאית בהון ד' רקיעין נחית לה פרנסא נחית לה פרנסא בתרי רקיעין וכר נחית בגופא דאיהו יעקב נחית לה מזונא על ידיה. וכר נחית בתרין שוקין ראינו שוקין עומדין שש דאית בהון ד' רקיעין נחית לה מזונא על ידיהו. וכר נחית בצדיק נחית לה מזונא על ידיה. וכר נחית בה' דאתחברו בה לא צריך לנחתא מזונא לה ע"י שליחא בעלמא אלא על ידית. וכר נפק בה אסתליק עד אין סוף דאיהו מזונא דיליה או כוונא דיליה לאו בזכותא חדא מלאה ולא בעי דאתינן אבא ואימא ולא בעי דאתינן רצות והוה אלא במילא תליא מלתא. וכר נחיתת מאתרהא ונחת קב"ה לדיירא עמה אתמר בה ובבנא איהו בין לישראל אלא קב"ה דאיהו אבא ואימא ואיהו ברך ומתפרנס על ידיה ראיהו עבד עולם עקב דיליה ובההוא זימנא איהי אתפרנסת ע"י שריו וכל דא כפום עובריהון דישראל הכי אתפרנסת. זכאה איהו מאן דסליק לה לאתראא ולקב"ה לאתריה ראתמר ביה (הנה יהוה רוכב על עב קל (ישעיה יט) הנה יהוה מוקומון זעיר כו') וכל דא כפום עובדיהון דשראל הכי אתפרנסת. זכאה איהו מאן דסליק לה לאתראא ולקב"ה לאתריה ראתמר ביה (הנה יהוה רוכב על עב קל (ישעיה יט) הנה יהוה מוקומון זעיר כו') וכל דא כפום עובדיהון דשראל דאמר (נ) אם אנון שעת לעיני לעפשי תנצוח עד אמצא מקום לוי' וכין ת"ח קלג) בההוא זמנא דבר נש אחזור ליה לאתריה מה כתיב ביה ממקום יפן ברחמיו לעמר ובמאי חוזרין ליה * לאתריה אלא בשלימו דתקונא דתקינו בצלותא וצוחא אובח רבדהו דאמר מסקומן פן ברחמיו לעמר. אמר החסידים אית שמו ערב ובקר תמיד בכל יום אומרים פעמים (ד) ואינון ה' דהו צריך לאחזרא לגבי ה' דאיהו מקום דלעילא ולאחזרא לי לגבי ה' דאתא ורזא דמנא לא אבא בער וגו' (קשע יט) והא אוקמת:

בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ מאי אלא הכי אוקמוה קדמאין כל אתין לרביא * דא אוריחא בילסלא מא ועדת דבה אברהם. שמא דאקרא יאדער את השמים שמים דא קב"ה דאיתו ואתון תשע השמים (מלכים פ') (פ) דא את בוניה עמיה. ואת צדיק ובת אינה הארץ מאנא דכללה לאפקא בה זרעין ואיבין ודא דמסת וכל שיח השדה טרם יהא באריקו (לפנות 6) אמר דא רכלא אתקן ברזא דאיהא הכא אע"ד דכלא אחברי ואתקן בשמא דליה דאתינן את השם יושב השלם דכלה דשמא דאמצעיתא. ולמה (כ) בגין דאדם אין דאיתונין הא ואן האלקער לאתא אדמתא. א"ל ר' אלעזר אבא שמי מ"ל דאיהו צדיק. א"ל ב"ה שבת ה' איהו י"ב אינהו כליל תלת צריכי צאן ראשר דאילנא ורא ח' עלמין דאיהו את בצבא דליה צבאות. וכל איתא עמהון כליל תלת דרגין לקבל תלת עפפין רש' ואת תלתא אבהן אינון. אלא ש קלאת עפפי אילנא (נ) ש תחתה שרשי אילנא וגבין רא וכל שמא דא צדיק. וכל דא כפום עובדיהון דשראל דאמר (נ) אם אנון שעת לעיני לעפשי תנצוח עד אמצא מקום לוי' וכין ת"ח קלג) בההוא זמנא דבר נש אחזור ליה לאתריה מה כתיב ביה ממקום יפן ברחמיו לעמר ובמאי חוזרין ליה * לאתריה אלא בשלימו דתקונא דתקינו בצלותא וצוחא אובח רבדהו דאמר מסקומן פן ברחמיו לעמר. אמר החסידים אית שמו ערב ובקר תמיד בכל יום אומרים פעמים (ד) ואינון ה' דהו צריך לאחזרא לגבי ה' דאיהו מקום דלעילא ולאחזרא לי לגבי ה' דאתא ורזא דמנא לא אבא בער וגו' (קשע יט) והא אוקמת:

<meta>This page continues the exposition on the mystical meanings of the word "Bereshit" (In the beginning) and transitions into Correction Forty-Nine, focusing on the sanctity of the Sabbath, the nature of the divine emanations, and the cosmic struggle against the "Other Side."</meta>

# Correction Forty-Nine

Correction Forty-Nine, which was made as a holy desire.

(It is taught that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, may he rest in peace, said that where the Sabbath resides, sadness should not approach. For sadness stems from the spirit of the "Other Side," which is the fire of Gehenna. Regarding this, it is said: *You shall kindle no fire in all your dwellings on the Sabbath day.* <note>Exodus 35:3</note>). What is the meaning of "to harness" <note>original: "לרתם" (lertam); likely a play on the word for the broom tree or harnessing spiritual forces</note>? It refers to the purification that makes a dwelling for the Sabbath. One must turn away from the Evil Inclination, who is the one who profanes the Sabbath. The "Covenant of Eternity" is the **Tzaddik** <note>The Sefirah of Yesod, represented as the "Righteous One"</note> who dwells within that Garden.

The children of Israel possess two kidneys <note>symbolizing advice and conscience</note>, which are called the "River" and the "Ancient Brook." The "Seventh" <note>the Sabbath</note> refers to the three Patriarchs who are the branches of the Sabbath. *A river went out of Eden to water the garden* <note>Genesis 2:10</note>. There is a "River" and there is a "Stream." This river is called the "Ancient Brook." Concerning this "Seventh," it is said: *No eye has seen, O God, besides You* <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>. This river is the letter **Vav** <note>representing the six lower Sefirot</note> that emerges from the Supernal Eden—which is the letter **Heh**—and passes through the "Father and Mother" <note>Chokhmah and Binah</note> for five hundred years until it reaches the seventh, the **Tzaddik**. From that bounty, it waters the Garden, which is the **Lower Shekhinah**.

(3) And the "Well" is the one who makes a dwelling for the Sabbath, which is the heart. No sadness or bitterness should approach there, for that is the fire of Gehenna. Regarding this, it is said: *You shall kindle no fire in all your dwellings on the Sabbath day.* This is certainly true; anyone who becomes angry on the Sabbath, it is as if they have ignited the fire of Gehenna. There are thirty-nine classes of forbidden work <note>original: "ארבעה מלאכות חסר חד"; literally forty minus one</note> corresponding to the "forty lashes minus one" <note>the judicial punishment</note>.

For Israel, this is why they say: "Move it from its place and leave it outside its place and its domain." Acting thus is as if one uprooted the tree of the "Sign of the Covenant" and placed it in a foreign domain. Whoever does this uproots their soul from its own domain and places it in another domain, which is the domain of bitterness and anger. This caused Israel to be uprooted from the Land of Israel and exiled to a foreign land, which is the "Public Domain" <note>Reshut HaRabim</note>. This is what happens to one who brings their "Holy Sign of the Covenant" into a foreign domain. 

**Saturn** <note>original: "שבתאי" (Shabbatai)</note> corresponds to the spleen, where evil is seen. The "Black Bile" is also Saturn, and of it, it is said: *The pit was empty; there was no water in it* <note>Genesis 37:24</note>. There was no water, but there were snakes and scorpions. This represents hunger, thirst, lamentation, mourning, and darkness. This is the exile where Israel must serve for two years in Babylon, as established. This corresponds to "mundane speech," which is forbidden on the Sabbath.

When the soul finds no place to rest there, it flees, just as it was said of the wicked one: *From the presence of my mistress I am fleeing* <note>Genesis 16:8</note>. Regarding the "Spleen," it is said: *Keep your foot from being bare* <note>Jeremiah 2:25</note>. A person's shoes should be prepared and not worn out. Because the place upon which you stand is "Holy Ground"—this refers to the Sabbath. Concerning this, it is said: *I have washed my feet; how can I defile them?* <note>Song of Songs 5:3</note>. Because of this, a person must change their clothes, their lamps, and their food on the Sabbath. One must add from the "mundane" <note>the Friday afternoon time</note> to the "holy" <note>the Sabbath</note>. Everyone who adds, God adds to them <note>blessing</note>; but for those who subtract, it is subtracted from them.

# Correction Forty-Nine (continued)

**In the beginning God created:** *Lift up your eyes on high and see: Who created these?* <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>. "Who" <note>Mi</note> and "These" <note>EleH</note> together form the name **Elohim**. *Lift up your eyes on high*—this is the secret of the "Shema" <note>The "Hear O Israel" prayer</note> that Israel recites to the Holy One, Blessed be He. This happens twice, making a total of fifty <note>representing the fifty Gates of Understanding</note>. How should it be recited? Like the dawn, as it is said: *Let the earth sprout grass* <note>Genesis 1:11</note>, a mystery that is hidden within the depths.

It is written: *He who brings out their host by number* <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>. Because of this, the "Shema" is recited at night, as the Masters of the Mishnah established regarding the Exodus from Egypt. A person must declare the Kingdom of the King, for He performs wonders within it. The "Morning" is the return to Him. This is the "Evening" of Isaac and the "Morning" of Abraham, and the "Covenant" is between them for Israel. *He who brings out*—this refers to "He who brings forth bread from the earth" <note>The blessing over bread</note>. Because of the Shema, the Priest gives him bread. This corresponds to the 248 words of the Shema.

*He calls them all by name*—as it says, *And the man gave names...* <note>Genesis 2:20</note>. This is what is said: *As the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house* <note>Isaiah 44:13</note>. He called names for all the "Holy Living Creatures" <note>Chayot HaKodesh</note>, the Seraphim, the Ophanim, and the Heavenly Host. He called them all by name to the place he inherited, so they would be preserved. From the place they originate, they are free and have dominion. 

*By the greatness of His might* <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>—this refers to the **Supernal Crown** <note>Keter</note>. And I say that "Power" <note>Koach</note> is that which returns. Or, "By the greatness of His might" refers to the "Middle Pillar" <note>Tiferet</note>, and His "Strength" refers to **Netzach** and **Hod**. I say that "Power" refers to the **Tzaddik**. *Not one is missing* <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>—this refers to the Man of Israel, the Levite.

*Lift up your eyes on high*—afterward, Rabbi Shimon stood and said: "This is how I heard this verse." *Lift up your eyes on high*: "On high" refers to the place where all eyes are lifted. This is the "Holy Wisdom" <note>Chokhmah</note>. *Who created these?* "Who" <note>Mi</note> is the Supernal Mother <note>Binah</note>, who created the world through "These" <note>EleH</note>. *He calls them all by name*—through their Father and Mother, who are the three Patriarchs. *He who brings out their host by number*—these are the hosts of heaven which are hidden and unique. What is the "Number"? It is not just counting, but the "Sefirah" and "Account" <note>original: "מספר וחשבן"</note>, which in its totality is the **Shekhinah**. *He calls them all by name*—this is the Shekhinah, who was called by name for Moses in the bush and was sanctified by the Name. From this comes the mystery of what is said: *And he shall increase greatly in the midst of the earth* <note>Genesis 48:16</note>. This is the **Tzaddik**, who is "Mighty in Power." The "Tzaddik" is the foundation. His strength is the "Power" of the work of Creation, of which it is said: *And now, I pray, let the power of my Lord be great* <note>Numbers 14:17</note>. *Not one is missing*—from the Shekhinah forever. And this is not difficult, for there are seventy faces to the Torah.

An old man said to him: "Old man, old man! This is truly hidden and concealed, and it was said: 'These' came first, and there was the wife of Isaac."

It also delves into the linguistic mysticism of "Elohim," formed by the union of "Mi" (Who) and "EleH" (These), representing the creative forces of the divine Sefirot.</summary>

It is the Soul, by whose benefit nourishment is converted into the substance of man, blood is diffused through the veins by a marvelous circulation, humors are tempered for the safety of the body, the vigor of the heart is fostered by the perpetual vicissitude of breathing, and flesh and bones are continuously nourished both for the tallness of stature and for the increase of strength. Finally, it is the Soul that, with no effort and no labor, tempers and bends the mass of the whole body; that preserves whole and inviolate that noble framework of limbs disposed in such singular order, the inexplicable conjunction of all nerves and vertebrae, and the admirable connections in the compacted bones for the sake of a longer life. Take the soul from the body, and instantly the face will collapse, the cheeks will turn pale, the eyes will wither, the tongue will go silent, the hands will grow weak, the feet will subside, the senses will become numb, the blood will freeze, the arteries will turn to stone, the limbs will grow cold, the entire structure of the human body will grow torpid like an immovable trunk, and finally the flesh will degenerate into worms, and the bones into the lightest dust. Thus, indeed, does the body depend upon the presence and conjunction of the Soul, that without it the body is nothing, but with it, it can do all things.

in that month began his first Consulship, brought an end to the civil wars after Egypt was reduced to the power of the Republic, and brought most splendid triumphs into the city, being so called by the decree of the Fathers), consecrated you as Augustus in August—and indeed on the first day of August, so that you might be both Julius and Augustus at once—through the solemn ministry of holy hands and the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, which is auxiliary to Heaven.

Now, therefore, by the festive birthdays, by the names of the first Caesars of your family, by the Monarchs who undertook the governance of the human race at the same age as you, and by the most fruitful part of the year, the three months sacred to the first Roman Caesars and to your own fortune, having already been made four times fecund in happy omens, we foresee that you will be five, nay six and seven times most happy thereafter, because you are the fifteenth of your one august House, and the fourteenth Emperor from Rudolph I, as if he were the Julius of your family, and you are a Helius Hadrian. Who, even if not a German, could deny that you are the Sun of Germany, given the Greek «Helius»? Now, the ancients said the sun comes from «solus» <gloss>alone</gloss>, because it is alone and unique in the world; and you, **LEOPOLD**, in the world,

are the sole and unique Emperor; you, who alone, even with the sun, obtain the leadership of all the other stars of the globe of the earth.

is spread out, and confesses how much it is divided. Numbers follow. Thus the old Samian <note>Pythagoras</note> knew how to solve them, thus he knew how to bind them, or the measurer of the sand <note>Archimedes</note>. Go on, nor stop your foot, captured by the sweetness of those things. There are arts which life demands for itself, and which it is pleasant to have learned, but so that they may be viewed by acting. What disputes do I see? From here the eloquent offspring of the house of Socrates, not one, from here the stern Porch will call you: from here the Gargettian <note>Epicurus</note> resting in his calm garden. 

You rather hear everyone, nor wish to devote yourself to one crowd or to have made sides. He judges badly who favors: the names of the authors hinder the truth. Therefore, but being your own, with reason alone as mistress, ask what the nature of the good is, whether it consists solidly in the honorable, or whether it is fitting that praises and wealth and the use of a healthy body be called the moments of a happy life. Now two crowds proceed from different camps: on the right, the sisters mindful of the upright, a pious crowd. One directs her heavy eyes now here, now there, seeing what is to come long before: the other holds savage death under her feet, and, overcome by no pain, feeds on adversities. There is one who holds the reins of character with certain moderation: captive pleasure follows. 

But another awaits where the weights of the scale incline, adding nothing herself: for anger and favor are far away. But Clemency takes something away from punishments: they fight gently and as if they were laws that did not want to win. For that one, the right hand flows more lavishly than the reddening Hermus, but she wishes to donate wealth, not to lose it: around her, Grace, with a smiling face, leads the dances. There is also she who admits offered honors, and thinks herself of such worth. Holy Faith stands as an immobile rock, nor is Love feigned: and Constancy, equal to herself, banishing the motions of the breast, just as the highest peak of Olympus hears the thunders and the hissing clouds below, nor does it shudder at the thrown fires of the lightning. But on the other side, Fear fixes its paling face on the earth: Cares approach in a tattered swarm, and lying Deceits. Insatiate Famine and the unhealthy love of having brood over stolen gold:

To Pharamundus succeeded his son Clodio the Long-Haired, to whom succeeded Meroveus, a man of such probity that the <term>Merovingi</term> <gloss>Merovingians</gloss>, who are now called Franks, were named from him. To this Meroveus succeeded his son Childericus, to whom succeeded Clodoveus, who was the first of the kings of the Franks to believe in Christ, baptized by the blessed Remigius. And these things you will find in the chronicles of the kings of the Franks and the princes.

Marica, according to some, is said to be Circe, the daughter of the Sun, the queen. <note>Refers to Virgil, Aeneid.</note>

Marius was a certain man of ignoble birth who became a Roman power of unheard-of cruelty; his fortune varied so that at times he was supremely happy, at times supremely unhappy. Lucan: "That was the mode of life for Marius, enduring all things that prior fortune can, and better than all." This is the same Marius whom we said above conquered Jugurtha by the advice and aid of Sulla. And note that the greatest slaughter followed in Rome from the civil war, with Marius and Sulla as authors, in which slaughter it is read that for ten years one hundred and fifty thousand Romans were killed. Marius is also a first name for a poet. <note>Refers to Ovid.</note> And Marius, a name written in every genre.

Marmaridae are certain people of Africa who live among snakes without injury, like Mars. Lucan in the ninth: "The unique race inhabits the lands, immune from the savage bite of snakes, the Marmaridae." For they are called Marmaridae from the place.

Maro is called Virgil, for he had many names, namely Publius Vergilius Maro. This Virgil, as Donatus testifies, was the most learned of poets, a man of great philosophy, a native of Mantua, who became a great friend to Octavianus Augustus, under whom the Lord was born, and to other magnates of the imperial court. He left many monuments of his genius. Among others, he made the <term>Bucolics</term>, the <term>Georgics</term>, and the book of the <term>Aeneid</term>. It is said he also made very powerful little books, of which one is called the <term>Copa Virgilii</term> <gloss>Virgil's Hostess</gloss>, another is called the <term>Moretum Virgilii</term> <gloss>Virgil's Salad</gloss>. His epitaph: "Mantua gave me birth, Calabria took me, Parthenope holds me; I sang of pastures, fields, leaders."

Mars, or Mavors, or Gradivus, is the god of arms, the god of war. He is feigned to be born without the union of Jupiter and Juno, by the touch of a certain flower, and is not accustomed to be appeased by human blood. Ovid, <term>Fasti</term> I: "Mars, you who edit the arts in the end of the year, I pray that Jupiter does not yet know of this." In the family and company of this Mars are fury, and anger, and fear.

And this very diversity will shine forth from the Medium, both natural and legal, through which any exchange must be recalled to equality, by which things to be exchanged are estimated, namely from the Need for things and Money. For need alone causes any thing to be so much more precious the more someone has needed it, and for that reason it is called by the Philosopher the cause of all exchange and communication of things, or as his words sound in Greek, <term>ἡ χρεία συνέχει πάντα</term> <gloss>need holds everything together</gloss>. Nor is this without reason. For if men needed nothing, there would certainly be no need for communication and exchange of things and services, which is openly false; since no mortal has yet existed who does not need the help of another. Money, however, the vicar and subsidy of need, was for this reason invented by men, so that since one often does not need that thing which another desires to exchange, money may then be offered in its place, by which the thing desired by us may afterwards be obtained. Just as if a farmer at that time does not need shoes, which the shoemaker needs grain, then in place of shoes the shoemaker counts money to the farmer for the grain, and thus money supplies the need of both.

§. IX. But what of Corrective or Punitive Justice? Since the law of Retaliation is most occupied with this, would it simply receive that without any consideration of circumstances? Let our Philosopher answer for us in this business:

XXXIII. HEALTH is indicated by sputum that receives concoction in a mature manner, which appears red or citrine in the first days, but on the fourth day it is matured and changes into white or sub-citrine; in substance and color it is well-behaved, namely white, light, equal, and continuous, not watery, nor foamy, nor viscous; and which is excreted easily and promptly.

XXXIV. The signs of DEATH, however, are: no sputum (unless the pleurisy is very slight), a pulse that is extremely hard, small, and very frequent due to heat; some flow of blood in the beginning without the alleviation of symptoms, diarrhea supervening as the liver and stomach are drawn into consensus, a sunken face, jaundice of the eyes, and dimness.

XXXV. The LENGTH of the disease is shown by raw or unconcocted pleurisies, but the BREVITY by concocted ones; and the more slowly the signs of concoction begin to appear, the longer the disease will be; but the more quickly signs, both good and bad, reveal themselves, the more quickly the pleurisy will tend either to health or to death.

XXXVI. Regarding the MANNER OF THE OUTCOME, we note only these things: if a pleuritic patient spits out white, smooth, and equal matter on the fourth day, the disease will terminate on the seventh. But if on the seventh, the pleurisy will not last beyond the eleventh or fourteenth day.

XXXVII. Whatever pleurisy is not resolved upwards by sputum within fourteen days, it is transformed into empyema. The same happens if neither the purging of sputum, nor a loosened bowel, nor bloodletting, nor medicine, nor diet could soothe the pains of the sides.

XXXVI. De Modo EVENTVS hæc tantùm notamus. Pleuriticus si quarto die album, læve & æquale exspuat, morbus in septimo terminabitur. Si verò septimo, ultra undecimum aut decimum quartum diem pleuritis non durabit.

XXXVII. Quæcunque pleuritis intra quatuordecim dies superne per sputum non solvitur, ea cum empyemate transmutatur. Idem fit si dolores laterum neque sputi purgatio, neque soluta alvus, neque sanguinis missio, neque medicamentum, neque victus ratio sedare potuit.

seed: ...of the healthfulness of the air, of the shape and arrangement of the sky and the heavenly paths, and most of all of the fixed and constant stars of the eighth sphere which were never seen or described by our ancestors, I will say hereafter. Therefore, first regarding the people, we found in these lands and regions so many and such great peoples, throngs, and nations that no one could recount them, as one reads in the Apocalypse. I saw a people mild, kindly, and skillful, and they all go naked, both women and men, and entirely without covering their bodies in any way. As they come from their mother's womb, so they go until they die. They are tall of body, square-built, well-formed, of good and beautiful proportions, and colored somewhat toward red, which I believe happens because they go naked and are colored by the sun. They also have long and thick black hair. They are active and agile in their walk and play, and have kindly, beautiful faces, which they nonetheless make ugly and distorted themselves, for they bore holes in their own cheeks, lips, noses, and ears. You should not think that such holes are small or that they have only one, for I have seen some who have seven holes in their faces, each so large that a pebble could easily fit into one. They plug these holes themselves with polished stones, crystals, marble, and alabaster, quite pretty and beautiful, and with white bone and other things made with art according to their custom and usage. And if you thus see such a strange, unusual, and very wondrous thing, namely a man who has in his cheeks alone and in his lips seven stones, some of which are half a span in length, you will not be without great wonder. For I have often observed and estimated that seven such stones weigh over sixteen <term>lot</term> <gloss>a unit of weight, roughly 16-18 grams per lot</gloss>, and besides that, their ears are pierced with three holes, and they carry other stones that hang in rings. And this way and custom belongs only to the men, for the women do not pierce their faces like this, only their ears. Another custom and way is also prevalent and among them, and contrary to all human belief: their women, who are quite lustful and wanton, cause their husbands' private parts to swell in such excessive measure that they appear deformed and shameful, and they do this with certain substances and the addition of certain poisonous animals. And from such a thing, it happens that many lose their member, which rots away due to a lack of medicine and they remain without a member. They have no cloth or covering, neither linen nor cotton, for they do not need it, and they have no private property, but all things are common to them. They all live together without a king and without a ruler, and each one is their own...

*Now that you have forgotten the winter, you possess a better breeze,*
    *Now it is pleasant to enjoy the desired honor of spring.*
*Am I mistaken? Or, now that your labor is overcome, O Leonhart,*
    *Do the joyful delights of spring also come to you?*
*Indeed, I am not mistaken: for while you sought the sacred halls*
    *Of the Muses, which are not to be approached with a soft tread:*
*The harsh winter had to be endured by you, and the pitiless rough roads,*
    *And a less happy fate often had to be borne.*
*The omen of your famous name has long suggested this,*
    *And the CROWN born to your race suggests it too.*
*You have the sublime name of the magnanimous LION:*
    *You truly possess the heart of an indomitable Lion.*
*With a Leonine mind you underwent every trial,*
    *While it was your concern to climb Parnassus.*
*With a Leonine mind the summits of the Clarian mount*
    *You conquered: so great a fervor is in your breast.*
*Hence therefore, the Muse who sits upon the Aonian peak*
    *Weaves for you a garland with a rosy flower.*
*Hence also the family of Krentzheim, fitting for you,*
    *Bestows it, a family celebrated in many places.*
*Hence Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> stands nearer to you with a laurel sprout,*
    *And covers your temples with the crown placed upon them.*
*And now you depart a Victor, the citadel of Pallas <note>Minerva, goddess of wisdom</note> overcome,*
    *And it is sweet to remember past hardships.*
*And now the Spring shines upon you with a lucky star: but one day*
    *There will be a plentiful harvest for you at the proper time.*

Age ergò, quomodo salva Legis Majestate Cogitationis poenam quis patitur? Non placet sententia distinguentium inter voluntatem merè nudam & conatum, illum quidem ipsum quoque nudam, sed nimiâ sui per actum in quem erumpit denudatione vestitae quodammodo speciem referentem voluntatem; istam legali poenae eximendo, hanc eidem semper & omninò subjiciendo. A controversy, agitated long ago many centuries before the jurisprudence was reformed by Justinian, is read concerning the punishment of the naked will between M. Cato and Tiro Tullius, the freedman of Cicero: the former, arguing in the Senate on behalf of the Rhodians, maintained it was unjust for anyone to be punished for the reason that he is argued to have wished to do evil: the latter, on the contrary, calling this a profession of folly, argued that one should not go to meet planned crimes, but rather to wait for them, so that when they have been perpetrated, then at last, when what is done cannot be undone, they may be punished. *See Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 7, chapter 3.* We embrace the opinion of Tiro for the cause at hand, and the faculty which the Law grants to a private person of preventing imminent harm by timely intervention—*last law, Code concerning in what causes restitution; law 1, Code when it is permitted to each one; law 4, Code to the Julian Law on Assassins*—we judge that this pertains to the Law and its minister much more according to the exigency of affairs. Magnanimus, strauit magna uirtute Viros Vir,
Imperium contra qui bella inimica gerebant:
Hunc super accedit fandi doctissimus Heros,
Ille tuus Genitor FEDERICVS, CAROLE, præstans,
Quem Regni Austriadûm non vltima fama RODVLPHVS

And Leaders, so that you may be a most grateful Author of these,
by which reason the people might be held under law.

<note>An ornate initial 'A' features foliate and floral motifs.</note>

Must I pass over LADISLAUS, who from the ancient origin of the race
of the TORRINGENI, derives his name and lineage,
in my poem? And shall I not raise him to the stars with praise?
For who will deny that he is worthy of praises?
Who, while youth, the first, sits upon his youthful face,
as a boy travels in the excellent gardens of the Muses;
so that, if the strength of the age of manhood should ever make him,
he may be able to add glory and praise to his race,
three hundred and seventy years having passed
(as the monuments of the ancients teach) which flourished before,
it still flourishes, and will flourish, while the earth shall remain.

    Therefore how happy would your father ADAM have been
by merit, who was most observant of equity,
and a lover of piety, and a hero renowned in war:
If the Fates had not yet broken his threads!
How he would have seen you, with such study and labor,
engaged in the liberal arts with great praise!
How he would have seen you, endowed with such virtues,
by which the ATHENS of Boia now admire you, a Youth!
How he would have seen you, following the grateful footsteps
of the heroes, once of your lineage, having set out!

    In addition, who would not think the Mother to be blessed
(who does not wish to join herself in any marriage bond,
after her first love has already failed through sad death)
since she has an offspring who might reign in the fortress of the Parent,
and brings back the Man in Piety and love of Virtue?

And <note>(z)</note> *all your children shall be taught by the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children; in righteousness they shall be established.* And <note>(a)</note> *no weapon formed against the children of God shall prosper, and every tongue that rises in judgment against them, these who are taught by the Lord shall condemn.*

We, who have been taught by the Lord [which is His clemency toward us], testify that the Lord has suppressed many weapons and various tongues rising against us; for God imbued His little children with power to refute deceitful tongues and lying judgments.

### *On the Manner of Singing and Praying.*

The opinion of the Apostle Paul regarding the manner of singing and praying was this: <note>(b)</note> *I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, but I will sing with the mind also.* The exhortation of the Apostle Jude to the Church of Christ was: <note>(c)</note> *that they should pray in the Holy Spirit.* Therefore, he did not commend to them books from which prayers might be uttered; but to pray in the spirit and with the mind seems in no way to imply the use of books.

The Apostle says: <note>(d)</note> *The Spirit helps our weaknesses; for we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered; now He who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because He makes intercession for the saints according to God.*

Therefore, that all may perceive the Spirit in their hearts, by which they may rightly pray for themselves and all others, and may follow the Lord with the highest praises for all His goodness toward them, which is forever, is what my sincere soul desires.

This Apostle said: God has revealed His secrets to us through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God. <note>(e)</note> And elsewhere: <note>(f)</note> *The righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith.* Relevant here is also this: <note>(g)</note> *I make known to you, brethren, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man; for I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came through the revelation of Jesus Christ.* From which arises this question: Can anyone rightly preach the righteousness of God, faith in Christ, the deep things of God, and the Gospel of Christ, unless these things are revealed to him by the Spirit of God, just as they were in the days of the Apostles?

The same Apostle says: But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, to reveal His Son in me, that I might preach Him among the Gentiles. <note>(h)</note> And Christ himself clearly says: <note>(i)</note> *No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.*

Can there therefore be any true Minister or Herald of the Son or the Father without such divine revelation? Ut ergo omnes spiritum in cordibus, quo pro seipsis & omnibus aliis rite orent, percipiant, & Dominum summis prosequantur laudibus pro omni sua erga se bonitate, quæ in secula est, exoptat mihi animus sincerus.
