If God is said to be everywhere because He contains, nourishes, and sustains all things (for He is the Creator) and the Body of Christ does not contain, nourish, and sustain all things (for it is a Creature). Therefore the Divine Omnipresence cannot be communicated to the Body of Christ. No Orthodox has ever doubted the Antecedent. Wherefore those who doubt the Consequent are not Orthodox.

### TH. X.

From various places of Hippocrates, such as *book 6, epid. 1, on diseases 11 and 14, book 7, aphorism 44*, it is clear that empyema patients should be burned, but since a double method of burning has been customary, the other which reaches as far as the pus, which <term>C. Celsus</term> wants in *book 8, chapter 9*, when he says:

> *If suppuration prevails, and it could not be resolved by what was written above, all delay is to be avoided, lest the bone be vitiated, but in the part where it will swell most, a glowing iron must be lowered until it reaches the pus, and that must be poured out:*

but the other which stopped in the skin and muscles: they argue among themselves which of those <term>Hippocrates</term> understood, and there are even today those to whom burning by a potential, rather than an actual, cautery is pleasing, either single or repeated. Little concerned about the mind of <term>Hippocrates</term>, I cannot approve of any of them. While a glowing iron is driven into the cavity, it terrifies the patient too much, excites greater pain, while it not only ruptures the fibers through which it passes but also injures the neighboring ones, and while it is driven in sometimes more easily, sometimes with more difficulty, according to how glowing it is, it happens very easily that by touching the lungs it injures them, or harms them with excessive heat. Those who burn the skin either with iron or caustic do nothing else but increase the pain, make the flesh that is to be cut more sensitive, and in many ways torture the patient, whom they could have relieved in one act; indeed, once the eschar is removed, all that remains to be done is what should have been done without that preceding it. Those who decline incision by applying repeated caustic are pressed by greater difficulties, for while it flows far and wide; it burns the parts with pain, inflammation, and swelling, which also compresses even a large opening so that the flow of matter is hindered, which, so that we may assist, the swollen lips of the wound must be depressed with a dilator, which is done without the patient's laughter, until separation happens,

### TH. X.

Ex Hippocratis variis locis ut *lib. 6. epid. 1. de morb. 11. et 14. l. 7. aph. 44.* empyicos urendos constat, cum vero duplex urendi ratio usitata fuerit, altera quæ ad pus usque pertingat, quod C. Celsus *lib. 8. c. 9.* vult, quando ait:

> *Si Suppuratio vicerit, neque per quæ supra scripta sunt discuti potuerit, omnis mora vitanda erit, ne os vitietur, sed quâ parte maximè tumebit demittendum erit candens ferramentum donec ad pus perveniat, idque effundendum:* 

altera vero quæ in cute et musculis subsistebat: controvertunt inter se quam illarum Hippocrates intellexerit, et sunt hodienum, quibus ustio non cauterio actuali, sed potentiali, vel unico, vel iterato arridet. Parum de mente Hippocratis sollicitus, nullam illarum probare possum. Ferramentum candens in cavitatem dum adigitur, nimis terret ægrum, majorem excitat dolorem, dum non solum rumpit fibras per quas transit, sed etiam vicinas lædit, et dum modo facilius, modò difficilius, prout candet, adigitur, facillimè fit, ut pulmones tangendo lædat, vel iis calore nimio noceat. Qui vel ferro vel caustico cutem exurunt, aliud nil agunt, nisi ut dolores augeant, carnem discindendam magis sensibilem reddant, et multis modis excrucient ægrum, quem uno actu absolvere poterant; nempe escharâ remotâ omne id agendum superest, quod illa non prægressa fieri debebat. Caustico iterato imposito qui sectionem declinant, illos majores urgent difficultates, dum enim diffluit longè lateque; exurit partes cum dolore, inflammatione et tumore, qui etiam magnum licet hiatum adeo comprimit, ut materiæ effluxus impediatur, quem ut adjuvemus tumida vulneris labia deprimenda decussorio, quod sine ægri peragitur risu, donec separatio fiat,

Dina Nicolai Dovelings, quae a primis annis ventris laboraverat, cum tensione gravi, intumescentia magna, quae circa pubertatis tempora, anno videlicet 13. et 14. mirum in modum increvit. concerning which we have read excellently warned many centuries ago by *Sextus Caecilius*, who excelled in that law and in knowing and interpreting the laws of the Roman People with knowledge, usage, and illustrious authority: *that we should not assign their obscurities to the fault of the writers, but partly to the ignorance of those not understanding, and most especially to the antiquity of the times, while the long age has obliterated the old words and customs by which words and customs the meaning of the laws was comprehended.* Nevertheless, it will be permissible to observe the same thing today in the Constitutions of other peoples as well, and especially of the Germans, composed in both Latin and vernacular language, which have been preserved for us from antiquity through the commendable solicitude of some; the obscurity of which, at any rate, must be ascribed almost entirely to archaic words that have been removed from our knowledge by the length of years. By what reason can we destine them for daily uses with happier success unless the impediments that obstruct the words themselves and their meaning from the outside are removed? Against which, a remedy cannot be expected more strongly from any other source than from critical erudition, commended by the praise of solid and true discretion and industry. Nor is there a lack of very learned men who, by either insisting on this path, left an example for others, or by running through it, desired to leave a suitable aid; those must be considered to have wished to exhibit a compendium who, in illustrating Roman institutions, have commented *on the signification of words that pertain to law, in imitation of Aelius Gallus, an ancient Jurisconsult*, or have commended to us their *glossaries* for declaring the laws of other peoples.

Furthermore, whatever is added contingent upon an uncertain event renders that stipulation conditional, whether it be casual, potestative, or mixed, as in law 46, section 2, law 208, and law 215, section 1 of the same title. In fortuitous conditions, fortune is always awaited. In arbitrary conditions, fulfillment depends upon the will of the person. Finally, in conditions that are partly fortuitous and partly arbitrary, both chance and will are observed. From a stipulation contracted under a condition, there is therefore only a hope that it will be owed, and on account of that hope, one is sometimes held as a creditor, who is called conditional, as in law 42 <term>de obligationibus et actionibus</term> <gloss>concerning obligations and actions</gloss>; indeed, he is sent into possession for the sake of custody, as in law 6 and law 11 of the <term>Digest</term> <gloss>the Pandects, the main collection of Roman legal writings</gloss>, concerning those to whom one is sent into possession. However, he cannot be sent into possession for the sake of holding and selling by what they call the second decree, as in law 19, final section of that same title. Plainly, a promisor suspected of flight can even be arrested, and indeed detained, until he has provided sufficient security for payment, according to Mat. Coler. <term>de processu executivo</term> <gloss>concerning executive procedure</gloss>, chapter 3, number 109. If, however, the promisor dies while the condition is pending, the right nevertheless remains in suspense, and the stipulation receives its force once the condition is subsequently fulfilled, such that the heir of the stipulator may sue, and the heir of the promisor may be sued, as Donellus notes in law 57 <term>de verborum obligationibus</term> <gloss>concerning verbal obligations</gloss>. For the existence or event of the condition is, by a legal fiction, drawn back to the beginning of the act of the transaction, and it is held as if it had been effective at the very moment of the agreement, as in law 11, section 1, concerning priority in pledges, and law 8, concerning risk and benefit. We apply a different law, however, in conditional legacies, in which it is held that if the legatee dies before the event of the condition, no hope at all is transmitted to his heir, as in law 4 and following, section 2, concerning when the day of a legacy arrives, and section 7, <term>Codex</term> <gloss>the Code of Justinian</gloss>, concerning lapsed legacies; Gomez, 2 <term>resolutiones</term> <gloss>legal resolutions</gloss> 11, number 12; and D. Tuldenus, <term>Commentarii</term> <gloss>commentaries</gloss>, chapter 7.

XIV. In stipulations conceived for the sake of extinguishing an obligation by the addition of a day, the obligation is understood as having been made purely.

For elephants, whenever they are troubled, are accustomed to turn back and consider those in front as enemies. And some, because of this lack of trust, call them common enemies. A disorderly flight of the Romans occurred. The Numantines, seeing this from the walls, leapt out, and pursuing, killed men hardly up to four thousand, and three elephants. They also captured many weapons and standards. Of the Celtiberians, about two thousand died. Nobilior, having recovered slightly from the disaster, attempted an assault on a certain marketplace of the enemies near a city named Azania, having accomplished nothing, but having lost many there too, he returned by night to the camp. From there, he sent Biesius, a commander of the horse, to a friendly nation for an alliance, needing cavalry. They sent some cavalry to him, whom the Celtiberians ambushed as they were coming. The ambuscade becoming apparent, the allies fled. Biesius, fighting, died himself and many Romans with him. Since these disasters kept happening to them, the city of Ocilis, where the marketplace and the money of the Romans were, transferred its allegiance to the Celtiberians. Nobilior, trusting no one, spent the winter in the camp, having set things in order as best he could, and keeping the provisions inside, and suffering from the scarcity of the provisions themselves and the frequency of snowfall and the harshness of the cold. So that many of the soldiers, some while gathering firewood, others inside, were dying from the confinement and the cold. Quádo li ſuoi vaſſalli gli portano oro, o altra coſa pretioſa, la mettono in queſta ſala, & dicono qſto ſia ad honor, & gloria del noſtro Santhoa Raia. Queſte genti di China come diſſe il detto moro, ſono bianche, & vannoveſti te, come noi, & mangiano ſopra tauole con noi, & hanno la croce, ma non fanno perche la tengono. In China naſce il muſchio da vna beſtia, che è ſimil ad vn gatto, qual mangia di vn legno dolce, groſſo vn dito, & è chiamato Comaru. Dietro alla coſta di China ſono molti popoli, come di Chenchii, doue ſi truouano perle, & qualche legno di Cánella, & li popoli detti Lechii doue è il Re di Moin, qual ha ſotto di ſe 22, Re, & lui è ſuggetto al Re di China, vi ſi truoua anche la gran Citta detta Cathaio orientale, & molti altri popoli in detta terra ferma, & tragli altri, alcuni di coſtumi ſi beſtiali, che come veggono il lor padre, & madre vecchi, & mal gagliardi gli amazzano, accioche non trauaglino piu in queſta vita, & tutti queſti popoli ſono Gentili.

A Lli. xi. di Febraio. 1522. partirono dall'Iſola de Timor ingolfando ſi forte nel mare grande, qual ſi chiama Lantchidol, & prefero il ſuo camino tra Ponente, & Gherbin, laſciando a' mandiritta la Tramontana, per paura che andando verſo la terra ferma, non fuſſero veduti da Portogheſi, & paſſarono di fuori dell'Iſola di Samotra chiamata come habbian detto dalli antichi Taprobana, laſciando pur a mandiritta ſopra la terra ferma Pegu Bengala Calicut Cananor, & Goa Cambaia Colfod'ormus, & tutta la Coſta de L'india maggiore. Et p paſſar piu ſicuraméte il Capo di buona Speranza che è ſopra l'Affrica, andarono verſo il polo Antartico circa. 42. gradi, & dimorarono ſopra detto Capo da. 7. ſettimane volteggiando ſempre con le vele ſuſo, perche li tirauan prua venti da Ponente, & da Maeſtro, che no gli laſciauan paſſare, & hebber anchora non poca fortuna. Il Capo di buona Speranza è verſo il polo Antartico di ſotto dall'Equinottiale gradi. 34. & mezo, & 1600. leghe dal capo di Malaccha, & è il maggiore, & piu pericoloſo Capo, che ſi veggha ſul mare di tutto il mōdo. Alcuni di noſtri ſi pmacamento di vertouaglie, come per eſſer amalati, voleuano andar ad vn porto ſopra l'Affrica de Portogheſi detto Monzanbich, li altri diceuan che piu preſto voleuan morire, che non andar al diritto in Spagna, pur finalmente cō l'aiuto del Signor Iddio paſſarono detto Capo nō troppo lontani, poi cominciarono a nauigare alla volta di Maeſtro duoi

mesi continui senza mai toccar porto alcuno, & in questo tempo ne morirono circa 21. di diuerse cause, quali buttauan in mare, & pareua che li christiani andassero al fondo con il viso volto in suso, & li indiani con il viso in giuso, & se Iddio no li haueffe dato buon tempo tutti moriuan di fame. Finalmente astretti da necessita trouandosi mezi morti andarono Isola di Capo verde detta San Iacopo del Re di Portogallo, doue subito sopra vn batello mandarono in terra a dimandar vettouaglie, facendo con ogni amoreuolezza a saper a Porthogesi li loro infortunii, & trauagli, & delle nuoue delli suoi, che si trouuano nele Indie, & con tanto buone parole, & carezze che seppero fare, hebbero alcune misure di risi, & volendo tornare pur per risi furono ritenuti 13. huomini, quali si erano assicurati dismontare in terra. Li altri restati in mare dubitando di non esser anchora loro presi con qualche arte, si partirono facendo vela, & alli 7. di Settembre con l'aiuto d'Iddio entrorono nel porto di San Lucar vicino a Sibilia, solamente 18. huomini, la maggior parte amalati, il resto di 59. che partirono dalle Molucche parte morirono di diuerse malattie, & alcuni anchora furono de capitati nel la Isola di Timor p suoi delitti, & giunti in questo porto di San Lucar per il conto tenuto di giorno in giorno, haueannauigato da quattordici mila quattrocento & sessanta leghe, circundando tutto il mondo dal Leuante in Ponente. Alli 8. di Settembre vennero in Sibilia, & scari carono tutta lartegliaria parallegrezza, & tutti in camicia, & scalzi con vn torchio in mano andarono a ringratiare alla chiefa maggiore il Signor Iddio che gli haueffe condotti salui fino a quel punto.

D Apoi alcuni giorni Antonio Pigafetta si parti, & ando alla Citta di Vagliadolit, doue si trouaua la Maesta dell'Imperadore, il quale non pote appresentare oro, o argento, o pietre pretiose che fossero degne della grandezza di tanto principe, ma li dette vn libro scritto di sua mano, oue erano notate tutte le cose accadute di giorno in gior no in questo viaggio Di li poi partitosi ando a Lisbona al Serenissimo Re di Portogallo, al qual disse tutte le nuoue delli suoi huomini, che hauean trouati si nell Isole delle Molucche come in altre parti. Dapoi di Spagna se ne venne in Francia, doue appresento alcuni doni delle cose portate di questo viaggio alla Serenissima Madama la Regente madre del potentissimo & Christianissimo Re di Francia. Finalmente venuto in Italia presento similmente questo suo libro al Reuerendissimo gran Maestro di Rhodi Messer Philippo Villiers Lisleadam.

seed: is called Siri Zacabedera. The cities are built like ours, subject to the King of Siam. After the realm of Siam is found that of Comagia and of Chiempa, where rhubarb is born, of which there are diverse opinions: one says it is a root, and another a putrefied tree, and if it were not putrefied it would not have such a great odor, and they call it Calama. Near this is found the great China, the King of whom is the greatest of all the Kings of the world, and he is called Santoa Raia. And all these things that will be told below, they understood from a Moor who was in the island of Timor, which we have not wanted to leave undescribed, just as they are, that is, that the said King has made his empire 70 crowned Kings, and has a sea port called Canthau, and two principal cities, that is, Nauchin and Conulaha, where he is accustomed to dwell, and he always keeps four of his principals near his palace, that is, one towards the East, the other towards the West, the other towards the South, and the other towards the North, and each gives audience to those who come from those parts. All the lords of Great India and of that above give obedience to said King, and as a sign that they are true vassals, each keeps in the square that is in the middle of their cities an animal called a Lynx, which is more beautiful than a lion, and the seal of the King of China is the Lynx, and all those who want to go to China carry this seal of wax, or upon an elephant's tooth; otherwise they would not let him enter the port. When any King is disobedient to the King, they have him flayed, and the skin salted, and dried in the sun, and they fill it with straw or other things, and make it stay with the neck down, placed in the square upon some eminent place, so that everyone sees it. The King never lets himself be seen by any person, and when his courtiers want to see him, he descends from the palace into a pavilion that is most rich, accompanied by six of his principal damsels, who are dressed as he is, and from that he enters into a serpent called Nagha, which is the most marvelous and rich structure in the world, and is placed in the main courtyard of the palace, and the King enters inside with the aforementioned women; so as not to be known among them, his men look through a glass that is placed in the chest of the said serpent, and they see the King and the women, but cannot discern which is the King. Said King marries his sisters, so that the royal blood does not mix with the blood of others. His palace is surrounded by seven walls, wide greatly one from the other, and in each of these such circuits stand ten thousand men, who keep watch at the palace, until a certain signal sounds; then come other ten thousand in each circuit, and thus they change by day and by night. In this palace are 79 halls where infinite women are who serve the King, and they always have lit torches to show greater

Dapoi il reame de Sian si truoua quello di Comagia, & di Chiempa, doue nasce il Riobarbaro, del quale sono diuerse oppinioni, chi dice che l'e radice, & chi arbore putrefatto, & se non fusse putrefatto non haueria cosi grande odore, & chiamanlo Calama. Appresso di questo si truoua la gran China, il Re dellaquale e' il maggior di tutti li Re del modo, & si chiama Santoa Raia, Et tutte qste cose che di sotto si dirano, itesero da vn moro che era ne l'isola di Timor, lequali no habbian voluto lasciar discriuere, tal qual le sono, cioe' che il detto Re ha fatto il suo imperio. 70. Re coronati, & ha vn porto di mare detto Canthau, & due Citta principali cioe' Nauchin, & Conulaha doue lui suol habitare, & sempre tien quattro de suoi principali appresso il suo palazzo, cioe' vn verso leuante, l'altro verso ponente, l'altro a' mezo di, & l'altro a tramontana, & ciascun da audientia a quelli che vengono da quelle parti. Tutti li signori della India maggiore, & di quella di sopra danno obedientia al detto Re, & per segno che siano veri vassalli, ciascun tien nella piazza, che e' in mezo le loro Citta, vn animal detto Lince, che e' piu bello, che vn leone, & il figillo del Re, di China e' la Lince, & tutti quelli che vogliono andar a China portano questo figillo di cera, ouer sopra vn dente di elephante, altrimente non lo lasciariano entrar nel porto. Quando alcun Re e' inobediente al Re, lo fanno scorticare, & insalata la pelle, & secca al sole la empiono di paglia, o di altra cosa, & la fanno star con il collo basso, posta nella piazza, sopra qual che luogo eminente, accioche ciascuno la vegga. Il Re no si lascia mai vedere da persona alcuna, & quando li suoi cortigiani il vogliono vedere, lui discende dal palazzo in vn padiglion che e' ricchissimo, accompagnato da sei damigelle sue principali, quali sono vestite come lui, & di quello entra in vn serpente detto Nagha, che e' la piu' marauigliosa, & ricca fabrica del mondo, & e' posto nella corte maggiore del palazzo, & il Re entra dentro con le prefate donne, per non esser conosciuto tra quelle, li suoi guardano per vn vetro che e' posto nel petto del detto serpente, & veggono il Re, & le donne, ma non possono discernere qual sia il Re. Detto Re si marita con le sorelle, accio che il sangue regale non si mescoli con il sangue daltrui. Il suo palazzo e' circundato da sette muri larghi grandemente vn dall'altro, & in ciascun di questi tali circuiti stanno dieci mila huomini, che fanno la guardia al palazzo, fino tanto che suona vn certo segno. poi vengono altri dieci mila in ciascun circuito, & cosi si mutano di di, & di notte. He did not blush, a few months later, to desert you when you had been driven into the war of the Genoese by his promises, betrayals, fraud, and cunning. He remembered the words of his grandfather, Cosimo de' Medici, which he was accustomed to preach: that Lucca should not be attacked by war by the Florentines, lest it be occupied by another once the Florentine strength was broken; but if war were brought upon the Lucchese by anyone else, the Florentines would easily gain possession of the city by their own ingenuity—for this is how he described crimes and betrayals. There are six hundred other testimonies concerning the treachery of the Florentines, and especially of the Medici family, against the Lucchese, which, if you did not know them clearly, you would never maintain these nocturnal and daily vigils with such labor of yours and such expense for so many years. What is the meaning of the citizens running through the city by night? What is the continuous inspection of the walls? What is the purpose of the guards at the gates? And other almost infinite things, which not even cities under siege and surrounded by enemy camps do so diligently. What do you fear? What do you suspect? Certainly, no one except the Florentines. O holy alliance with the Florentine tyrant, during which you have more need of a guard than if the most powerful enemy were besieging your city with a victorious army and pressing you with all the evils of war. These things are approved by you, men of Lucca. But your mind is still distracted by one knot, namely, you fear that if the Florentines are superior in war, they will turn their victorious army against you if you join war councils with the King and the Pope against their tyrant. As if the Florentines have not always—especially since the Medici family became powerful—plotted against you in every way they could. Do not labor in the hope that fortune will allow them to spare you, for they have never forgiven you, nor will they ever forgive you. Although I fear that I may seem to be flattering you, when the King and the Pope will achieve their just wishes in any way, even without you, though not quite as easily. ### L.

For most of the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>legal scholars</gloss> hold that for one knowingly purchasing a feudal object, the price need not be returned even if a stipulation regarding eviction was interposed, which, however, we leave in the middle.

### LI.

Regarding a dowry, the matter is not without difficulty. For one may find not a few who distinguish between the giving of a dowry that began from a promise and that which owes its beginning to delivery, establishing the provision of eviction in the former case and denying it in the latter.

### LII.

But since that distinction is proven neither by solid reason nor by text sufficiently validly, it will perhaps be safer if we distinguish regarding the present business thus: Either a promise of eviction has been added to the giving of the dowry, or no such pledge was interposed. In the former case, a recovery action or an action from stipulation <note>original: "actio ex stipulatu"</note> is competent for the husband. In the latter, however, it must again be distinguished whether the dowry was given as appraised or unappraised. In the latter case, if indeed the object is given in dowry in good faith, no action is competent for the husband; but if deceit intervened, an action for deceit <note>original: "actio de dolo"</note> will have a place, or where that infamous action cannot be instituted, an action on the facts will. But in the former, since an appraisal is a sale, an action from purchase <note>original: "actio ex empto"</note> is competent once the object given in dowry is evicted.

### LIII.

In legacies, the matter must be expedited by a distinction: Either the testator knew that the object belonged to another, or he was ignorant. If, knowing it, he bequeathed a third party's object, since in this case the heir is compelled to redeem it if he can, he is entirely held in its name for eviction.

<summary>This page discusses the complex legal standing of dowries and legacies when the objects involved are claimed by third parties, focusing on the conditions under which a husband or legatee can seek restitution through various civil actions.</summary>

### L I.

Circa dotem res difficultate non caret: Haud parum multos enim invenire licet, qui distinguunt inter dotis dationem quae â promissione coepit, et eam quae initium suum traditioni debet, illo casu evictionis praestationem statuentes, hoc negantes.

### L I I.

Verùm cum distinctio ista nec solidâ ratione, nec textu satis validè probetur, Tutius fortè erit, si circa praesens negotium ita distinxerimus: Aut enim ad dotis dationem promissio evictionis accessit, aut nulla pollicitatio ejus interposita est: Priori casu marito competit hoc nomine condictio vel ex stipulatu actio: Posteriori verò rursus sub distinguendum venit, an dos aestimata data fuerit, an inaestimata: posteriori casu si quidem bona fide res in dotem data fit, nulla marito competit actio, sin verò dolus intervenerit, de dolo actio, vel ubi famosa actio institui nequit, in factum locum habebit: Priori verò cum aestimatio venditio sit, evicta re in dotem datâ ex empto actio competit.

### L I I I.

In legatis res distinctione expedienda est: Aut enim I. scivit testator rem alienam esse, ut ignoravit: Si sciens rem alienam legaverit, cum hoc casu heres, si possit, eam redimere cogatur, omninò ejus nomine de evictione tenetur.

Not the former: for it would be either dead or living. If dead, the seed is lacking, the power of generation is lacking, natural application is lacking, and thus, the cause of generation being removed, the generation itself as an effect will be removed. If it is living, the principle of generation would reside in the body, not in the demon, about which, however, the dispute exists. It is not the latter; for it would be either brute or forced from elsewhere. It cannot be a brute body; otherwise, a human would not be generated from it, since like generates like in species, not unlike. But if it is forced from elsewhere, namely from air, as they believe, it cannot be that either, for it would be inanimate and inorganic, which is in no way productive of an animate being. It follows, therefore, that the assumed body cannot accomplish this.

<margin>§. 12.</margin> We argue further: Whoever is destitute of his own seed, he cannot generate; but the demon is destitute of his own seed; therefore, he cannot generate. The major premise is manifest; for no substance can be produced without a certain medium and vehicle, let alone for a human to be generated from no pre-existing matter. The minor premise is proven thus: The demon either has seed from himself or from another: not from himself, since seed is a part of a living corporeal substance and the residue of food excellently digested; but demons are incorporeal substances, destitute of their own bodies, and therefore cannot provide corporeal seed from themselves.

<margin>§. 13.</margin> Not from another, as will be said shortly; therefore, they are clearly destitute of seed. The adversaries indeed object that the Devil can collect seed from men, when he acts as a <term>succubus</term> <gloss>female demon tormentor</gloss>, outside the natural vessels, and acting as an <term>incubus</term>, pour it into

<margin>§. 14.</margin> a woman's womb. Truly, I answer: (1) Logicians themselves know that from power to existence is a weak

<margin>§. 15.</margin> consequence. (2) Posited, but not conceded, that something might be generated from such stolen seed, the Devil would not have generated; for he should be considered to have generated whose the seed was, and who emitted it, not he who transferred and carried it elsewhere.

<margin>§. 16.</margin> See Weyer on Witches, chapter 13. (3) That part of the seed in which the generative power is contained, by the long interval in which it is collected and instilled elsewhere, is very easily annihilated and evaporates, for it is clearly aerial, most thin, most subtle, foamy, and thriving with the most gentle warmth, akin and related to the heat of the stars, and therefore most easily expirable and dissipatable. See Aristotle, book 2, *On the Generation of Animals*, chapters 2 and 3; and the witches themselves confess, having experienced such union, that the sperm was extremely cold. If, therefore, the seed is cold, it has lost the generative power.

But we can acquire jurisprudence for ourselves—so that we may understand the laws, know their history, and apply them to new cases—if, according to the advice of *Emperor Justinian*, individual matters are handed down to us first by a light and simple path, and then afterwards by a most diligent and exact interpretation. ### XIX.

Hence, as it is elegant, so a question resulting from the vehemence of the disputes distracted into various opinions arises: What if a pact has been entered into between the contracting parties that the interrupted payment of the Rent will not result in any peril of deprivation for the Emphyteuta: whether a pact of this kind is valid or not? And although the negative opinion has pleased some: yet because such a convention is by no means considered to be against the form of a perpetual colony, we will defend with Bartolus that it can subsist.

### XX.

On the contrary, it has been established by supreme reason of law that as long as the census is paid at the appointed times, it is not permitted for the direct Lord either to revoke the emphyteusis or to change anything in it by which it might be made worse.

### XXI.

Moreover, if the Lord has not accepted the paid pension, and the Emphyteuticary has deposited it when offered and sealed at a fitting place and time according to the law, he will avoid the penalty of rejection.

### XXII.

God is Most Great, as long as the noise rises, and the pilgrims gather, and they run in the pilgrimage and complete the Hajj and the Umrah for God. But if you are prevented, then offer what can be obtained of sacrificial animals. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of slaughter. And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then an expiation of fasting or charity or sacrifice. And when you are secure, then whoever performs the Umrah during the Hajj months, then he offers what can be obtained of sacrificial animals. And whoever cannot find [one] then a fast of three days during Hajj and seven when you have returned. Those are ten complete. This is for those whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque.

For just as in ancient times there were those who placed study and effort into emulating the poems of the most excellent poets, so also were found those who, captured by the sweetness of the subject and the ease of Anacreontic diction, although against the will of Minerva <note>Note: meaning without natural talent</note>, nevertheless worked in the same genre <note>28</note>. Confer Ilgen in the preface to the Homeric hymns, pages XII—XIV.

However, those arguments which they take from the manner of the thing, we do not admit as being weak. The rule that "the manner does not vary the thing" admits of various instances and various limitations, whether you take it concerning the manner of constituting, or concerning the manner of usurping. Nor do we admit those arguments which they take from the denial of real Majesty. For this distinction of Majesty, into real and personal, can be defended in the way the Lord Justus Synold Schütz does in *I. P.* vol. 1, disp. 3, or rather in another way, which, if opportunity is given in the assembly, we shall indicate. Join this with Theod. Grasvv. on the Right of Majesty, chapters 10 and 11.

For who would say, where the kingdom is elective or hereditary, upon the failure of the ruler and before a designation has been made, that the people wander about like wild beasts? See Colotes in Plutarch, book 1, *against Colotes*, p. 1124. The very disposition of GOD protests. See Lord Boecler in his commentary on Grotius, chapter 3, book 1, p. 200, 201. All effects protest, which sufficiently demonstrates that Majesty is present wherever judgments remain and the good are affected by rewards and the bad by punishments (Romans 13). And these things are not to be restricted to some certain place, as if some peoples were at least capable of Majesty and others were not, contrary to the mind of those from whom they attempt to prove this, and contrary to sound and right reason.

Let these things said about the Tyrant, who seized power by force, suffice. But what if it was brought about by arts and fraud that someone was elected King? And, since God in this case seems to have wished to employ the ministry of the people, and to transfer Majesty from the people through the people to some one person, by that very fact, while He left the choice of electing to the people, as long as error concerning the person did not impede the consent of the people, the matter seems to receive an easy decision.

However, when an error of person led the people into fraud, just as it is established to have happened in this century with the Pseudo-Demetrius, the matter is doubtful whether the successor is even then bound; and whether a right acquired with a burden can be taken away by others; because it appears that the people retained Majesty, and under this condition, if this or that person were [the candidate], they finally transferred it, and that not having followed, the transfer itself is void. Nec illas admittimus, quas sumunt à negatione Majestatis realis. Haec enim distinctio Majestatis, in realem et personalem, vel eo modo potest defendi, quo Dominus Justus Synold. Schütz I. Quis enim diceret, ubi regnum est electitium, vel successorium, deficiente imperante, ante designationem factam, populum instar ferarum oberrare. vide Colotem apud Plutarchum l. 1. adv. Colot. p. 1124. reclamat ipsa DEI dispositio. vide Dominus Baecl. in comment. ad Grotium c. 3. l. 1. p. 200. 201. reclamant omnes effectus, qui Majestatem adesse, ubicunque judicia supersunt, et praemiis boni et poenis mali afficiuntur, satis demonstrat Rom. 13. Et haec non sunt restringenda ad certum aliquem locum, quasi quidam populi saltem essent capaces Majestatis, quidam vero non, contra illorum mentem, ex quibus hoc conantur probare, et contra sanam et rectam rationem.

Haec de Tyranno, qui vi imperium rapuit, dicta sufficiant. Sed si artibus et fraude esset effectum, ut quis in Regem eligeretur? Et, quandoquidem DEus, hoc in casu videtur ministerium populi voluisse adhibere, et à populo per populum Majestatem in unum aliquem transferre, eo ipso, dum eligendi arbitrium populo reliquit, quamdiu error circa personam, populi consensum non impedivit, res videtur facilem accipere decisionem.

Locus porrò tribuitur huic beneficio legi 2. dationi in solutum tam uoluntariæ et extrajudiciali, quæ similis est uenditioni, ejusque uicem subit, lex finis. Digesta Quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. quàm judiciali et necessariæ, quemadmodum cum allegatis Doctores et responsis hoc ipsum probat et confirmat Dominus Richter. dicta decisione numero 49. ### THESIS XXVIII.

Hence it is hotly debated among the Doctors: *Can this remedy of ours have a place in a transaction as well?* There are those who deny it; there are those who affirm it. On the side of the former stand the Gloss, Innocent, and others on Chapter "When from cause," On buying and selling, and the Gloss on Law "Lucius," § last, Digest, On the SC Trebellianum; Zasius in counsel 18, book 1; Alciatus in counsel 24, no. 3 and 89, no. 4; Cravetta, counsel 151, no. 26; Menochius in counsel 401, no. 157, book 5; Afflictus, decision 220; Gail, book 2, observation 70, and many others may be seen in Fachin, book 2, chapter 26, and thus hold Vinn. tr. on transaction, ch. last, no. 11 and following; Mynsing. 1, observation 33; Zoesius on the Digest, on this title, no. 26. But as the truer and far more equitable opinion of those who affirm it, namely, that this benefit also finds a place in a transaction, it is established and asserted by Law 5, Code, On deceit, joined with Law 36, Digest, On verbal obligations, Law 65, § 1, Digest, On the claim of indebtment. And this is held by Bartolus on this Law 2, and on the Law "If anyone with otherwise," no. 5, Digest, On verbal obligations; Decius in counsel 60, no. 4; Pinellus on this Law 2, part 1, chapter 4, nos. 14 and 15; Petr. Rebuffus, On the rescission of contracts, article sole, gloss 15, no. 18; Wesenbeck in the paratitla On transactions, no. 8; Scotanus, D. 17, thesis 25; Struve and others. Nor is only the Latin word, but also the German word <term>Keiser</term> <gloss>Emperor</gloss>—which, with a slightly changed pronunciation, is derived from it—used to designate that Majesty in our Empire. I am not unaware that there are indeed other Monarchs in the orb of the world whom Europeans, and among them the Germans, distinguish by the same name. Thus it is established that the Monarch of the Turkish Empire, the Monarch of China, Japan, Monomotapa, and so forth, are commonly called Caesars, *Keiser*. Indeed, I would think that the scarcity of words was the cause for that name being assumed. For these Monarchs, since they have—either in reality or by their own claim—power greater than a king, and because no other peculiar name abounds among the Germans by which Majesty superior to a king can be signified, it had to be expressed by the title of *Caesar* in some way. From which matter, however, it seems nothing can be taken away from the dignity of the title. I would distinguish, as the schools speak, between the univocal and analogous concept of a word, or perhaps more clearly, between the grammatical and courtly style, and I would say that, grammatically or analogically, the name of *Caesar* is sometimes attributed to recent monarchs because of a certain similarity they have with our Caesar, in that, just as he does, they arrogate the Empire to themselves (by what right, I do not dispute); but univocally, and, if I may say so, courtly, or in its genuine and native signification, it is asserted only for our Emperor, and is estimated with the same honor as the <term>Catholic Majesty</term> <gloss>of the Spaniards</gloss>, <term>Most Christian Majesty</term> <gloss>of the French</gloss>, the <term>Sultan</term> <gloss>of the Turks</gloss> (or rather <term>Chakan</term> <gloss>Great Khan</gloss>), the <term>Chan</term> <gloss>of the Tartars</gloss>, the <term>Sophi</term> <gloss>of the Persians</gloss>, the <term>Mogor</term> <gloss>of the Indians</gloss>, and so forth, and other names of that sort, which are proper to the monarchs of those nations, or at least are accustomed to be held as such. The title of Emperor is indeed common to the Turkish Sultan with our Caesar, by a pact entered into between Rudolph II and Achmet in the year 1606, by which it was cautioned on both sides that upon the arrival of the legates of either party, they should use only the appellations of *Father* and *Son*, in such a way that the Sultan would hold our Caesar in the place of *Father*, and the Caesar the Sultan in the place of *Son*; but in letters, the title of Emperor, not King, should be attributed to both (Becman, *Civil and Geographic History*, p. 431). The same surname is also attributed to other monarchs by historiographers (Becman, *Not. Dign. Ill.*, Diss. 1, Ch. 2, § 3 sqq., p. 16). But the title of *Caesar* in public, solemn, and courtly formulas admits no other into a share of glory, but is proper today to our Invincible Emperor, and may it be perpetual to the Most August House of Austria. There remains, finally, that which we asked last: Is the title of the Grand Duke of the Muscovites, by which he is called <term>Czar</term>, or <term>Zaar</term>, or as others write <term>Tzar</term> (for thus the stronger part of the title is reported to hold itself: "The Great Lord Zaar and Grand Duke, All-Russia’s Self-Holder, of Vladimir, Moscow, Neugard Zaar, Zaar of Kazan and Astrakhan, Zaar of Siberia," etc.; *Func. Orb. Hodie-Imper.*, Vol. 1, p. 172, and you may read in our newspapers from time to time "the Czarish Majesty"), the same thing as *Caesar*, and does it derive its origin from there? Georg Hornius defends the affirmative opinion. “From the year 1500,” he says, “Basil first called himself *Czar*, i.e., *Caesar*, when until then they were called *VVelikiknesa*, Grand Dukes. For the Russians had understood that the Supreme Prince of the Christians was called *Caesar*, wherefore, so that they themselves would not be inferior, they themselves [took] the name.”

Esse quidem et alios in terrarum orbe Monarchas, quos Europæi, inque illis Germani eôdem nomine insigniant, non ignoro. Sic Monarcham Imperii Turcici, Monarcham Sinæ, Japoniæ, Monomotapæ, et cetera. Cæsares, *Keiser* / vulgò appellari constat. Enimverò existimarem, id nominis ut assumeretur, penuriam vocum exstitisse causam. Hi quippe Monarchæ cùm potestate Regiâ majorem sive revera habeant, seu sibi vindicent; nec apud Germanos peculiare nomen aliud suppetat, quô significari Regiâ superior Majestas possit, *Cæsaris* titulo exprimenda utcunque fuit. Quâ tamen ex re dignitati tituli nihil decedere posse videtur. Distinguerem, uti scholæ loquuntur, inter conceptum vocis univocum et analogum, aut fortè clarius, inter stylum Grammaticum et Curialem, diceremque, Grammaticè aut analogicè tribui *Cæsaris* nomen modò recentis Monarchis ob quandam similitudinem, quam habent cum Cæsare nostro, eô, quod non secus ac ille Imperium (quô jure, non disputo) sibi arrogant; Univocè verô et, ita dicam, Curialiter, aut in significatione sua genuina ac nativa soli Imperatori Nostro asseri, eâdemque æstimari dignatione, quâ *Hispanorum Catholica Majestas, Gallorum Christianissima Majestas, Turcarum Sultan, vel potius Chakan, Tartarorum Chan, Persarum Sophi, Indorum Mogor*, et cetera. et id genus nomina alia, quæ singula gentium illarum Monarchis sunt propria, aut certè pro talibus haberi solita. Imperatoris quidem titulum Sultanus Turcicus cum Cæsare Nostro habet communem, initô inter Rudolphum II. et Achmetem A. 1606. pactô, quô utrinque cautum, ut sub adventum utriusque partis Legatorum non nisi *Patris* et *Filii* appellationibus utantur, ita, ut Sultanus Cæsarem nostrum in *Patris*, Cæsar verò Sultanum in *Filii* loco habeat; in literis autem utrique Imperatoris, non Regis titulus tribuatur. Becman. Hist. Civil et Geogr. p. 431. Tribuitur et Monarchis aliis idem agnomen ab Historiographis. Becman. Not. Dign. Ill. Diss. 1. c. 2. §. 3. sqq. p. 16. At *Cæsaris* titulus in Formulis publicis, solemnibus et Curialibus nullum alium in partem gloriæ admittit, sed Invictissimo nostro Imperatori hodieque proprius est, atque utinam Augustissimæ Domui Austriacæ perpetuus.
